summary: Fixes for macOS 27.2, where v0.4.0 fails to compile native attention and returns wrong results from pivoted LU, plus a round of signal-processing, linear-algebra and special-function additions. 63 commits since v0.4.0. macOS 27.2 If you are on macOS 27.2, upgrade: v0.4.0 is affected by both of these. Native bridge programs compile again. The framework now rejects a bridge bundle with two or more weight files ( verifyBundleAtPath: invalid model ), which broke af.sdpa , causal decoder blocks and fused ONNX attention. Such a bundle is retried with its weights merged into one file (#309). A slice offset on the last axis no longer loses its offset. Two such slices at different offsets feeding matmuls in one fused program returned the wrong column or failed to compile on an M5 Pro, which made linalg.lu_pivoted , det , slogdet , solve and inv return wrong or non-finite results. The compiler now lowers a last-axis-offset slice_by_size (and so crop and static gather) off the last axis; ANEFORGE_ROUTE_WIDTH_SLICES=0 restores the old lowering (#311, #314). bench/slice_offset_probe.py shows whether a machine has the underlying behaviour (#313). Verified on an M5 Pro under macOS 27.2.1: the full on-device suite and the corpus are green. Other chips on 27.2 have not been checked. See the new "macOS 27.2" section of the FAQ. Signal processing dsp.hilbert (analytic signal, #265), dsp.detrend (#278), and the sawtooth , square and chirp generators (#264). Windows: flattop , blackmanharris , nuttall , cosine , gaussian (#268). fft.irfft (#261). Linear algebra and special functions linalg.kron (#262), linalg.polar (#259), linalg.matrix_rank and linalg.cond (#260). special.digamma and special.beta (#250), special.bessel_j1 and special.bessel_i1 (#251). Models and LLMs MPNet encoders (all-mpnet-base-v2) in the sentence-transformers drop-in (#255); RoBERTa-family encoders apply the pad_id + 1 position offset (#257). load_resnet accepts a Hugging Face repo id (#256). Qwen2/2.5 attention biases are loaded; the dense adapter dropped them (#253). Deep small-dimension models no longer hit the ANE op ceiling in decode (#254). MoE top-k selects exactly k experts on exact fp16 ties (#298). ONNX MeanVarianceNormalization , Hardmax and the hyperbolic ops (#263). onnx.coverage_report lists a model's unsupported ops before you try to compile it (#269). Compiler The compile cache is reused instead of forcing recompilation (#284). A compress= request that falls back to a wider encoding now warns (#249). Benchmarks Rooflines for M1 (MacBook Air), M2 Max, M4 Pro, M4 Max and M6, and a re-run of the M1 MacBook Pro. ANE power from the SMC rail where powermetrics reports none (#294), with follow-up fixes for chips whose rail or IOReport layout differs (#305, #307, #308). A run whose idle baseline was not idle is flagged, and its perf/W is withheld from the table (#306). Result files are strict JSON: no bare NaN (#307, #312). Examples Conway's Game of Life (#272), the Mandelbrot set (#273) and the Lorenz attractor (#274), each stepped on the ANE. The whisper.cpp backend exports a usable encoder bundle (#275, #276). Install: pip install -U aneforge (pretrained loaders: pip install "aneforge[models]" ).
title: ANEForge: Python for direct computation on the Apple Neural Engine

summary: This replication package accompanies the manuscript “Reliability, Faithfulness, and Stability of Self-Directed Context Selection in Open-Weight Large Language Models.” It contains source code, experiment configurations, the frozen confirmatory item manifest, processed experimental outputs, statistical-analysis scripts, generated figures, and detailed reproduction instructions. The study evaluates self-directed evidence selection using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Phi-3.5-mini-instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 across HotpotQA, QASPER, and ERASER MultiRC. The confirmatory selection experiment comprises 7,650 model outputs. Raw copies of the public datasets are not redistributed.
title: Replication Package for "Reliability, Faithfulness, and Stability of Self-Directed Context Selection in Open-Weight Large Language Models"

summary: This dataset record contains seven curated microscopy image segmentation datasets with image files, corresponding mask annotation files, and predefined train, validation, and test splits. The datasets are derived from public or previously published sources cited in the associated manuscript: Grain (Warren et al., 2024), EMPS (Yildirim and Cole, 2021), Aachen-Heerlen (Iren et al., 2021), UHCS (DeCost et al., 2017), MetalDAM (Luengo et al., 2022), and Super/EBC (Stuckner et al., 2022). The files were reorganized for a unified benchmark, split into train, validation, and test subsets, and subjected to annotation review, supplementary annotation, and quality control. The depositor has confirmed that the curated files can be redistributed for research use. The deposit includes 3,625 image files, 3,625 mask label files, and 163,901 mask instances counted as 8-connected non-zero connected components within the label images. The datasets included are Aachen-Heerlen, EBC, EMPS, Grain, MetalDAM, Super, and UHCS. File-level checksums, dataset statistics, class-wise mask-instance counts, source mapping, and documentation are provided to support reuse and reproducibility.
title: Microscopy image segmentation datasets with mask annotations

summary: the zipped file is a self-contained replication package for the paper "The Cost of Restricting Access to Natural Areas: African Swine Fever Containment Zones and Local Income". The execution requires locally installed recent versions of both Stata and R and the download of a package of external data from official websites of the Government of Italy. All steps are documented in the readme file and discussed in the paper. ABSTRACT The spread of African Swine Fever in the European Union since 2014 has triggered a policy response that, in several cases, included severe restrictions on access to forests and other natural areas. In most cases, pig farming and, to a lesser degree, the agricultural sector were compensated for the costs incurred as a consequence of the disease and its containment measures. The indirect costs borne by outdoor-based local economies, on the contrary, have been typically excluded from compensation schemes and, for the most part, remain unmeasured. This paper estimates these costs in the context of the African Swine Fever outbreak that affected North-West Italy from 2022 onward. Using municipal-level taxable income data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate the effect of access restrictions on local income. We find a decline of self-employment income per taxpayer of about 18–23 percent relative to control municipalities. The effect is weaker and below statistical significance for small business income and absent for wage income and pension income. The result is also unaffected by pre-outbreak pig-farming intensity in the municipality, indicating that the impact of direct costs is negligible. These findings suggest that the portion of containment policies that restricted access to natural areas shifted a significant part of the economic burden of disease control on sectors unrelated to pig farming and on municipalities where pig farming has a very limited presence. They also raise a compensation-design issue: containment policies generate broad public benefits, but also appropriable benefits for pig producers outside the outbreak zone. In those circumstances, when indirect costs remain uncompensated and sector-specific benefits from containment measures are not internalized by the beneficiaries we should expect distorted incentives and sub-optimal policy responses. The paper discusses policy options to improve both the efficiency and fairness of compensation for disease-containment measures that restrict access to natural areas.
title: Full, self-contained replication package for "The Cost of Restricting Access to Natural Areas: African Swine Fever Containment Zones and Local Income"

summary: An open educational engineering module on hypersonic waverider aerodynamic design, cone-derived shock capture, and lift-to-drag maximization. Covers inverse design from conical shock flowfields, shock-riding leading edges, and zero-spillage lower-surface pressure capture; the osculating cones method for non-axisymmetric planforms and scramjet inlet integration; hypersonic drag polars, lift-to-drag (L/D) maximization, the Küchemann barrier, and leading-edge bluntness versus aerothermal heating trade-offs; worked numerical calculations for caret-waverider pressure lift, wave drag, and polar L/D; an interactive waverider L/D and shock-capture explorer; and conventional delta wing versus waverider comparisons. Aligned with Washington Accord graduate attributes (WA1–WA3) and published on Prep4Uni.Online.
title: Waverider Aerodynamic Design Explained: Cone-Derived Leading Edges & L/D Maximization

summary: This dataset contains the complete experimental sequencing data generated for the study "Thermodynamically Constrained Encoding Improves Reliability in DNA Data Storage" . The study investigates the impact of thermodynamic constraints, based on Gibbs free energy (ΔG), on the reliability and efficiency of DNA-based digital data storage. Two encoding strategies are compared: the reference JPEG DNA encoding and a thermodynamically constrained version designed to improve the representation and recovery of encoded information during DNA sequencing. summary: STARLI | F051–F060 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Quantum Sensing, Reference Integrity and Trustworthy Biosensor Qualification Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection joins two five-theme research units from the STARLI 300-theme atlas. Research Unit II (F056–F060) develops common-mode failure identification, biological ground-truth validation, low-photodamage operation, trustworthy metrology and full-lifecycle qualification. The common challenge is whether a measured improvement survives independent references, hidden nuisance variables and resource-matched classical controls. The ten English working editions contain 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 one-page investigations, 2,000 separate Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Version 1.3 revises the six notes beneath each Gate question: causal mechanism, independent witness, blinded falsifier, competing explanation, stop rule and successor interface. These numbers describe editorial architecture and proposed research designs, not experimentally established originality or quantum advantage. The Ten Research Directions F051  Microscale Quantum Sensor Long-Term Stability At The Limit — Studies whether sensitivity remains stable across prolonged acquisition, replacement references and biological-matrix changes. Compares a quantum channel with identical-optics quantum-off ablation; tracks detection limit, calibration drift and interval coverage. Hidden reference drift or undercoverage of blinded truth defeats the proposed advantage. F052  Quantum Magnetic-Field Sensing And Microrobotic Motion Decoupling At The Limit — Separates quantum magnetic-field readout from motion-induced field changes in microrobotic experiments. Tracks Allan deviation, field sensitivity and photon budget against a strong classical sensor. Equal-photon comparisons test whether an apparent gain comes from photon count rather than quantum coherence. F053  Quantum Optical Microfluidic Interface Loss At The Limit — Examines losses and nuisance coupling at an optical quantum-sensing interface within microfluidic systems. Uses recorded photon budgets, contrast, drift and a locked reference instrument to test end-to-end readout integrity. Post-selection and loss of reference identity are explicit rival or stopping conditions. F054  Quantum Biosensor Autonomous Fault Diagnosis At The Limit — Designs autonomous detection of biosensor failure states without equating a model alert with an independently verified fault. Hidden reference-drift challenges, quantum-off ablations and withheld measurements interrogate field sensitivity, contrast and coherence-time estimates. Uncalibrated uncertainty intervals must trigger abstention. F055  Multisite Quantum Sensing Network Calibration At The Limit — Proposes traceable calibration transfer between quantum sensing sites, including independent references and shared-drift injection. Compares sensitivity, Allan deviation and cross-site reproducibility with classical optical or magnetic sensors. A site-consistent improvement is insufficient if extra photons explain the difference. F056  Quantum Sensor Common-Mode Failure Identification At The Limit — Investigates common-mode faults that can make multiple quantum sensors agree while all are wrong. A locked reference instrument, masked reference substitution and covariance-aware uncertainty audits separate shared errors from true agreement. Missing reference identity or selective retention of good readings invalidates release. F057  Biological Sample Quantum Readout Truth

summary: Observable forms are frequently used to identify, classify, and evaluate systems. However, an observable form does not necessarily provide a complete account of the internal processes that produce or govern the system. In some situations, the external representation becomes the dominant basis for interpretation, replacing a more direct examination of the system's internal structure, functional relationships, and causal processes. The Surface-Process Inference Paradox (SPIP) is proposed as a general theoretical framework for examining this problem across different classes of observable systems. Its central question is whether what is externally observed adequately represents the system's actual internal processes, or whether the observer becomes restricted by the external form and consequently fails to understand what is occurring within the system. The framework distinguishes two principal pathways. The first is structural observational ambiguity, in which different internal processes can produce indistinguishable observable forms. The second is observer-mediated surface capture, in which the observer gives excessive interpretive importance to an external category or representation despite the availability of relevant process evidence. A primary case study, the Genre-Bound Musical Evaluation Case (GBMEC), is used to preserve the original observation concerning music genre and internal musical structure. The framework is then generalized to human behaviour, visual art, literature, social practices, institutions, software, artificial intelligence, biological systems, and physical systems. Mathematical formalization is developed through state-space models, observation functions, observer representations, process-inference errors, mutual information, observability, and controlled category interventions. Eight theoretical propositions, boundary conditions, hypotheses, and falsification criteria are established. SPIP is presented as a testable and potentially cross-disciplinary framework, not as a completed universal law. Its scientific contribution will depend on whether its mechanisms can be operationalized, distinguished from existing explanations, and independently reproduced across relevant domains.

title: THE SURFACE-PROCESS INFERENCE PARADOX

summary: Processing code, derived maps and result tables for a study of urban expansion, summer land surface temperature (LST) and residents' potential surface-heat exposure in Baghdad, Basra and Erbil, Iraq, from 2000 to 2025. Contents: (1) the complete code, comprising a Python/Google Earth Engine pipeline with its full configuration, local robustness checks, a built-up agreement analysis and the scripts that draw every figure of the article; (2) a harmonised 30 m four-class land-cover series (GLC_FCS30D, 2000–2020) and annual built-up masks; (3) Landsat summer LST and NDVI epoch composites (2000–2025), also expressed as anomalies relative to a rural ring; (4) MODIS Terra/Aqua night-time LST composites (2005–2025); (5) hot-pixel frequency and Getis–Ord Gi* hotspot maps; (6) GHS-POP and WorldPop population grids clipped to each study area and scaled to the 2024 Iraq census; (7) analysis zones (core, new growth, rural ring) as GeoJSON; and (8) all result tables, including SUHI by zone, trends, matched conversion contrasts, exposure metrics, and the rural-reference, threshold, multiple-testing and placebo robustness checks. All files are derived from open datasets (Landsat, MODIS, GLC_FCS30D, GHSL, WSF Evolution, WorldPop, JRC Global Surface Water, SRTM, ERA5-Land). See 00_README.md for file contents, raster codes, limitations, run order and source citations.

summary: THE DEVICE MUST EARN ITS RELEASE An Integrated Technical Guide to Trustworthy Autonomous Neural Nanomanufacturing STARLI / YULI | Research Family 16 | Flagships F151–F160 of 200 | Author: 33 / STARLI–YULI | Research Design and Technical Integration Edition | 7 November 2026 The central question of autonomous neural nanomanufacturing is not whether an intelligent manufacturing line can produce a visually convincing neural electrode. It is whether the line can demonstrate, by evidence accessible to an independent examiner, that the fabricated object meets its declared physical and functional criteria, that its apparent efficiency was not created by quietly excluding unsuccessful attempts, that its defect assessment is not dependent on a shared mistake, and that the machine would refuse an unsafe or unqualified decision even when the optimization algorithm prefers to continue. Neural nanomanufacturing brings a remarkable variety of engineering disciplines into contact. Lithography controls geometry; material preparation establishes the initial chemical state; microscopy and electrochemical measurements create partial views of a device; statistical models infer hidden quality; control systems change recipes; safety interlocks restrict what the equipment may do; and qualified people determine whether the resulting evidence is sufficient for release. Each discipline can work well in isolation while the complete manufacturing claim remains false. This guide proposes a way to make the interfaces between them scientifically accountable. The basis for this essay is a set of ten prospective STARLI / YULI research introductions, F151 through F160. Their research questions concern autonomous recipe selection, closed-loop nanoelectrode fabrication, intelligent nanomaterial quality control, adaptive microstructure formation, AI-based defect detection, process digital twins, cross-batch electrochemical stability, energy efficiency, autonomous stopping, and trustworthy release authority. Those ten investigations are treated here as interacting duties within one nonclinical experimental program, not as ten completed demonstrations and not as proof that an integrated factory already exists. Their common physical perimeter is a controlled neural nanoelectrode manufacturing bench, with coded material lots, instrument-calibration records, machine event logs, independent inspection, and hardware-level ability to stop. Their common scientific demand is falsifiability. A device receives no special status because its manufacturer calls the controller intelligent, autonomous, quantum, or advanced. Its status comes from comparisons with an appropriate conventional line, independent measurement and a complete record of the attempts that failed. A newcomer can enter the topic through a simple thought experiment. Imagine two production benches that receive nominally similar precursor materials and seek to produce a defined pattern of neural electrodes. The first follows a fixed qualified recipe and relies on manual inspection. The second can alter processing settings when a sensor reports a deviation. After a week, the adaptive line displays more attractive device images and announces lower production energy. Have we learned that it is better? Not until we know the denominator of attempted devices, the calibration condition of the metrology, the origin of its defect labels, whether defective parts were discarded before counting, whether the energy calculation included idling and rework, and whether a safety stop would still work if the optimizing software failed. The appropriate research object is therefore not a single successful coupon. It is the documented manufacturing episode, from material receipt to independent release or justified refusal. This episode becomes the basic unit that connects the ten flagships. 1. From a collection of manufacturing improvements to a single evidence contract The ten source themes are easier to understand when
title: STARLI / YULI / FAMILY 16 / F151 - F160 AUTONOMOUS NEURAL NANOMANUFACTURING - TEN RESEARCH DESIGNS F151 / Ai Autonomous Neural Nanomanufacturing At The Limit Primary endpoint: first-pass automated manufacturing yield [%]. Concealed challenge: concealed precursor material-lot replacement. Rival: selection of only the best finished coupons. Physical limitation: count all aborted runs and do not permit autonomous release. F152 / Closed-Loop Neural Nanoelectrode Fabrication At The Limit Primary endpoint: nanoelectrode patterned line-width error [um]. Concealed challenge: blinded exposure focal-plane displacement. Rival: machine-stage thermal drift. Physical limitation: reject any uncalibrated metrology feedback. F153 / Intelligent Quality Control Of Neural Nanomaterials At The Limit Primary endpoint: nanomaterial inspection false-negative rate [%]. Concealed challenge: blind seeding of trace-defect specimens. Rival: biased manual defect annotation. Physical limitation: stop if even one predefined safety-critical defect is not declared. F154 / Adaptive Neural Microstructure Manufacturing At The Limit Primary endpoint: adaptive microfeature height-following RMSE [nm]. Concealed challenge: concealed design-mask topology change. Rival: unreported manual post-processing. Physical limitation: stop if topography extrapolates beyond the height standard. F155 / Ai Defect Detection In Neural Interfaces At The Limit Primary endpoint: neural-interface defect-detection recall [%]. Concealed challenge: concealed introduction of unseen defect morphologies. Rival: learning illumination features instead of defects. Physical limitation: reject release when hidden critical defects are missed. Research method parent: supplied 780-page F02 research monograph. Structural and visual anchor: Family 10 F091-F100 v1.1. Science targets derive from the F101-F200 flagship atlas; all proposals are untested. STARLI / YULI / FAMILY 16 / F151 - F160 AUTONOMOUS NEURAL NANOMANUFACTURING - TEN RESEARCH DESIGNS F156 / Process Digital Twins For Neural Nanodevices At The Limit Primary endpoint: process digital-twin signed width residual [um]. Concealed challenge: blinded swap to a second manufacturing machine. Rival: leakage of reference measurements into the fitted twin. Physical limitation: recalibrate or abstain on unseen machine geometry. F157 / Cross-Batch Stability In Neural Nanomanufacturing At The Limit Primary endpoint: cross-lot electrode-impedance coefficient of variation [%]. Concealed challenge: concealed material supplier substitution. Rival: differences between impedance measurement fixtures. Physical limitation: reject cross-batch claims without independent EIS. F158 / Energy Efficiency Of Neural Nanomanufacturing At The Limit Primary endpoint: energy per independently qualified manufactured device [J/device]. Concealed challenge: blinded inclusion of idle and rework energy. Rival: lower reported energy through greater reject rates. Physical limitation: halt energy claims if defects or rejects rise. F159 / Autonomous Stop Conditions In Neural Nanomanufacturing At The Limit Primary endpoint: autonomous hardware hard-stop missed-event rate [%]. Concealed challenge: concealed injection of out-of-envelope process commands. Rival: counting delayed alarms as normal operation. Physical limitation: stop the bench immediately upon an interlock miss. F160 / Trustworthy Autonomous Neural Nanomanufacturing Platforms At The Limit Primary endpoint: independent quality-release assessor agreement [%]. Concealed challenge: blinded replacement of quality inspectors. Rival: false consensus from shared evaluator software. Physical limitation: no release without independently reconstructable adjudication. Release status: complete prospective research manuscripts with independent expert review pending on mathematical assumptions, semantic repetition and reproducibility. No clinical efficacy is asserted. Join the STARLI Research Community: https://zenodo.org/communities/starli-research-gate/ We do not need to know which door future generations will choose to open. We only hope that when they open it, they will find a little light to guide their way. 🌈🚪✨

summary: Flight safety and the reliability of aircraft operations under the extremely low temperatures of the Arctic Zone depend directly on the stability of the low-temperature properties of aviation fuels. The critical parameter determining the cold-flow properties and uninterrupted pumpability of fuel is the freezing point (the onset of crystallization, TNK); exceeding it leads to the precipitation of a solid phase and the risk of fuel filter blockage. This article presents a comparative analysis of the freezing point of TS-1 aviation kerosene produced by four leading Russian oil refineries (coded as A, B, V, and G). The tests were conducted in a certified laboratory using the GOST 5066 method with the "KRISTALL-20" automatic analyzer. Significant differences in coldflow properties depending on the manufacturer were revealed. Samples from manufacturers A, B, and V demonstrated high phase stability (freezing points from −62.3 °C to −66.8 °C), ensuring a reliable safety margin relative to GOST 10227 requirements (not higher than −60 °C) for polar aviation. The product from manufacturer G showed a freezing point of −58.7 °C, which meets the baseline standard but imposes operational limitations according to GOST 16350. Additionally, an analysis was conducted on the impact of seasonal temperature fluctuations in Arctic regions on the permissible storage duration of fuel at airfields without loss of low-temperature characteristics. Typical operational scenarios in remote airports, where the possibility of prompt replacement of a fuel batch is absent, were considered: under such conditions, even a slight deviation of the freezing point from optimal values can lead to a critical reduction in fuel system throughput. It was concluded that the manufacturer factor must be taken into account during the incoming quality control of aviation fuels for Arctic regions. It is recommended to include in acceptance procedures not only verification of compliance with baseline standards but also an assessment of the freezing point margin, taking into account forecast minimum temperatures in the area of operation. This approach will minimize the risk of fuel system failures and enhance the overall reliability of aviation equipment under extreme climatic conditions.
title: Comparative Analysis of the Onset Crystallization Temperature of TS-1 Aviation Fuel from Different Manufacturers.

summary: This paper examines the emerging possibility of organised data marauders and data warriors for hire as a structural feature of the liquid order. Drawing on the analysis of trans-sovereign force, algorithmic neo-contractors, cyber-mercenaries and private sector offensive actors, it traces historical precedents of private violence and information operations through to contemporary zero-day markets, commercial spyware, narrative laundering and LLM data poisoning. These actors operate across strategic, infrastructural, algorithmic and cognitive domains, exploiting the inverse law of sovereign accountability. The paper connects this development to the rise of independent security constructors who offer Dual-Core compatible, contestable services rather than pure extraction. Within the Flow Sovereignty and Reserve of Humanity framework, such constructors can be integrated as peripheral agents whose morphisms remain auditable, while unconstrained data marauders constitute a cohomology threat. The analysis closes with architectural propositions for containing the former and constraining the latter under Permanent Systemic Instability. KSCCN article (3 pages).
title: Data Marauders and Organised Data Warriors for Hire in the Liquid Order: From Historical Private Force to Algorithmic Neo-Contractors and the Rise of Contestable Security Constructors

summary: This paper addresses the fundamental question of the precise extent to which spectral bounds for fractional Schrödinger operators transfer to their magnetic counterparts, and delivers five major results that together form a complete map of what survives, what fails, and what must be proved to close the remaining gaps. The central objects are the magnetic Laplacian H_A = (−i∇ + A)² defined as a Friedrichs form extension from the quadratic form q_A[u] = ∫ |(−i∇ + A)u|² dx for A ∈ L²_loc(ℝᵈ; ℝᵈ), its fractional powers H_{s,A} = (H_A)^s defined via the spectral theorem, and the Aharonov–Bohm potential A_α = (α/ρ)ê_θ with flux parameter α in the cylindrical coordinates of ℝᵈ = ℝ² × ℝ^{d−2}. The negative eigenvalue counting function is denoted N(K) = Tr 1_{(−∞,0)}(K), the Riesz means are Tr(K)^−_γ = Σ |λ_j|^γ for γ > 0 with the convention Tr(K)^−_0 = N(K), and the abbreviated notation T^γ_α = Tr(H_{s,α} + V)^−_γ and N_α = T^0_α is used throughout. The semiclassical constants are L^{cl}_{0,d} = (2π)^{−d}|B_d| and L^{cl}_{γ,d,s} = (2π)^{−d} ∫(1 − |ξ|^{2s})^γ_+ dξ, where |B_d| is the volume of the unit ball in ℝᵈ. The first and most striking result is a definitive negative one: the diamagnetic inequality, which states that |e^{−tH_A}(x,y)| ≤ e^{tΔ}(x,y) for almost every x, y and all t > 0, implies no comparison whatsoever of eigenvalue counting functions or of Riesz means between magnetic and non-magnetic operators. The physical intuition that a magnetic field, which raises the ground-state energy, should also decrease the number of bound states and the sums of powers of negative eigenvalues, is shown to be false by explicit counterexamples. The mechanism of failure is a flux-induced change of degeneracy: at half a flux quantum, the lowest angular channel of an axially symmetric system becomes doubly degenerate, so that two shallow magnetic bound states may replace a single deeper non-magnetic one. The ground-state energy still increases in accordance with the diamagnetic inequality, but the count and even the sum of binding energies may increase. The primary counterexample is constructed in three dimensions with s = 1, R = 1, and V = −8·1_{|x|<1}, a spherical square well of bounded, compactly supported potential belonging to L^∞_c(ℝ³) ⊂ L^{3/2}(ℝ³), the natural CLR class. The channel with angular parameter l ≥ 0 possesses a negative eigenvalue if and only if √λ R exceeds the first positive zero of the spherical Bessel function j_{l−1}, and the number of negative eigenvalues in that channel equals the number of positive zeros of j_{l−1} below √λ R. This follows from matching logarithmic derivatives at r = R between the interior solution u = r j_l(kr) with k = (λ − κ²)^{1/2} and the exterior decaying solution u = r^{1/2} K_{l+1/2}(κr), and taking the limit κ ↓ 0 where the exterior solution behaves like r^{−l}, reducing the threshold condition to j_{l−1}(√λ R) = 0. The relevant thresholds in the variable λR² are: for l = 0, the first threshold is π²/4 ≈ 2.467401 governed by j_{−1}(x) = cos x/x; for l = 1/2, the first threshold is j²_{0,1} ≈ 5.783186 governed by j_{−1/2} ∝ J₀; for l = 1, the first threshold is π² ≈ 9.869604 governed by j₀(x) = sin x/x; for l = 3/2, the first threshold is j²_{1,1} ≈ 14.681971 governed by j_{1/2} ∝ J₁. At α = 0 the channels are l ∈ ℕ₀ with multiplicity 2l + 1, and since 2.467401 < 8 < 9.869604, only l = 0 is active, carrying exactly one eigenvalue since 8 < 22.206610, giving N(H₀ + V) = 1. At &al
title: Aharonov–Bohm Flux and Magnetic Eigenvalue Bounds: Failure of the Diamagnetic Comparison, a Sharp Factor-Two Substitute, and Magnetic Lifting of Lieb–Thirring Constants

summary: This dataset contains two types of files: Replication Package Benchmark Logs (.zip) Below, we explain each file. 1) Replication Package: This Excel file documents the framework selection process and presents the benchmark results and their analysis. It includes five sheets that describe the framework selection process, benchmark results, and analysis used in the study. Sheet 1: Search_String This sheet provides the search strings used to identify candidate frameworks from GitHub, along with the inclusion and exclusion criteria applied during the framework selection process. Sheet 2: Initial_Frameworks_Extraction This sheet contains the initially extracted 164 repos, followed by the refined set of 55 frameworks shortlisted from the original pool. Sheet 3: Final_Frameworks This sheet presents the final set of frameworks selected for the experimental evaluation. It also includes the selection criteria used to finalize these frameworks for further benchmarking. Sheet 4: Benchmark_Results (RQ1–RQ3) This sheet reports the benchmark results for each agentic framework across the three reasoning benchmarks: BBH, GSM8K, and ARC. It includes the accuracy of each framework, the time taken per task, the total execution time per framework, and token consumption at both the task and framework levels for each benchmark. Sheet 5: Analysis This sheet contains the analysis of the benchmark results and summarizes the comparative performance of the evaluated frameworks. 2) Benchmark Logs (.zip): This ZIP file contains the benchmark execution logs for all 22 evaluated agentic frameworks across two reasoning benchmarks: BBH and ARC. The file is organized into separate folders for each benchmark, containing the execution logs of all frameworks, including those that failed to complete the evaluation. These logs provide detailed task-level information, including accuracy, token consumption, and execution time. However, for four frameworks, token consumption was not recorded in the logs and was instead obtained from the OpenAI usage dashboard. Across both benchmarks, the dataset covers 9,881 tasks, and the total ZIP file size is 19.1 MB.
title: Agentic Frameworks for Reasoning Tasks: An Empirical Study

summary: Every LLM request SWAN AI-SQL (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWAN-AISQL) and the baselines issue on SemBench MOVIE/ECOMM/MMQA, the 30-query hybrid bench of the PLOP paper and the SWAN 2.0 benchmark (https://github.com/ZhaoFuheng/SWANBench), with the provider's answer, its measured latency and its cost, as a DuckDB file (gzip-compressed, 1.02 GB; 4.8 GB unpacked; 2,541,389 recorded calls) for the repository's cache proxy (serve/ai_cache_server.py). It holds SWAN AI-SQL, LOTUS 1.2.4, PLOP (the public Morrila fork, DP cost-model mode), BlendSQL 0.1.27, ThalamusDB 0.1.15 (exact mode) and Palimpzest 1.5.3 (Abacus optimizer) on every benchmark each of them runs. Each prompt is kept with its most recent recording; this version is the one behind the tables of both repositories as of 2026-11-21, every row a replay on one machine. Always use the latest version: the concept DOI and serve/fetch_cache.sh resolve to it. Every table in the repositories replays without a provider key: run serve/fetch_cache.sh (it downloads, checks and unpacks the latest version), then the benchmark harnesses; the proxy replays each recorded answer with its recorded latency and cost. Model: gpt-5.6-luna, temperature 0, each system's default prompts (zero-shot). Replay matches requests byte for byte; an edited query, another model, or a client library that renders the request differently is a fresh request. The systems' may have their own run-to-run variance (LOTUS's ranking order, result assembly in BlendSQL and Palimpzest, ThalamusDB's sampler, PLOP's parallel operator order).
title: SWAN AI-SQL replay cache: recorded gpt-5.6-luna answers of SWAN, LOTUS, BlendSQL, Palimpzest, ThalamusDB and PLOP on SemBench, the PLOP hybrid bench and SWAN 2.0

summary: Data and Stata code for the article "Institutional Trust, Social Networks and the Shadow Economy: A Joint Test Across Three Measures of Informality". The package contains a country-year panel of 167 countries for 2007–2020 (2,338 observations; the balanced estimation sample is 130 countries and 1,820 observations), the Stata do-file that reproduces the tables and Figure 1, and two transcribed series used for comparison: the EY (2025) currency-demand shadow economy estimates and the SSE Riga Shadow Economy Index for the Baltic states. Variables combine informal output estimates from the World Bank Informal Economy Database (Elgin, Kose, Ohnsorge and Yu 2021), social capital and rule-of-law elements from the Legatum Prosperity Index 2023, civil society indices from V-Dem v16, and controls from the World Development Indicators. All underlying data remain subject to the terms of their original providers, who should be cited. summary: Postoperative complications remain an important concern in the surgical treatment of cicatricial esophageal strictures. Identifying risk factors before surgery is clinically relevant for treatment planning and for correcting potentially modifiable factors. To identify factors associated with the development of postoperative complications in patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures. A retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures treated at three surgical institutions in the Kyrgyz Republic between 2015 and 2025. The overall study cohort comprised 194 patients; the analysis of postoperative complications included 154 patients who underwent surgical treatment: minimally invasive surgery (n=143) or open surgery (n=11). Postoperative complications were recorded according to the Esophagectomy Complications Consensus Group criteria and graded using the Clavien–Dindo classification. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with postoperative complications. Postoperative complications occurred in 55 of 154 surgically treated patients (35.7%). In univariate analysis, open surgery (OR=5.45; 95% CI 1.38–21.48; p=0.015) and the presence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (OR=2.19; 95% CI 1.02–4.68; p=0.043) were associated with postoperative complications, whereas higher serum albumin levels (OR=0.85; 95% CI 0.76–0.96; p=0.010) and a higher prognostic nutritional index (OR=0.88; 95% CI 0.80–0.96; p=0.005) were associated with lower odds of complications. In the multivariable model, ASA class III–IV (OR=3.14; 95% CI 1.44–6.85; p=0.004) and serum albumin level (OR=0.85 per 1 g/L increase; 95% CI 0.74–0.97; p=0.014) remained independent predictors. After adjustment for baseline characteristics, open surgery was not independently associated with postoperative complications (OR=3.36; 95% CI 0.74–15.15; p=0.115). The risk of postoperative complications in patients with cicatricial esophageal strictures was independently associated with higher ASA physical status and serum albumin level. These findings highlight the importance of preoperative assessment of the patient’s general condition and nutritional status when planning surgical treatment. The association between open surgery and complications observed in the unadjusted analysis was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for baseline characteristics; therefore, differences between surgical approaches should not be interpreted as an independent effect of the operative technique.
title: Risk Factors for Postoperative Complications in Patients with Cicatricial Esophageal Strictures: A Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: This preprint presents an existence and local uniqueness certificate for a family of collision-free periodic choreographies in the planar, equal-mass Newton–Yukawa three-body model. In dimensionless units, the pair potential is Vα(r) = −[1 + α exp(−r)]/r, with the gravitational constant, individual masses, and inverse screening length set to one. The certificate covers every coupling value in the closed interval α ∈ [0.00997, 0.01003] at the specified fixed initial separation. The construction starts from a symmetric collinear configuration and imposes three endpoint equations at one-sixth of the period. Reversing symmetries and cyclic relabeling extend a collision-free shooting solution into a periodic choreography in which all three bodies traverse the same closed path one-third of a period apart. The numerical argument combines outward-rounded enclosures of the flow and its first derivatives, collision exclusion over the fundamental arc, and a strict uniform Krawczyk inclusion. Subject to the correctness of the interval implementation and its rounding guarantees, these bounds imply exactly one shooting root in the stated box for each coupling. The manuscript documents the original MPFR Taylor–Picard calculation. A subsequent CAPD 6.0.0 implementation, using a different validated ODE solver, reports strict inclusion in all three shooting coordinates, a contraction bound below 0.495687, and pairwise separation above 0.688548 throughout the fundamental arc. The manuscript and source audit record the earlier stage of the work, when the CAPD run had yet to be executed. Independent technical review of the CAPD implementation and rounding remains open. The result concerns the specified orbit family and coupling interval. A certified connection to the Newtonian orbit at α = 0, geometric figure-eight topology, and orbital stability remain open for this family.
title: Collision-Free Three-Body Choreographies in Newton–Yukawa Gravity: A Uniform AI-Verified Certificate

summary: HYOWON v0.1.1 — Maintenance Release HYOWON v0.1.1 is a maintenance update to v0.1.0. It changes numerical support code, checkpoint reading, MPI error handling, source provenance capture and documentation. The release does not introduce a new physical model or gravity solver. Paper 0 provenance: The Paper 0 manuscript identifies HYOWON v0.1.0 as its simulation source. Version 0.1.1 was not used to generate those results and should not replace v0.1.0 in their software citation. Changes CIC geometry: Reuse validated mesh geometry and the upper coordinate bound within a deposition or interpolation operation. The per-particle wrapping, division, clamping and interpolation-weight calculations retain their existing order. Exact sums: Partition non-negative segment sums among host workers and combine exact integer accumulators before rounding the result to binary64. SHA-256: Process complete input blocks without copying them byte by byte into a staging buffer, and encode hexadecimal digests without a formatting stream. The hash algorithm and persisted identity encoding are unchanged. Checkpoint loading: Decode particle state, timestep and associated provenance into temporary state before publication. Distributed reads require agreement on the manifest digest and successful validation of each rank's checkpoint shard before publishing the loaded state. The manifest is hashed while reading the opened stream, and bound HDF5 descriptors are rewound before descriptor-backed opening and hashing. MPI failure handling: Synchronise errors in force-storage preparation and acceleration publication. Unrecoverable MPI startup or communication failures use an abort path rather than allowing a rank to unwind independently. Text and build provenance: Use the classic locale for machine-readable text and Linux memory observations. Refresh Git source information before executable builds. The reported commit and tree describe Git HEAD, not uncommitted contents or the resulting executable. Documentation and metadata: Update build and usage guidance and the version information in CITATION.cff . Numerical scope and verification The tagged changes leave the gravity and FFT solver implementations, initial-condition generators, cosmological drift/kick calculations and native snapshot/restart schema definitions unchanged. Changes to CIC support routines and force-preparation error paths do not guarantee identical results in every execution environment. The [ v0.1.1 changelog ](https://github.com/youngjinphys/HYOWON/blob/v0.1.1/CHANGELOG.md) records Linux Release builds with and without MPI, the existing smoke test, and matched-input 64-particle comparisons. These are bounded software checks, not evidence of cosmological convergence. Bitwise agreement across arbitrary FFTW plans, thread counts or MPI decompositions is not claimed. The HDF5 descriptor-offset correction was not exercised on macOS. summary: Source code and experimental result data accompanying the paper "A bi-objective optimization of multi-robot inspection planning and charging infrastructure design under energy constraints" (Avossevou, Guenounou, Nait Chabane, Beddiar; submitted to Transactions of the Institute of Measurement and Control). This repository implements a bi-objective optimization framework for multi-robot industrial inspection, jointly deciding robot routing and task allocation, partial recharge scheduling, and the placement and technology of charging stations. The problem is solved exactly via a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (weighted-sum and epsilon-constraint scalarization) and approximately via three tailored multi-objective metaheuristics: NSGA-II, a Multi-Objective Ant Colony Optimization approach (MOACO), and a Decomposition-Based Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithm (MOEA/D). See the included README.md for repository structure and reproduction instructions.
title: Code and data for: A bi-objective optimization of multi-robot inspection planning and charging infrastructure design under energy constraints

summary: Background: Introduction: basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant skin neoplasm. Its nasal location poses a challenge for surgical oncology and reconstructive plastic surgery, particularly in recurrent lesions with infiltrative histologic patterns and involvement of multiple anatomical subunits. Case report: We present a case report of a 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and systemic arterial hypertension, with a history of previously excised basal cell carcinoma of the right nasal ala. She subsequently developed recurrence with growth toward the contralateral ala. Preoperative biopsy revealed infiltrative basal cell carcinoma with an adamantinoid component. Wide oncologic excision was performed under general anesthesia, with a planned clinical margin of 1 cm. The excision included skin and subcutaneous tissue, with documented operative dimensions of 10 × 2 cm. Immediate reconstruction was performed using a frontonasal rotation flap designed through a t-shaped incision. Definitive histopathologic examination demonstrated tumor-free margins. No intraoperative complications were documented. Conclusion: the management of recurrent nasal basal cell carcinomas requires integration of oncologic and reconstructive principles. Negative histopathologic margins represent a favorable initial result. Long-term follow-up is essential to assess recurrence, nasal function, and reconstructive outcomes.   Keywords: basal cell carcinoma; nasal neoplasms; tumor recurrence; oncologic excision; frontonasal flap; reconstructive surgery.
title: Recurrent infiltrative basal cell carcinoma involving both nasal alae: wide oncologic excision and reconstruction using a frontonasal rotation flap. A case report

summary: Reproducibility package (v6, final submission with structural revalidation and updated Fig. 6C/Fig. 10) for the manuscript The single Rho GTPase of Trypanosoma cruzi signals to actin through a non-catalytic OCRL-family RhoGAP . Contents: 01_figuras.zip — all 23 submission figures exactly as embedded in the manuscript (10 main-text figures Fig1–Fig10, 12 supplementary figures FigS1–FigS12, and GraphicalAbstract.png); 02_dados_de_origem.zip — 78 standardised source tables and sequence files (including per-figure datasets, invariant-set microarray re-normalisation tables, ex vivo midgut adhesion totals, and GenBank QB139547 TcOCRL sequences); 03_proveniencia.zip — 61 per-result provenance records tracing each figure and table to its laboratory source file, plus the numbering crosswalk; 04_scripts.zip — 124 analysis and figure-generation scripts; 05_reconstrucao_3d.zip — autonomous 3D confocal reconstruction package for GFP-TcOCRL epimastigotes (raw confocal z-stacks of Series019, isotropic volumes for 16 cells, silhouettes, STL meshes, and localisation classification); 06_codigo_de_analise.zip — 259 files preserving the directory layout cited in Methods and Data Availability ( pipeline_reanalise/ , in_silico/ , tools/ , and raw_data/14_Tabela1_insilico_toolkit/ ). Linked public accessions: Polysomal microarray data are deposited in NCBI GEO under accession GSE354409 (platform GPL1061). The corrected full-length TcOCRL mRNA sequence from T. cruzi Dm28c (2,537 bp; 5′ UTR isoforms of 191 and 10 nt; 781 aa) is deposited in GenBank under accession QB139547 . The subcellular localisation prediction code is maintained at github.com/luizdione/Software_subcellular-localization-prediction . Numbering notice. The final manuscript carries 10 main-text figures, 12 supplementary figures and 10 supplementary tables. Relative to v1–v3, former Fig. 6 moved to Fig. S11, former Fig. 7 D–E moved to Fig. S12, former Fig. 7–11 were renumbered Fig. 6–10, and Fig. 5 / Fig. S6 reflect the invariant-set microarray re-normalisation. Always resolve by subject using MAPA_NUMERACAO_v13.md , placed outside the ZIPs for direct reading. Interpretation caveats are detailed in README.md , including that co-folding confidence scores do not discriminate binding (a paired GFP negative control outscores the canonical positive control), that score comparisons require the same bait, and that human RhoA numbering does not transfer directly to TcRho1. The manuscript itself is not deposited here: this record contains data, figures, provenance records and analysis code only.

summary: Most installed machines watch themselves only with fixed limit alarms. We propose agentising: an AI check layer, learned from healthy operation, added beside those alarms, plus an agent that would turn warnings into actions for a person to approve. Only the detection layer is tested here. We tested it on five public machine datasets that map onto Germany’s largest manufacturing sectors: CNC milling (AI4I 2020), a hydraulic rig (ZeMA), the Tennessee Eastman chemical plant, NASA C-MAPSS turbofans and the SKAB pump test bed. Thresholds were set for 1% false alarms on healthy calibration data; measured test false-alarm rates were 0.85–4.0% on the milling, hydraulic and chemical-plant data and up to 31% on the pump test bed. Adding the AI check to a simulated per-sensor limit baseline at least doubled caught milling failures (14% to 30% with a random split, 8% to 20% with a row-order-preserving split), raised mean detection over 18 observable chemical-plant faults from 82% to 91% while halving detection delay, and warned on every held-out engine with median leads of 50 to 76 cycles depending on the split. Hydraulic valve and pump faults stayed invisible without pressure sensors. Fresh GitHub-hosted runs reproduced the five- machine benchmark outputs and the split-sensitivity outputs exactly. A separate camera-inspection demonstration was run in a browser app and is not part of that automated reproduction.
title: Agentising Existing Machines: An AI Check Layer for Current Machinery, Tested on Five Industrial Simulations and Test Rigs

summary: Data, code, result tables and figures for: El-Samra, R., El-Fadel, M. “A Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index for the Jordan River Basin: Observed Stress 1981–2020, SPEI Benchmark and CMIP6 Projections to 2050”, submitted to Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies (manuscript EJRH-D-26-04528, revised version R1). The Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index (CHSI) is the difference between standardized annual precipitation and temperature anomalies, rescaled to unit variance over 1981–2010. It is computed from NASA POWER data for 11 grid cells (0.5° × 0.625°) covering the Jordan River Basin, grouped into three hydro-climatic zones, for 1981–2020. The decade 2011–2020 is withheld from standardization and used for evaluation. CHSI is benchmarked against SPEI-12 with FAO-56 Penman–Monteith reference evapotranspiration. It is projected to 2050 with 30 NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, each standardized against its own 1981–2010 historical run. This version accompanies the revised manuscript. It adds the sensitivity of the projections to the standardization, the reference period, the threshold and the weight given to temperature; seasonal CHSI; CHSI for each grid cell and on a 0.1° grid (ERA5-Land temperature, CHIRPS precipitation); significance tests and effect sizes; and a comparison with soil moisture and runoff from MERRA-2 and ERA5-Land. It also contains the Word files of Supplementary Tables S1–S14. Only this version matches the revised manuscript. Contents: raw extracts (data_raw/), configuration of cells and weights (config/), Python scripts (scripts/), and derived series, tables and figures (outputs/). See README.md for the folder structure, how to reproduce each table and figure, and data sources and licences. ERA5-Land extracts contain modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information; neither the European Commission nor ECMWF is responsible for any use of this information.
title: Combined Hydro-Climatic Stress Index (CHSI) for the Jordan River Basin: data, scripts and results

summary: AquaTrajectories is an open-source R and Python research-software toolkit for aquatic animal 2D and 3D movement analysis, video-based fish-tracking interfaces, multiview reconstruction, camera geometry, behavioural methods, conditional uncertainty assessment and reproducible scientific visualization. Version 0.2.0 adds evidence safeguards for estimator sensitivity, mixed coordinate units, independent-unit interpretation, spatial support, measurement-geometry associations and descriptive falsification checks. Its synthetic numerical oracles and cross-platform qualification do not certify biological identity, real-video tracking generalization, physical underwater XYZ metrology, causal feeding responses, fish welfare outcomes or hardware safety.
title: AquaTrajectories: Aquatic Animal Movement and Multiview Trajectories

summary: This archive contains the occurrence datasets, environmental predictor sets, projected habitat-suitability rasters, derived tables and analysis code supporting the study "Climate-driven shifts in the potential distributions and spatial overlap of pear (Pyrus spp.) and the oriental fruit moth (Grapholita molesta) in China" (Geng et al.). Contents 01_occurrences/ - Spatially filtered occurrence records used for modelling: Pyrus_spp_occurrences.csv (n = 1063) and G_molesta_occurrences.csv (n = 108), with fields record_id, taxon, longitude, latitude, source (GBIF / iNaturalist / literature) and year. Derived from 2327 Pyrus and 139 G. molesta raw records by removing duplicates and applying 5 x 5 km spatial filtering in ENMTools. 02_environmental_variables/ - The 40 candidate variables (19 bioclimatic, 3 topographic, 18 soil) with their provenance, the sets retained after Pearson (|r| < 0.8) and VIF (< 5) screening, and the final predictor sets at 2.5 arc-min: Pyrus spp. = Bio2, Bio4, Bio6, Elevation, Aspect, Slope, T-CaCO3, T-CaSO4; G. molesta = Bio1, Bio4, Bio19, Elevation, Aspect, Slope, T-CaCO3, T-pH-H2O. 03_kuenm_optimisation/ - kuenm calibration output: 600 candidate parameter sets (regularization multiplier 0.1-4.0 crossed with 15 feature-class combinations) ranked by delta AICc. Selected settings: RM = 0.8, FC = LPT for Pyrus spp.; RM = 3.7, FC = QT for G. molesta. 04_suitability_rasters/ - Projected habitat suitability (GeoTIFF, 2.5 arc-min, China extent) for the current baseline (1970-2000, WorldClim) and the 2050s, 2070s and 2090s under SSP126, SSP245 and SSP585 (BCC-CSM2-MR), for both taxa, from the optimised MaxEnt models and the Biomod2 committee-averaging (EMca) ensembles, together with the species-level MaxEnt models for P. pyrifolia, P. ussuriensis and P. bretschneideri. 05_area_overlap/ - Suitable area by suitability class (threshold >= 0.2), change rates relative to current, spatial overlap extent, Jaccard indices among species-level models, and centroid displacements for each period and scenario. 06_scripts/ - R and shell scripts for MaxEnt and kuenm calibration, Biomod2 ensemble modelling (10 algorithms, 10 replicates, pseudo-absence to presence ratio 10:1 with a 5 km minimum distance), MESS extrapolation diagnostics, thresholding, area and centroid calculation and overlap analysis. Run order and required package versions are given in README.txt. 07_tables/ - Manuscript Tables 4-7 as csv: variable percent contribution and permutation importance, projected suitable areas and species-level model performance. Methods summary MaxEnt 3.4.4 was run with kuenm-optimised settings; ensemble models were built in Biomod2 with the six top-performing algorithms and integrated by committee averaging; calibration and evaluation followed a 75/25 split, and performance was assessed with AUC, TSS and Kappa. All layers were standardized to 2.5 arc-min. Notes The Pyrus occurrence set comprises genus-level records rather than verified commercial orchard locations, so the projections represent climatic suitability for the sampled Pyrus occurrences and not cultivated pear production area. Raw records originate from GBIF (https://www.gbif.org) and iNaturalist (https://www.inaturalist.org) and remain under their original licences; this archive provides the filtered, modelling-ready derivatives. Author contributions are given in the additional description. Contact: gengqf@sdau.edu.cn

summary: Overview This versioned reproducibility archive supports the manuscript Earthquake Waiting Times Adjusted for Seismicity Rate: Implications for Short-Term Forecasting . The study evaluates whether adjusting earthquake waiting times for the seismicity rate estimated by an epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model can improve short-term earthquake forecasts. The proposed model (M2) is compared with temporal ETAS (N0), a constant-weight two-component model (M1), and a model using ordinary waiting times with a fixed reference rate (D1). Synthetic experiments also consider a magnitude-weighted alternative (N1). What's New in Version 1.1 Version 1.1 preserves the original version 1.0 archive and adds: Available protocols and results from additional historical earthquake sequences, including exploratory Cohort B and the 18-sequence geographically stratified Cohort C. Event catalogs, forecast scores, model-fitting outputs, and diagnostic analyses. Profile-likelihood investigations of practical parameter identifiability. Parameter-boundary sensitivity experiments involving the Omori decay exponent and exponential triggering timescale. Detailed analyses of the 2011 Tohoku, 2012 Haida Gwaii, and 2017 Iran–Iraq earthquake sequences. Reproducibility documentation, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks. Main Scientific Findings Forecast performance varies across earthquake sequences. Although rate-adjusted waiting times improve retrospective forecast scores in some cases, the results do not demonstrate consistent superiority over ETAS or matched ordinary-waiting-time alternatives. Some apparent improvements depend on the fitted model parameters and their allowable bounds. Nearly equivalent calibration fits can produce substantially different forecasts, including reversals in model ranking. Scope and Limitations The additional global evaluations are retrospective hindcasts, not independently issued prospective forecasts. The available Cohort A component contains the study protocol but not complete final scored results. The Vanuatu audit addendum does not establish verified prospective forecast skill. The parameter-sensitivity analyses are diagnostic and do not establish structural parameter identifiability. Reproducibility The archive contains source code, available input catalogs, fitting outputs, forecast scores, documentation, and checksum manifests. Users should consult README_START_HERE.md , RELEASE_NOTES_v1.1.md , and CLAIM_TO_ARCHIVE_MAP.csv before reproducing individual experiments. The original version 1.0 archive is preserved unchanged within the version 1.1 package.

summary: Description This repository provides the data and Python code supporting an extended triple collocation (ETC)-based fusion of daily transpiration-to-evapotranspiration ratios (T/ET) across 47 sites of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON).  Four categories of T/ET estimates are included: HFT: High-frequency Turbulence RSA: Remote Sensing Model GSP: Gridded Land Surface Product BIO: Biogeophysical Process Model ETC-based fusion framework The accompanying Python code implements an ETC framework to estimate the time-varying random errors of the four T/ET methods and combine them into a dynamically weighted fused product. The ETC system is reconstructed independently for each target day using a centered 30-day moving window, with at least 15 fully collocated daily observations required for estimation. This moving-window approach allows method-specific error variances, error covariance, fusion weights, fused T/ET, and fused uncertainty to vary with phenological and environmental conditions. HFT defines the common reference scale to which the other three estimates are rescaled, but it is not assumed to be error-free. The default ETC configuration permits correlated errors between HFT and BIO because both methods are derived partly from tower eddy-covariance observations and may share footprint and energy-balance-closure effects. The identifiability of the specified error-correlation structure is checked before the fusion is performed. For each valid moving window, the ETC equations are assembled as an overdetermined linear system and solved by ordinary least squares. If an ETC solution cannot be obtained, the program attempts a standard triple collocation solution without correlated errors. Method weights are subsequently calculated using best linear unbiased estimation based on the full error covariance matrix. Complete fusion dataset The principal file, NEON_TET_Fusion_47sites.csv , is a long-format dataset containing 85,654 daily site records and 16 variables. It includes: Daily fused T/ET; Estimated uncertainty of the fused T/ET; Daily T/ET estimates from HFT, RSA, GSP, and BIO; Dynamic fusion weights assigned to the four methods; and Method-specific random error variances. T/ET values, fusion weights, and fused uncertainties are dimensionless. Method-specific error variances have units of ((T/ET)^2). The four method weights sum to one within floating-point precision. Missing observations are represented by empty fields and were not filled during conversion of the fusion workbook to CSV. Figure-specific datasets Figure-specific tables Figures 2 and 3: Figure2_Figure3_NEON_Site_Data_Aligned.csv contains site coordinates, error variances, error standard deviations, and mean fusion weights. Error standard deviation is the square root of the temporal mean error variance. Figure2c_Figure3c_Statistics_Check.csv lists the plotted summaries alongside values recomputed from the 47 site records. Figure 4: Figure4_NEON_Fusion_Weights_by_Site_and_Vegetation.csv contains site and display coordinates, vegetation classes, and site-level mean fusion weights. Figure 5: Figure5_Plot_Data.csv documents the displayed trends, correlations, variance inflation factors, regression coefficients, and explained-variance contributions for the environmental-driver analysis. summary: Description This repository provides the data and Python code supporting an extended triple collocation (ETC)-based fusion of daily transpiration-to-evapotranspiration ratios (T/ET) across 47 sites of the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON).  Four categories of T/ET estimates are included: HFT: High-frequency Turbulence RSA: Remote Sensing Model GSP: Gridded Land Surface Product BIO: Biogeophysical Process Model ETC-based fusion framework The accompanying Python code implements an ETC framework to estimate the time-varying random errors of the four T/ET methods and combine them into a dynamically weighted fused product. The ETC system is reconstructed independently for each target day using a centered 30-day moving window, with at least 15 fully collocated daily observations required for estimation. This moving-window approach allows method-specific error variances, error covariance, fusion weights, fused T/ET, and fused uncertainty to vary with phenological and environmental conditions. HFT defines the common reference scale to which the other three estimates are rescaled, but it is not assumed to be error-free. The default ETC configuration permits correlated errors between HFT and BIO because both methods are derived partly from tower eddy-covariance observations and may share footprint and energy-balance-closure effects. The identifiability of the specified error-correlation structure is checked before the fusion is performed. For each valid moving window, the ETC equations are assembled as an overdetermined linear system and solved by ordinary least squares. If an ETC solution cannot be obtained, the program attempts a standard triple collocation solution without correlated errors. Method weights are subsequently calculated using best linear unbiased estimation based on the full error covariance matrix. Complete fusion dataset The principal file, NEON_TET_Fusion_47sites.csv , is a long-format dataset containing 85,654 daily site records and 16 variables. It includes: Daily fused T/ET; Estimated uncertainty of the fused T/ET; Daily T/ET estimates from HFT, RSA, GSP, and BIO; Dynamic fusion weights assigned to the four methods; and Method-specific random error variances. T/ET values, fusion weights, and fused uncertainties are dimensionless. Method-specific error variances have units of ((T/ET)^2). The four method weights sum to one within floating-point precision. Missing observations are represented by empty fields and were not filled during conversion of the fusion workbook to CSV. Figure-specific datasets Figure-specific tables Figures 2 and 3: Figure2_Figure3_NEON_Site_Data_Aligned.csv contains site coordinates, error variances, error standard deviations, and mean fusion weights. Error standard deviation is the square root of the temporal mean error variance. Figure2c_Figure3c_Statistics_Check.csv lists the plotted summaries alongside values recomputed from the 47 site records. Figure 4: Figure4_NEON_Fusion_Weights_by_Site_and_Vegetation.csv contains site and display coordinates, vegetation classes, and site-level mean fusion weights. Figure 5: Figure5_Plot_Data.csv documents the displayed trends, correlations, variance inflation factors, regression coefficients, and explained-variance contributions for the environmental-driver analysis. Figure 6: Figure6_TET_Consistency_and_Distributions.csv contains the daily category-level and fused T/ET series, with 68,047 valid pairs per comparison. contains the displayed density grids, histograms, curves, and statistical annotations, with recomputed metrics identified separately. Figure 7: contains site–comparator records for the error-reduction maps and Taylor diagram, including error reductions, correlations, normalized standard deviations, and centered root-mean-square differences. Figure 10: Figure10_Data.csv contains daily trajectories, centered seven-day means, a non-drought baseline, and peak-season summaries for SOAP, TEAK, and SJER. Figure 11: docum

summary: What does it mean to say that looking at an atom changes it? A detector can register the same initial average light signal for two proposed measurement processes, even when the processes disturb a trapped ion in different ways. This preprint asks whether a second measurement of the ion’s motion can tell them apart. In a protected three-level calcium-ion benchmark, moving the beam inward at equal calibrated optical gain reduces the initial two-quantum excitation rate by 7.09% under a least-energy-exchange rule and increases it by 23.47% under an energy-frame rule. A scalar optical channel gives zero direct excitation at the inner position. A separate test allows the ion to leave the three levels. Twelve equally sampled preparations give a pooled return probability of exactly one half for original positive rank-one detector events ending within the measured levels. The calibrated scalar model gives 0.999082 at the outer position. Both tests await a matched physical experiment. Published Maryland and Innsbruck apparatus parameters delimit the necessary optical calibration and motional readout. A successful blinded replication would establish which specified rule predicts the disturbance across settings on that instrument. Ordinary quantum measurement theory accommodates the alternatives. The ERU kernel supplies no positive event rate with the probe switched off. This preprint extends An Operator Formulation of the Equation of Relational Unity (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24382197). The deposit includes the experimental protocols, editable manuscript source and reproducibility files.
title: ERU and Wavefunction Collapse: Relational Dynamics, Definite Outcomes and Falsifiable Predictions

summary: Data, fitted models, forecasts and reproducibility code accompanying “Consistency Distillation with Soft Feasibility Penalties and Copula Coupling for Joint Wind-Solar-Load Probabilistic Forecasting”. The archive contains Belgian wind, solar and load hindcasts at 1 h and 24 h, strong tree baselines, retained neural weights and ensembles, calibration and joint-dependence diagnostics, figure source data and table-generation code. Separate experiments examine archived-weather wind forecasts under matched training budgets and complete inference costs for fixed core policies. The weather-budget experiment and inference-cost benchmark use different models and must not be combined into one accuracy–latency claim. The eight ZIP files together form a self-contained archive. Download all parts and extract them into the same directory; each is an ordinary ZIP, not a split volume. ARCHIVE_PARTS.md lists the required files. README.md and REPRODUCE.md describe the directory structure and reproduction commands; MANIFEST.json provides per-file SHA-256 values. Results include negative findings and do not establish qualified-teacher accuracy retention or operational superiority. Author-owned code: MIT. Original experimental results: CC BY 4.0. Third-party data and software retain their source rights and attribution requirements; see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, DATA_SOURCES.md and the file-level scope map. Open-Meteo snapshots use best_match; per-value upstream model identities were not retained. The provider API-data licence and this provenance limitation are documented separately.

summary: We establish a deterministic algorithm that computes the exact closed meandric number M_n from the order n in 2^{O(sqrt(n) log n)} bit operations. The main construction splits each crossing into two points and gives a bijection between closed plane meanders and a prescribed class of straight-line Hamilton cycles on a rational point set of size 4n. A polynomial-size system of local annotations selects exactly one constrained Delaunay triangulation for each cycle. Applying the annotated-triangulation counting theorem of Marx and Miltzow then yields the subexponential bound. We make the geometric construction, the uniqueness of every annotation and the integer-arithmetic cost explicit. A technical appendix gives a periodic-depth realization with canonical rooted-path states and the same asymptotic bound. As a separate consequence, an interval decomposition and formal Lagrange inversion give an exact coefficient formula and a subexponential algorithm for an associated core count; these cores are exponentially rare among all meanders. Reproducible finite checks are reported separately from the proof and from larger reference counts. Version 2.0 (22 November 2026): revised and simplified proof of the main reduction, with an explicit c*N^15 bound for the essential annotation catalogue; clearer attribution to the general Marx--Miltzow counting framework; the depth-augmented realization moved to a technical appendix; removal of the former core-coverage theorem section; expanded bibliography and precise reference-count provenance; and reproducible positive, negative and rank-feasibility diagnostics. The accompanying source archive contains editable LaTeX, BibTeX, vector figures, standard-library Python checks and raw records. It does not implement or benchmark the full subexponential counting engine at large orders. This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.
title: Exact Subexponential Counting of Closed Plane Meanders

summary: This paper proposes the Theory of Asymmetric Resource Dissipation and Nullification (ARDN), a general systems-level framework for examining the relationship between internal resource expenditure, local functional returns, and additional value obtained by entities outside an operational system boundary. The central observation is that resource expenditure within a system does not necessarily produce a proportionate functional benefit for that system. Under specified conditions, internal agents may consume time, energy, attention, information, computational capacity, labour, or other measurable resources while failing to produce sufficient net functional output relative to their defined objective. At the same time, some result of their activity may pass through an identifiable transfer pathway and create measurable additional value for an external beneficiary. The framework distinguishes the internal system, the external reference, the transfer pathway, and the external beneficiary. It formulates a conditional resource-output-gain relationship and separates four possible systemic outcomes: decision dilemma, functional divergence, structural contradiction, and local functional nullification. The primary case is the Friends Celebrity Quarrel Case (FCQC), in which two friends expend conversational and cognitive resources while arguing about a celebrity who may be unaware of their existence. The case is used as a recurring human illustration rather than as the definition of the general mechanism. The distinction between the celebrity as an external reference and a digital platform as a possible external beneficiary is made explicit. The paper develops a fourteen-layer architecture, twelve principal disciplinary domains, operational definitions, a mathematical notation system, conditional scaling models, falsifiable propositions, counterexamples, and a proposed computational and empirical research programme. ARDN is presented as a theoretical proposal, not as an established universal law. Numerical parameter estimation, empirical replication, and cross-domain validation remain necessary before its broader claims can be accepted. summary: The Default Relative Domination Principle (DRDP) is a proposed human psychological framework concerned with the possibility that an individual may experience an unearned sense of relative self-elevation after observing the decline, failure, or downward movement of another person. The central proposition is that an observer may experience a favorable comparative shift without making a corresponding objective improvement, acquisition, or additional effort. The proposed framework includes familiar and unfamiliar individuals, relationship-independent activation, spontaneous self-other comparison, relative-gap perception, latent ego-related activation, conscious and unconscious processing, and possible affective gratification, relief, stability, and perceived security. The framework preserves a five-stage human mechanism: observed decline, spontaneous comparison, relative-gap perception, ego-related activation, and possible affective gratification. It further distinguishes conscious ego-gratification from unconscious ego-gratification and both from the possible activation of a latent ego-related tendency. DRDP does not assert that every human being experiences pleasure whenever another person declines. Rather, it proposes a potentially recurring human tendency whose activation may depend on comparability, perceived relevance, relationship conditions, empathy, self-evaluation, and other contextual factors. The manuscript distinguishes the proposed construct from social comparison, schadenfreude, downward comparison, self-evaluation maintenance, and related psychological explanations. A formal mathematical architecture is developed to separate objective position, subjective relative position, latent ego-related activation, self-elevation, gratification, and perceived security. Sixteen theoretical layers, multidisciplinary research domains, ten hypotheses, boundary conditions, alternative explanations, operational definitions, and an empirical validation roadmap are specified. No new participant data or experimental findings are reported. The present work is a theoretical formulation whose distinctiveness, reliability, causal structure, and generalizability require independent testing. Keywords: Default Relative Domination Principle; Relative Self-Elevation; Latent Ego Activation; Social Comparison; Schadenfreude; Unconscious Processing; Conscious Ego Gratification; Human Psychology; Self-Evaluation; Affective Psychology.
