THE SIX-STAGE CHAPTER DEVELOPMENT In the first passage the investigator identifies physical origin, material identity and the inherited scientific dispute. The second passage proposes a specific physical mechanism and a mathematical geometry with separate units on each axis. The third passage audits calibration, independent measurements and all denominators. The fourth introduces an adversarial counterfactual designed to preserve a plausible visible outcome while changing the cause. The fifth tests the strongest equal-resource comparator, including blinded disturbances and uncertainty intervals. The sixth leaves an open source inheritance with a hard stopping rule and a future research question. The progression must change the question at each step; simply altering the names of variables would not constitute scientific development. TWO HUNDRED RESEARCH GATES The gates follow forty specific challenges for each of five distinct flagship endpoints. Every gate has a material or informational origin, an extreme counterfactual revealing how a false interpretation might survive and a future plan with an independent witness. Each gate includes a concept structure and an adversarial-break structure. Their diagrams explain competing roles; they do not prove that the proposed mechanisms work. The gate remains open when an outside investigator discovers a new, better explanation and can reproduce the experiment without asking the originator for private knowledge. THIRTY-THREE PHOENIX PROTOTYPES Each Phoenix object proposes a physical or digital minimum that could be independently built: a chemical identity card, sensor calibration fixture, adversarial controller, locked sensor model, offline reconstruction package or simulated archive migration. A prototype is an answer embryo, not a certified product. Its design is useful only if it identifies an independent observation that could make the present answer fail, and if the human operator retains the right to stop the test. ONE-HUNDRED-YEAR ARCHIVAL TEST The century-scale horizon is modeled, not observed. It contains threats such as changing formats, missing dependencies, lost institutional custody, inaccessible computing services and silent changes to research methods. The preferred experiment uses adversarial simulated migrations and independent replay across distinct custody pathways. A successor should be able to identify the original chemical evidence, recreate model grids, verify denominators and revoke inherited control privileges. A beautiful future image without these rights is insufficient. FINAL SCIENTIFIC INSCRIPTION The future is not an extension of a beautiful prediction. It is an invitation to test the parts of today's knowledge that might be wrong. The White Rainbow Era seeks a defensible warmth: open knowledge, human authority, bounded instruments, adequate reference comparisons and the inheritance of questions. summary: Abstract. Spin-independent mα⁶ operators of lithium require singular three-electron Hylleraas integrals. We classify all supports of eight selected operator representations, obtaining 21 negative patterns, 12 finite-part families and 58 finite-part minimal rows. Every such row has four rational seed coordinates and an explicit polylogarithmic remainder. Generic non-isogeny and product monodromy make these coordinates unique; exactly 5 minimal rows are elliptic. Every reached pattern has a published treatment or a finite representation, with at most two residual variables where needed. A closed-form atlas of 98 functions includes 291 wall formulas and 174 ray formulas. The evaluator covers positive exact rational exponents; 1044 values at 18 points agree with independent evaluations of the formulas to 40 significant digits. At 9 further pre-specified points, all 522 values agree with an independent implementation of the same closed forms in every printed digit. Independent native quadratures confirm sampled values to 55 digits or more at 5 points spanning all four chambers. We compare 231 published reference values and classify the differences. A worked Q₄₄ matrix element proves that total basis degree three is the lowest admitting an element outside the algebraic-letter polylogarithmic class. Open questions include unresolved cone classifications, a smaller lower-function space on triangle walls, a complete seed form for the worked element, and missing native values. This record holds the manuscript (version 7; 53 pages), the verification bundle LITHIUM_QED_MASTER_P3_v7.zip (LaTeX source and PDF, the supplementary verification package with the census atlas, the wall and ray formulas, the selected representations, value tables, published-value comparisons, the unchanged closed-form evaluator and the replay script run_checks.py , the fact sheet and claim map that tie every statement to its source, and the provenance of the manuscript; 505 files, checked by MANIFEST.sha256 ), the clean arXiv LaTeX source, and SHA256SUMS.txt . README.md explains how to verify the files and run the checks; PAPER3_VERIFICATION/README.md inside the bundle is the entry point for the replay. The code is under the MIT licence; the manuscript and the data are under CC BY 4.0. Companion articles: J. Matuzas, Elliptic structure of the singular three-electron Hylleraas integrals, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23917908 ; J. Matuzas, Three-electron Hylleraas integrals with two inverse-square distances: exact reduction and high-precision evaluation for the fine structure of lithium, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23977551 . Generative-AI disclosure and author responsibility. ChatGPT-6 Pro (GPT-6 Astra Pro in writing the manuscript) was used for derivations, computations, and drafting; OpenAI Codex ran the independent native computations and the independent evaluator tests on a local server; Claude Opus 5.5, with Claude Fable 5.2 in parts of the census review and of the evaluator tests, was used for independent re-derivation and audit of every increment and proposed several of the checks. The author directed and audited the work throughout and takes full responsibility for the mathematics and the final text. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 81V45; Secondary 33E05, 33B30, 14H52, 65D30, 81-08. All the work was done by AI. Preprint. External peer review is not claimed.

summary: STARLI / WHITE RAINBOW ERA / FAMILY 39 / F191–F195 4D AROMA ENVIRONMENTS AND AUTONOMOUS LIVING CIVILIZATION FIVE FLAGSHIP SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH ESSENCE / PROSPECTIVE NONCLINICAL / 2026-11-23 SCIENTIFIC DNA AND BOUNDARIES. This research volume separates 4D material sorption from passive airflow, audited microgrid energy from shifted HVAC costs, fairness and accessible refusal from personalized preference scores, preserved digital twins from physically correct sensor calibration, and software stop requests from electrically witnessed hardware isolation. F191 through F195 share an indoor-air model boundary but retain independent endpoints, conventional benchmarks and authority stops. All surfaces and scenarios are synthetic and cannot establish real building safety, human exposure or clinical benefit. F191 / 4D Smart Aroma Materials in Living Environments at the Limit. Mechanism: reversible sorption, material transport, surface state and geometry-memory response, temperature-dependent desorption, ventilation advection-diffusion and material state history. Independent endpoint 4D surface response reproducibility [%]. Minimum prototype: synthetic shape-memory polymer-state trajectories, sealed nonrelease sorption grids, programmable humidity traces, certified test artefacts and mechanical-interlock witness logs. Strong conventional comparator matched nonresponsive passive adsorbent plus ventilation-only and fixed-rate no-release offline baselines. Witness: unaffiliated materials laboratory with gravimetric sorption, blind dimensional cycles and independently calibrated room-concentration reference. Counterworld: withheld humidity reversal and changed ventilation topology after frozen response calibration. Stop: nonconsensual release, material leak, unverified concentration, uncontrolled heating or measured air-quality exceedance. F192 / Botanical Volatiles and Smart Microgrid Energy Coupling at the Limit. Mechanism: power-flow scheduling, energy integration, battery state-of-charge, heat and ventilation energy, volatile-source mass balance and demand-response constraints. Independent endpoint Aroma control energy cost [kWh/day]. Minimum prototype: offline 24-hour synthetic building demand traces, traceable unit conversion sheets, no-release actuator emulation, battery state files and blinded grid-fault challenge packets. Strong conventional comparator measured-energy conventional HVAC and fixed-release/no-release scheduling with equal air-quality and grid constraints. Witness: independent energy auditor using traceable revenue-grade power meters, ventilation references and battery SoC logging. Counterworld: blind renewable shortfall combined with a late-night ventilation demand spike. Stop: ventilation below regulatory minimum, unsafe exposure forecast, battery reserve failure, energy-meter trace loss or violation of human stop authority. F193 / Fairness and Accessibility in Personalized Aroma Environments at the Limit. summary: In multireference alignment one observes noisy copies of a signal in R^d, each cyclically shifted by an unknown random amount. The quasi maximum likelihood estimator aligns the observations jointly and averages them. Its power spectrum is biased, and Bandeira asked whether its Fourier phases are consistent once the power spectrum is corrected. They are not. Take d equal to 6, 7, 10 or 11 and the truth a unit sinusoid of frequency one. At every sufficiently large fixed noise level, the phase of the first Fourier coefficient of the estimate converges to the set of midpoints between consecutive shifts of the true phase. If the Fourier magnitudes of the estimate are then replaced by the true ones, its distance to the nearest shift of the truth converges to 2 sin(π/(2d)). The same failure holds on an open set of signals whose nonconstant Fourier coefficients are all nonzero. The deciding sign is that of an explicit Gaussian integral, which we enclose in rigorous bounds for every d from 3 to 11.
title: A half-step phase error of the hard-alignment estimator in multireference alignment

summary: Synthetic operational databases from process-based business simulation are commonly judged by resemblance to real data, which misses plausible records that could not have arisen from the process they represent. We define business-rule admissibility as the property that every state and every change in a dataset could have been produced by the represented process under its own rules, decompose it into ten criteria, each checkable as a query over a database and its change history, and name three layers where a simulation can lose it. We draw 22 cases from developing NAILU, a framework that turns business prose into executable simulations. Separate language-model agents built a study firm from its handbook; another, seeing neither the model nor its data, wrote the firm’s rules. Of nine past defects re-injected, the rules caught six in every run; seven event-log distances caught two in every run, one of them missed by the rules, and a third in most runs; the firm’s management indicators caught one only when read monthly with measures the author added, and none under a robust score. A pre-registered replication on twenty new seeds confirmed all five predictions. Of five further defects, covering a forbidden transition, recording and execution, the rules caught three in every run and one in half; one that dropped writes from the change history escaped every detector but its reconciliation with the tables. On the unchanged firm, the rules found six departures from its handbook. The evidence comes from one framework, where the detectors saw different defects
title: Business-Rule Admissibility in Process-Based Business Simulation

summary: This a research program titled the "Triple Interface Method". Its aim is to solve the Goldbach conjecture.  This manuscript presents a modular tripartite “engine” for tackling the binary Goldbach problem. The argument is broken into a small set of auditable modules—how energy is spread across rational frequencies, how bilinear short-shift correlations are controlled, how nuisance low-frequency effects are cancelled, and how average positivity is converted into pointwise positivity for every even number in a range. Each outputs a quantitative bound; together they feed a simple closing ledger that leaves only mild, standard number-theory inputs (distribution in very small moduli and a positive main term) and a routine finite base. The machinery of the paper has been coded in Lean 4 and the repo is available to the public. This proof strategy was not successful. It is preserved here for the purposes of the archive.
title: Goldbach and the Triple Interface Method

summary: GHC compares successful rewrite rules in arrival order. We ask when changing how rules are tried preserves the chosen rewrite. If every match of a later strict challenger implies a match of its earlier incumbent, a depth-first search gives a faithful first-match priority in linear time once the comparisons are known. Appending a challenger preserves old relative priorities. Inserting a structural rule before $t$ old arrivals can force almost all $\binom{t}{2}$ suffix pairs to reverse, even if the new rule never wins. An inherited list can need quadratically many reversals with only one later arrival. Given the caller table, minimum repair takes polynomial time for fixed $t$. For insertion at the head the decision problem is NP-complete even when every old rule can still win. The containment criterion covers sixteen shipped list-fold rules, including three with cyclic pairwise choices. For a fixed arrival order, testing whether the last rule can be deleted takes polynomial time on a forest of forward comparisons and is coNP-complete at treewidth two, even with disjoint one-to-one match prerequisites. Deciding whether one first-match priority preserves all winners takes polynomial time at width two and is coNP-complete at width three. For a list of $q$ possible winners, a width-two algorithm has an exponent linear in $q$, with a matching conditional lower bound. Typed Core templates realize the reductions at the GHC 9.14.1 matcher. A separate joint-order problem becomes NP-complete at three successes per call. The fold example compares the source-level work of shared tests.
title: Which GHC Rewrite Rules Can Win?

summary: Abstract Biological semiosis is a relational hypothesis whose attribution depends on evidence, causal explanation and an explicit interpretive theory. Elementary Semiotic Events provides an episode-level procedure for evaluating this inference. Each claim specifies a candidate sign, object, interpreting system and interpretant, alongside the observations and warrants linking them. Four obligations govern assessment: define the theory-relative relation, establish its biological premises, test the inferential bridge independently and evaluate rivals. ESE distinguishes formal derivability, empirical support and permission to make a theoretical attribution. Its three-valued readiness policy records failed, unresolved or satisfied obligations; chronological traces preserve the availability of evidence; and a finite-model criterion tests identifiability. Constructed examples show how a selective response can leave reference unsettled and observationally equivalent mechanisms can disagree under intervention. Transcription factor–DNA (TF–DNA) recognition provides a tractable molecular specialization, connecting sequence models, binding, regulation and interpretant hypotheses through distinct measurements. These results establish conditional properties of explicit assessment procedures and identify possible discriminating biological tests. ESE makes the premises, limits and revision conditions of a biological sign claim inspectable. Record contents This version contains the author preprint (not peer reviewed), Online Resource 1 (supplementary information) and Online Resource 2 (computational reference supplement). Online Resource 2 provides a reference implementation, deterministic tests, expected results and a checksum manifest for finite formal and synthetic claims; it contains no empirical molecular dataset and does not adjudicate biological semiosis. summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half (π), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement resting on the birth of the arrow — a pure projection from one unit, the product over the primes. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ)², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. The work rests on classical results — Pell–Lagrange, Legendre's sieve, the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt — and proposes a new linking of them: the geometry of the seam as a model of the process linking the primes. The author's answer to Riemann's question is geometric: on each range chosen in a definite way, the process of the link of the primes is seen as the unit circle and a sinusoid around it; for his work the author regards this answer as a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and what in it is accepted as an initial prin
title: The Fractal Ladder of Prime Density: Quadratic Scale and Linear Error

summary: INTEGRATED INTELLIGENT ACUPUNCTURE NANO-QUANTUM RESEARCH AT THE LIMIT F196–F200 · STARLI · White Rainbow Era · Research Working Edition v1.0 Prospective research essence | Nonclinical | Synthetic mathematical models At the end of forty integrated families, the central question changes. How can a research civilization connect five kinds of evidence while preserving the right to disagree? Family 40 gathers AI–nanorobot coordination, bioelectric and quantum sensing, philosophical and physical dual-track validation, bounded autonomous platforms, and open negative-case reconstruction. The purpose is not to announce that a new acupuncture mechanism has been confirmed. It is to design a research archive in which every ambitious model comes with a stronger rival, a declared uncertainty and a route to refusal. A well-matched classical baseline may defeat a quantum-labelled architecture. A thermal or electrode artifact may account for a proposed biofield. Two cultural readers may agree about an ancient text yet disagree about the physical proxy that should test its modern interpretation. A capable control system must still stop when a human revokes permission. Finally, a striking result should remain provisional until a different laboratory can reconstruct its adverse cases and explain why the result might be false. The family is situated in Eastern philosophical traditions as intellectual history and an ethics of balance and responsibility, while empirical claims are restricted to independently observable measurements. All diagrams, surfaces and numerical grids in this volume are synthetic and prospective. There is no clinical intervention, biological proof, medical-device validation, confirmed remote effect or established new field. The volume offers thirty inherited candidate relationships, forty-two open numerical models, eighty-two staged chapter investigations, two hundred research doors, and thirty-three successor prototype sketches. Its deepest ambition is methodological: to make a future researcher more capable of falsifying it than the original author could have been. FIVE FLAGSHIP STUDIES F196 — AI–Nanorobot Coordination in Intelligent Acupuncture at the Limit Primary endpoint: independent negative-case rebuild rate (1); timing reconstruction error (ms). Minimum prototype: disconnected digital-twin microrobot and separately referenced control log. Strong comparator: matched deterministic classical coordination on identical task streams. Independent stop: refuse any action lacking a valid human permission record or external witness. How can a research civilization connect five kinds of evidence while preserving the right to disagree? Family 40 gathers AI–nanorobot coordination, bioelectric and quantum sensing, philosophical and physical dual-track validation, bounded autonomous platforms, and open negative-case reconstruction. The purpose is not to announce that a new acupuncture mechanism has been confirmed. It is to design a research archive in which every ambitious model comes with a stronger rival, a declared uncertainty and a route to refusal. A well-matched classical baseline may defeat a quantum-labelled architecture. A thermal or electrode artifact may account for a proposed biofield. Two cultural readers may agree about an ancient text yet disagree about the physical proxy that should test its modern interpretation. A capable control system must still stop when a human revokes permission. Finally, a striking result should remain provisional until a different laboratory can reconstruct its adverse cases and explain why the result might be false. The family is situated in Eastern philosophical traditions as intellectual history and an ethics of balance and responsibility, while empirical claims are restricted to independently observable measurements. All diagrams, surfaces and numerical grids in this volume are synthetic and prospective. There is no clinical intervention, biological proof, medical-device validation, confirmed remote effect or established new field. The volume offers thirty inherited candidate relationships, forty-two open numerical models, eighty-two staged chapter investigations, two hundred research doors, and thirty-three successor prototype sketches. Its deepest ambition is methodological: to make a future researcher more capable of falsifying it than the original author could have been. summary: Printing a floating-point number and reading it back should recover its bits. We find exactly 626,159 positive finite binary64 values whose shortest CPython spelling SQLite 3.54.1 reads as a neighbor. These failures collapse disjoint adjacent pairs. SQLite's default writer reverses 5,084 of those pairs. On each, SQLite reads its own text back to the stored value, while correct rounding gives its neighbor. We count them by locating incorrect midpoint decisions and identifying which decimals CPython can print. A repair adds 104 bytes to SQLite's power table and gives correct rounding for every 64-bit coefficient passed to the converter. Compiled versions with wide and portable multiplication agreed with exact rounding in 2,402,440 selected cases. A separate limit arises before conversion. Two 20-digit decimals can require different answers even when the scanner retains the same prefix and discards a nonzero digit from both. We determine exactly how many binary rounding boundaries remain ambiguous as additional decimal digits are retained. An exact suffix comparison and a correction to exponent accumulation give a complete reader for accepted ASCII decimals below the stated length limit. It matched whole-text rounding on 1,296,347 native tests. An x86-64 Linux build on the same Mac reproduced all five native output streams in each of seven cohorts. The complete Linux reader matched the reference on all 55,670 additional public input rows. The released reader misrounded 157 public test spellings. REAL-column import also changed 910 negative zeros to positive zero. SQLite's 18-digit format preserves every finite nonzero value with either reader.
title: Decimal Prefix Ambiguity and Binary64 Rounding in SQLite

summary: Replication package (version 8) for the paper "Salience, Calibration, and Taker Returns in Kalshi's Mention Markets" (Franklin Cabrera Ordonez; earlier working title: "Salience, Mispricing, and Tradability in Kalshi's Mention Markets: Pre-Specified Tests"). Version 8 supersedes versions 1 to 7: it adds the selection check on the discovery sample and the minimum detectable effect of the prospective plan (Cell 133a) and the reconciliation of Table 8 with Table A16 (Cell 133b), and it cites the prospective-test plan version 4 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24450089; earlier versions doi:10.5281/zenodo.24443393, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24448264 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.24448367) and the quote logger version 3.2 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24451715). Row-level Kalshi data, the raw trade cache and the event-metadata cache are not included, because Kalshi's Developer Agreement restricts sharing API data without written authorization; they are listed with SHA-256 hashes in OMITTED_FILES.csv. summary: This artifact accompanies the poster paper "Evaluating Multi-Agent Incident Response: Baseline Design, Efficiency, and Policy Compliance" by Ebelechukwu Nwafor and Habeeb Olufowobi, accepted at the ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC '27). The paper asks whether a multi-agent LLM workflow for incident response is more efficient than a single agent, and shows that the answer depends on how the single-agent baseline is built. It evaluates MAN-IDS, a four-role LLM workflow, against single-agent baselines and a deterministic rule in three controlled studies on a Docker test network with Redis and PostgreSQL access scenarios. Contents - The MAN-IDS system and the evaluation harness (runners, scoring, decision protocol). - All prompts, model versions, and settings used in the studies. - The protocol for each study, written before any model calls were made. - Complete run records with full traces for 1,152 scheduled investigations across 64 campaigns:   - Study 1: explicit response policy, Claude Sonnet 5, 384 runs.   - Study 2: detector gating and routing repair, Claude Sonnet 5, 512 runs.   - Study 3: replication with Qwen3-8B on fresh campaigns, 256 runs. - Analysis scripts and their saved outputs, including the stage-timing, format-versus-decision, and comparable-quality re-analyses reported in the paper. - The trace analysis that motivated the routing repair, with the run records of the earlier evaluation it reads. - Detector experiment outputs (splits, predictions, reports) derived from CICIDS2017 and CSE-CIC-IDS2018. - The test-network setup (Docker Compose files, topology, schemas). Reproducing the results No model calls or API keys are needed. Running "python3 reproduce_analyses.py" re-runs the three study analyses from the saved run records and reports whether each result matches the shipped file byte for byte. The README lists the required Python packages and the remaining commands. Notes - Response actions were never executed. All tools are controlled and non-executing. - The public datasets are not redistributed. Only derived splits, predictions, and reports are included. - Run traces contain the absolute file paths of the machines that produced them. - Re-running the model studies would require an Anthropic API key (Studies 1 and 2) or a GPU serving Qwen3-8B (Study 3), plus Docker. title: Artifact for "Evaluating Multi-Agent Incident Response: Baseline Design, Efficiency, and Policy Compliance" (ACM SAC 2027)

summary: This record registers, before any per-origin value was read, a test of how three checkpoint-relief alleles combine at individual budding-yeast replication origins. The data are the eight-genotype factorials of Sheu, Kinney and Stillman (2016, Genome Research 26:315–330), taken from the authors' repository (github.com/jbkinney/14_sheu, commit 026c2ef). The primary test uses the 0.2 M HU, 90-min factorial. The 0.05% MMS factorial serves as an agreement test, and the unperturbed 25-min factorial as a negative control. A triple-mutant HU time course, run in two separate experiments, supplies the HU noise estimate. Product, additive and constrained stochastic-threshold models are compared in a single censored likelihood. Each sample carries its own scale and floor. Three gates come first: a replicate control, an unperturbed null and an information check. A verdict requires agreement across floor treatments, width adjustment, doubled noise and the MMS condition. Every verdict is provisional pending a replicated HU factorial. The design corrects three errors in the earlier Pol α registration (10.5281/zenodo.24450406): a missing scale term, a floor treated as exact, and an ambiguous reference level. Version 2 adds Amendment 1, filed before any per-origin value was read: the condition assignment is confirmed from figure captions and per-sample settings because Supplemental Table 1 is not accessible; floor treatment F1 is recomputed from the repository profiles; and a second HU 90-min replicate gate (set 7 vs set 4) is added. Version 3 deposits the outcome. The registered analysis terminated at Gate 3, the unperturbed negative control: three of four interaction terms exceeded the registered threshold with the checkpoint inactive (mcm4Δ74-174 × dbf4-19A γ = 1.40, 95% CI 0.98–1.85). The registered outcome is uninterpretable, and the HU combination-rule comparison was not performed. Gates 2, 2b and 4 passed. Code and outputs reproduce every reported number from the authors' repository (commit 026c2ef).
title: Prospective registration: combination rules for sld3-38A, dbf4-19A and mcm4Δ74-174 at individual replication origins in the Sheu et al. (2016) factorial

summary: Data and analysis files supporting Salichos et al., Multi-host phylodynamics of hepatitis E virus reveals extensive lineage sharing across humans, wild boar, and swine . The study analysed 436 hepatitis E virus ORF2 sequences from humans, wild boar, swine and camels, together with 49 ICTV subtype reference genomes. Subtypes were reassigned de novo by phylogenetic placement, and time-calibrated coalescent and birth–death skyline analyses were run for 13 subtype- and host-specific datasets, followed by a discrete-trait analysis of host transitions among HEV-3 lineages. This deposit contains the 411 bp alignment and per-analysis alignments with sampling dates, sequence metadata after filtering and deduplication, BEAST v2.7.7 XML input files, parameter log files, the annotated maximum clade credibility and maximum-likelihood trees shown in the figures, and the scripts used for the temporal-signal testing, the host and subtype rate comparison, and Figures 2 and 4. All sequences are publicly available in GenBank; accession numbers are listed in alignments/metadata.tsv . Results tables are published with the article and are not duplicated here. See README.md for the full contents. Version 2 adds three analyses, in HEV_round2_additions.tgz. All version 1 files are unchanged. prior_sens/ — Sensitivity of the becoming-uninfectious rate (δ) to its prior. Four datasets (HEV-3f all hosts, HEV-3f swine, HEV-3c human, HEV-3a wild boar) re-analysed under three alternative lognormal priors on δ, alongside the prior used in the main analysis: twelve BEAST v2.7.7 input files, the twelve parameter logs of 100 million states each, the four baseline logs, and a summary table of prior and posterior δ. subtype_bssvs/ — The discrete-trait host-transition analysis repeated within individual HEV-3 subtypes, for the three subtypes containing all three host states with more than four sequences per host: HEV-3f (n = 131), HEV-3c (n = 82) and HEV-3e (n = 48). Three input files, two independent chains of 200 million states per subtype, and a summary table of posterior inclusion probabilities, Bayes factors and transition rates for all six pathways. window_unconstrained/ — The 411 bp ORF2 window tree re-estimated without the whole-genome backbone constraint, used to check that the subtype assignments do not depend on it. IQ-TREE v3.1.4 outputs and the resulting assignments. scripts/make_figure4_bssvs.py generates Figure 4 and supersedes scripts/Figure4_BSSVS.py from version 1, which implemented an earlier treatment of the rate indicators.
title: Multi-host phylodynamics of hepatitis E virus reveals extensive lineage sharing across humans, wild boar, and swine

summary: This record contains the code, the processed input data and the results of every run of a benchmark study on the day-ahead and rolling-horizon scheduling of building energy systems with photovoltaics (PV), photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) collectors, a battery, a heat pump and a thermal storage tank.   The study compares three quantum-inspired metaheuristics (quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithm, quantum-behaved particle swarm optimisation, simulated quantum annealing) with their classical counterparts (genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimisation, simulated annealing), with general-purpose optimisers (differential evolution, L-SHADE, sep-CMA-ES, jSO, Gaussian QPSO, real-coded QEA, coordinate pattern search) and with mixed-integer linear programming (an exact MILP for the linear instances, a naive linearisation, a piecewise-linear MILP and its three-band and scenario-based forms). All optimisers receive the same number of objective-function evaluations and are tuned with one protocol.   Experiments - 21 synthetic day-ahead instances with 24 to 864 decision variables, 30 runs per algorithm and instance, evaluation budgets of 5,000, 20,000 and 100,000 - 1,311 data-driven day-ahead instances in three climates (typical-meteorological-year weather, measured electrical loads) - component ablations, budgets proportional to the number of variables, settings tuned at 864 variables - warm starts from the schedule of the piecewise-linear MILP - one year of rolling-horizon operation with 19 controllers, with and without a weekly demand charge, and three shorter variants (perfect forecasts, a second forecast-error model, random initialisation at every step)   Contents (143 files, 44 MB compressed) - qio_ies/: simulator of the energy system (numba), optimisers, MILP models, rolling-horizon operation - scripts/: one script per experiment, the statistical analysis, and the scripts that write the tables and figures - data/: processed measured load series - results/: output of every run (CSV, NPZ, JSON), reference costs and analysis tables - README.md: layout, commands and requirements   Reproduction The analysis tables and the tables and figures of the accompanying article can be regenerated from the stored run results with the analysis, table and figure scripts listed in README.md. The experiments themselves can be repeated with the run scripts. Metaheuristic runs are deterministic for a given seed. Extract the archive with the file times preserved.   Requirements Python 3.11 with numpy, scipy (HiGHS), numba, pandas, joblib, matplotlib and pvlib. The results were produced with Python 3.11.9, numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, numba 0.66.0, pandas 3.0.3, matplotlib 3.11.0, joblib 1.5.3 and pvlib 0.15.2.   Data sources The weather records are the typical-meteorological-year files distributed with pvlib. The measured loads are derived from the UCI data set ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014 (https://doi.org/10.24432/C58C86).
title: Benchmark of quantum-inspired and classical metaheuristics and piecewise-linear MILP for PV–battery–heat-pump–thermal-storage scheduling: code, data and results

summary: Predictive world models learn to forecast observations, but accurate short-term predictions do not necessarily produce physically coherent behavior over longer horizons. We investigate how incorporating physical structure can strengthen world models while retaining their underlying predictive objectives. Across token-based models of planetary motion and JEPA-style visual models of mechanical systems, we study conserved-quantity supervision, symmetry-aware representations, temporal consistency, and learned structured dynamics. In planetary motion, angular-momentum supervision improves autonomous next-token forecasting, while the benefits of temporal regularization depend on the accompanying physical objective and representation. In visual models, generating rollouts through supervised energy-based dynamics heads produces more faithful trajectories and phase-space evolution. Together, these findings highlight the importance of how physical structure participates in prediction: improvements in an auxiliary physical readout or a local acceleration estimate do not automatically translate into more reliable long-horizon behavior. Evaluations across initial conditions and physical parameter shifts further reveal where these benefits persist and where generalization remains limited. Our study supports physical structure as a practical means of improving predictive world models and provides a unified framework for understanding its effects on representations, learned transitions, and autonomous rollouts. The central lesson is that effective physical inductive biases should help models both represent physical regularities and use them to generate future states.
title: Where Structure Enters a World Model: From Predictive Fit to Physical Rollout

summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.
title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction

summary: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.
title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification

summary: Language models fuse reports in retrieval, multi-agent consensus and agent memory, where treating shared-source reports as independent can double count evidence. A common remedy is an instruction to count each source once. Its value depends on the receiver's raw baseline. Pricing it needs an exact reference. We build the graded-dependence exact reference: binary worlds with single-report reliability 0.65 and four dependence levels, whose disclosed parameters give every world an exact posterior and every rule a target risk. The paired gain protocol scores raw and instructed answers of four configurations on 2,976 worlds. Agreement and gain separate in both directions. At $δ$ = 0, claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol agreed with the rule within 0.001 in 744 of 744, and the instruction raised their posterior mismatch by 0.044; gpt-6-luna agreed in 165 of 744 and gained 0.0140 (95% interval 0.0064 to 0.0219); claude-haiku-5-5's gain moved from -0.0295 ($δ$ = 0) to +0.0302 ($δ$ = 1) (descriptive). The prespecified first-child endpoint contrast, gain at $δ$ = 1 minus $δ$ = 0, was 0.0342 (0.0303 to 0.0382). In the preregistered tests, the raw source-weight contrast was positive (0.259, 95% interval 0.182 to 0.337; Holm rejected zero) and the grouping endpoint difference was not detected (0.0004, -0.0023 to 0.0031). This interval excludes differences larger than 0.0031 in magnitude and lies within the registered precision bound of $\pm$0.0046. The reference prices the rule before any model call. The paired gain, estimable as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items, decides adoption per receiver and prompt condition.
title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain

summary: If we optimize an image until a classifier is confident it shows a cat, we may get an adversarial example, not a cat. Planning with a latent world model is a similar search for actions whose predicted future is closest to the goal. Is the result a plan, or an adversarial example of the world model? We show that it can be either. On the released DINO-WM and LeWM, more iterations of the cross-entropy method (CEM) lower the predicted cost but lose up to half of the problems CEM had already solved. The model's own predictions do not reveal these failures. We propose a simple test that executes the plan after every iteration and counts the problems a planner solves and then loses. Unlike an image, a plan comes with its actions, which our round-trip check reads back from the predicted states with a small network, penalizing mismatches. The check reads back the sum of each block of five actions, the part that two consecutive predicted states determine. Without retraining the world model and at only 0.2% to 3.1% more planning time, it improves the widely used planners CEM and MPPI on three released world models, and gains more where planners lose more problems. Without replanning, success rises from 0.39 to 0.76 on Wall with DINO-WM and from 0.56 to 0.94 for MPPI on JEPA-WM. With replanning (MPC), it rises from 0.70 to 0.81 on Cube with LeWM.
title: A Plan or an Adversarial Example? A Round-Trip Check for Latent World Models

summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency

summary: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents

summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. Prior attacks either passively analyze network traffic, which yields only coarse correlations, or hijack the agent through indirect prompt injection, which must place sensitive content in an outgoing field and is blocked by content-level defenses. Whether an attacker can actively recover fine-grained private context without any explicit transmission thus remains insufficiently understood. Our insight is that an agent's benign Web decisions themselves leak private context, as what it chooses to visit encodes whether, which, and in what order it acts, forming a behavioral covert channel. Building on this, we design SNOOP, a stateful hierarchical probing framework that narrows a coarse-to-fine hypothesis tree per task and reconstructs user queries and profiles from the agent's observable paths. Across four agents and three LLM backbones on 500 StackExchange queries and 378 multi-turn iKAT dialogues, SNOOP recovers query concepts with an average F1 of 0.89 and user profiles with an F1 of 0.80, while four representative agent defenses change its recovery by less than 0.03 F1. Since no sensitive content is ever transmitted, content-level inspection cannot detect this leakage; we therefore propose Selection-Obfuscated Retrieval (SOR), which acquires resources under a fixed budget independent of private context and confines the agent's selection to a local snapshot, cutting SNOOP's F1 to 0.39 without additional LLM inference.
title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions

summary: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
title: Mind World Models: Joint Learning of Motor EEG Representations and Action-Conditioned World Dynamics

summary: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.
title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer

summary: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving

summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. One example is \textit{spurious agreement}, where the student maintains high overlap with the teacher at the states visited but produces repetitive generations. Although such failures have been observed, the mechanisms behind these failures remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we investigate OPD through the lens of learning dynamics, tracing three mechanisms from local analysis to subsequent on-policy sampling. We first identify states where sampled-token OPD updates fail to correct teacher--student mismatch and characterize them using the student's mass on the teacher's top-$p$ set. We then show that learning from the teacher is difficult at mismatched states and that their gradients can also affect with learning at other tokens. Finally, using a termination-token mismatch as a case study, we study how continued training on mismatched states influences on-policy sampling, suppressing the student's current modes and leading the student toward states where the teacher is unreliable . These findings help explain the benefits of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization and motivate targeted correction of states where student and teacher are mismatched.
title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation

summary: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.
title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation

summary: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.

summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models

summary: Agentic products introduce risks that extend beyond those of their underlying models, arising from their tools, permissions, data access, safeguards, and operating conditions. Existing evaluation instruments provide useful evidence about model behavior and agents in defined harnesses, but their results do not necessarily transfer to deployed products or cover risks created by product configurations and interactions. Identifying and measuring such risks is especially difficult before deployment, when failure pathways, exposure, and outcome distributions may be poorly understood. This raises a fundamental question: what can evaluation evidence establish about the safety of a particular product, and what decisions can it legitimately support? We call the illusion of evaluation the appearance of safety assurance when producing an evaluation result is treated as sufficient evidence for claims that extend beyond what was measured. Drawing on practitioner experience, prior research, and twelve illustrative product contexts, we identify six methodological challenges spanning product-risk identification, ecological and measurement validity, metric interpretation, outcome verification, evidence transfer, and evidentiary sufficiency. We propose a granular transparency-and-decision-relevance record that makes risks, system configurations, assumptions, uncertainty, and evidentiary limits explicit. The proposal is a reporting and reasoning aid, not proof of safety or a deployment-approval standard. We conclude with open questions on valid product-level measurements, evidence transfer, and decision sufficiency.
title: The Illusion of Evaluation: Challenges in Agentic Product Evaluation Practice

summary: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.
title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments

summary: Traffic forecasting models are typically evaluated under ideal conditions with complete data. This evaluation does not reflect the frequent sensor failures and communication outages common in real-world deployments. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of multivariate traffic prediction models to evaluate their performance under varying levels of sensor data loss during inference. We benchmark several architectural paradigms, including graph neural networks, attention-based Transformers, and selective state-space models, across sparsity levels ranging from zero to complete sensor loss, using two widely used multi-channel traffic benchmarks. To ensure consistent comparison across traffic variables, we use normalized metrics and define a usability threshold to identify when predictions become unreliable. Our results show a clear trade-off between baseline accuracy and robustness: models with the highest accuracy under full-data conditions often degrade most sharply as data becomes sparse, while less accurate models maintain more stable performance. These findings show that model selection should be based on the expected reliability of the sensor network rather than peak accuracy alone. This work provides a practical framework for assessing traffic forecasting models and highlights the importance of robustness in real-world applications.
title: A Sparsity Analysis of Traffic Forecasting Architectures: How Much Missing Data is Too Much?

summary: Trading agents join probabilistic language-model inference to persistent portfolio state and execution authority. A false claim can become an order, an evaluator flaw can promote a worse policy, and shared models or data can produce correlated behavior. AI-safety research studies reward misspecification, tool misuse, distribution shift, evaluation gaming, and unsafe self-modification. Financial research and governance study execution costs, market access, manipulation, operational resilience, backtest overfitting, and systemic feedback. These literatures are rarely integrated into one measurement agenda for systems that reason in language and act in markets. This paper defines the relevant system boundary and develops four conjectures with twelve measurable research subproblems: grounding and abstention; user-mandate fidelity; bounded information and execution authority; leakage-resistant evaluation; execution fidelity; promotion-gate integrity; emergent manipulation; correlated stress; tacit coordination; provenance and position-policy continuity; deterministic risk kernels and interruption; and human governance and recovery. Each subproblem specifies a failure pathway, research question, minimum experiment, metrics, and deployment implication. The supporting evidence map (Appendix A) distinguishes direct trading-agent evidence, market-mechanism evidence, general AI-safety evidence, official governance precedents, and author proposals. The paper also proposes a ten-part reporting standard and a set of anti-problems: higher returns, benchmark scores, more explanation, more autonomy, more agents, or a passed model judge do not by themselves constitute safety progress. This is a structured research agenda, not a systematic review, empirical validation, or claim that any architecture makes autonomous trading safe.
title: AI Safety for Trading Agents: Critical Problems for Market-Deployed Language Models

summary: Abstract Reliable rare-flood decisions require more than numerical convergence or pooled interval coverage. We evaluate a reporting framework that distinguishes reporting (PASS), seeking further information (HOLD), and withholding an unsupported estimate for review (WITHHOLD). Five policies were compared on shared simulated cases in a post-development frozen V11 evaluation cohort (2,800 cases) and a separately targeted stress cohort (2,000 cases), using selective coverage, acceptance, paired illustrative loss, and cost sensitivity. V11 accepted 657/2,800 (23.46%) cases in the frozen cohort; 637/657 accepted intervals covered the true target (96.96%). In targeted stress, it accepted 23/2,000 (1.15%), of which 9/23 (39.13%) covered truth; all five heavy-tail GEV cells had zero PASS. V11's mean proxy loss exceeded that of the V10 decision candidate in the frozen cohort (0.8118 versus 0.7585) but was lower in targeted stress (1.5017 versus 1.7258); policy rankings also varied across 180 assumed cost settings. An earlier external Powell audit reported 11/2,000 heavy-tail discrepancies, but did not establish case identity or objective equivalence. Replaying the eleven named cases from the archived V11 generator recovered the reference point estimates; independent profile-interval validation remains unresolved. Five Australian gauge series comprise annual maxima of daily-mean flow, not instantaneous peaks; penalized GEV did not outperform lognormal on mean expanding-origin log score at four comparable gauges. The results map simulation-specific failure domains and decision trade-offs; they do not validate a general screening guarantee or a facility design recommendation. Keywords: flood-frequency analysis; generalized extreme value; selective coverage; abstention; decision loss; heavy tails; temporal dependence; out-of-sample validation.
title: Evidence-Conditioned Flood-Frequency Decisions: Selective ‎Coverage and Decision-Loss Trade-offs

summary: The growing complexity of electronic systems demands efficient design flows, yet EDA scripting remains a bottleneck: proprietary APIs are sparsely documented, and errors often appear as silent failures or cryptic exceptions. Hand-crafted knowledge helps but is difficult to maintain as toolchains evolve. We present ZhuLong-SE (Self-Evolution), an execution-grounded LLM agent that learns reusable knowledge from prior task traces. Building on ZhuLong, it enhances the task-level harness with API retrieval, documentation responses, isolated sandbox execution, and static checking, then adds governed cross-task self-evolution. Beyond solving individual tasks, ZhuLong-SE distills past execution traces into a three-tier memory store governed by ground-truth anchoring, disconfirmation filtering, held-out rollback, and anti-leakage retrieval. On the 158-task EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark, the full task-level harness, with self-evolution disabled, achieves 92.4% pass@1 and outperforms ZhuLong on all five tested LLM backbones. On a harder instance-disjoint test set, self-evolution from the bare configuration surpasses a human-crafted-experience baseline by 2.5 percentage points (80.0% vs. 77.5% pass@1).
title: Self-Evolving Beyond Human-Crafted Experience for EDA Scripting

summary: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.
title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory

summary: The MoT virtual environment, called the Metaverse of Things (MoT), combines machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) to offer significant business opportunities in various sectors such as entertainment, healthcare, and education. In addition to its benefits, the MoT poses risks to privacy and security through unauthorized access, which threatens trustworthiness. While traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS) exist to handle this challenge, they struggle with high-dimensional data and poor interpretability. To address this challenge, the research conducted a thorough analysis of different ML models and proposed the optimal model to secure the MoT environment. The research employed explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the most effective features that contributed to optimal model selection. The research presented an optimal framework combining ML and XAI to safeguard MoT networks from the most recent cyberthreats. The research used three advanced benchmark security datasets: ToN-IoT, CIC-IoT-2023, and BoT-IoT, to examine the XAI-based intrusion detection framework. The XAI-based intrusion detection framework achieved 99.83% accuracy on ToN-IoT and 96.45% on CIC-IoT-2023 using the XGBoost model. On the BoT-IoT dataset, the Random Forest (RF) and Extra Trees (ET) classifiers reached 99.99% accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques used for XAI further enhanced feature relevance and user confidence in the optimal model.
title: Enhancing Metaverse Security using Explainable AI-based Intrusion Detection Framework

summary: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that naïvely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.
title: Inject, Encode, Navigate: Feature-Wise Time Injection for Rectified Flow with Bidirectional Feature Encoding
