summary: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.
title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance

summary: Everything behind the paper "A Memory Note Can Change What a Formal Proof Checks: Experiments with an LLM Verification Agent on OpenTitan" (M. Ghonim and X. Song) except the prover and the models: the registered protocols with their SHA-256 hashes; the decision log; for every campaign, the harness, prompts, plans, stores, trial order, dispatch state and analysis; one directory per trial with the executed run.tcl , parsed verdicts, licence receipt, property and assumption files, the store written back and a transcript summary; the agent-free controls, mutation-gate reports and formal-coverage runs; and every generator with the tables and macro files it writes. One command regenerates every number in the paper without an EDA licence ( rm paper/manuscript/tables/*; bash paper/finalize.sh ; Python 3.9+ with numpy and matplotlib). The manuscript itself is not included. Raw JasperGold logs and consoles are not included; the parsed verdicts and the executed Tcl are. Full trial transcripts are summarised, home-directory paths are replaced by <home>/ , and journal names in the decision log are masked. Re-running the trials needs JasperGold 2026.06, OpenTitan at the commit given in the protocols, and access to the named models. Built from commit <commit> by paper/package_artifact.py ; MANIFEST.txt lists every file and memory-study-artifact.sha256 gives the archive's checksum.
title: Artifact: A Memory Note Can Change What a Formal Proof Checks: Experiments With an LLM Verification Agent on OpenTitan

summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

summary: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.
title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?

summary: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation

However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.

summary: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

summary: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?

summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.
title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.

summary: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention

summary: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents

summary: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. summary: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce Low-Rank Multimarginal Optimal Transport (LRMOT), which restricts transport plans to tensors with bounded multilinear rank, providing a compact and structured representation of multimarginal couplings. This structure enables efficient algorithms with a low memory footprint. We establish approximation bounds for the resulting low-rank formulations and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed algorithms substantially reduce computational time while achieving solutions with low transport cost.
title: Low-Rank Tensor Representations for Efficient Multimarginal Optimal Transport

summary: Galois Shadows in the Spectrum of Quadratic Tensor Contractions: A Note on Associativity Indices and Exact Arithmetic over ℚ(φ) C. J Tully Independent Researcher Engineer TTG-41/42 Cryptosystems ·   Australia 23 November 2026 Abstract This note records a precise adjustment to a quasi-associativity index (QEI) together with an independent spectral observation concerning the quadratic contraction of a 52-component tensor. The revised index QEI′ is bounded in [0, 1] by the triangle inequality and differs from the original only by a constant rescaling. The spectral result shows that the contraction decomposes into a pair of conjugate eigenvalues in ℚ(√5), each of multiplicity two, whose sum recovers a previously noted integer invariant. The appearance of the Galois conjugate pair inside the tensor’s own spectrum is recorded and verified. Both contributions are acknowledged.

summary: This record provides the Actual Vapor Pressure (AVP) component of the H igh-resolution ( d aily and 1 km) atmospheric M oisture I ndex C ollection over China (HiMIC-Daily) . AVP is essential for water vapor transport calculations and complements the other five moisture indicators in the collection. The dataset was generated using the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) algorithm for spatial reconstruction, integrating meteorological station observations with multiple high-resolution datasets, including land surface temperature (MOD11A1/MYD11A1), land cover (MCD12Q1), topographic variables (MERIT DEM), column water vapor (MCD19A2), vapor pressure (TerraClimate), 2-m temperature and dew point temperature (ERA5-Land), and population density (WorldPop). LightGBM was selected for its higher efficiency and robustness compared to other tree-based algorithms. For AVP, the reconstruction achieves an R ² of 0.989, MAE of 0.677 hPa, and RMSE of 0.933 hPa. The product has a spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km and a daily temporal resolution, covering China from January 1, 2003, to December 31, 2025. The dataset is organized into annual NetCDF files, one file per year, with daily data indexed by the time coordinate. The dataset is referenced to the World Geodetic System (WGS) 1984 Coordinate System. Comprehensive information on file naming and other specifications is documented in the "README.pdf". The HiMIC-Daily dataset is organized into annual NetCDF files, with one file per indicator per year. summary: The Hi gh resolution ( d aily and 1km) atmospheric M oisture I ndex C ollection over the China  ( HiMIC- Daily ) provides a comprehensive dataset of six moisture indicators: Relative Humidity (RH, %), Dew Point Temperature (DPT, °C), Actual Vapor Pressure (AVP, hPa), Mixing Ratio (MR, g kg -1 ), Specific Humidity (SH, g kg -1 ), and Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD, hPa). These indicators are essential for characterizing atmospheric moisture conditions: RH has been widely used in human comfort assessment and weather forecasting; AVP is essential for water vapor transport calculations; VPD serves as a key indicator of moisture stress on vegetation and fire risk; DPT has been applied in frost prediction and evaporative cooler design; MR has been used for hydrograph separation and identification of groundwater recharge sources; and SH is crucial for total precipitable water and longwave radiation assessments. To generate this dataset, the study adopts the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) algorithm for spatial reconstruction by integrating meteorological station observations with multiple high-resolution datasets, including land surface temperature (MOD11A1/MYD11A1), land cover (MCD12Q1), topographic variables (MERIT DEM), column water vapor (MCD19A2), vapor pressure (TerraClimate), 2‑m temperature and DPT (ERA5‑Land), and population density (WorldPop). LightGBM is selected for its higher efficiency and robustness compared to other tree‑based algorithms. The dataset demonstrates high accuracy with R ²/MAE/RMSE values of RH (0.877, 4.849 %, 6.520 %), AVP (0.989, 0.677 hPa, 0.933 hPa), VPD (0.906, 0.983 hPa, 1.411 hPa), DPT (0.985, 1.120 ℃, 1.608 ℃), MR (0.988, 0.459 g kg -1 , 0.633 g kg -1 ), and SH (0.988, 0.451 g kg -1 , 0.620 g kg -1 ). With a high spatial resolution of 1 km × 1 km and a daily temporal resolution, this dataset covers China from January 1, 2003, to December 31, 2025. HiMIC-Daily provides a reliable data foundation for research in meteorology, ecology, environmental science, and human health.  The dataset is organized into annual NetCDF files, each containing daily data indexed by the time coordinate. To optimize storage and maintain precision, each index is scaled by a factor of 100 and converted to 16-bit integer (int16) format prior to archiving, with original values restored by dividing the stored data by 100. The dataset is referenced to the World Geodetic System (WGS) 1984 Coordinate System, and comprehensive information on file naming and other specifications is documented in the “README.pdf”. summary: Hilberg's hypothesis states that block entropy of text grows as hn + An^beta. We connect maximal entropy random walk (Parry) sequence ensembles, ANS-like equipartition of surprisal, Santa Fe processes with an HCR-motivated Gaussian world model, and LLM-based entropy measurements into a picture of text as progressive revelation of a world state. Calibration on Santa Fe processes shows that PPMd compression slopes barely respond to the true Hilberg exponent, while a word-level Pitman-Yor coder recovers it but measures lexicon occupancy. A permutation-calibrated lexical index detects word-order effects in anthologies. For compression, a self-contained coder cannot remove a genuine An^beta source term; explicit word and recency models reduce predictive log loss by 1.5-3.4% over a context-mixing base, and shared dictionaries pay off mainly for small independently coded documents. Supplementary files contain all code and results.
tags: Hilberg's law; Zipf's law; Heaps' law; Santa Fe process; maximal entropy random walk; asymmetric numeral systems; hierarchical correlation reconstruction; text compression; neural scaling laws
title: Hilberg's law as learning a world state: implications and limits for text compression

summary: Reconstructing an editable music score requires musical events, sung text and the instructions that organise them on the page. Existing recognition targets often omit part of this information, while direct MusicXML prediction repeats substantial structural markup. We introduce Cecilia, a compact representation of canonicalised MusicXML that retains musical content, lyric attachments and layout instructions. Cecilia-OMR predicts this representation through metadata and measure-bounded music segments from shared visual memory. A learned count head determines the number of output segments. Across paired complete scores under a common tokeniser, the ratio of mean MusicXML to Cecilia sequence lengths is 27.73. Cecilia-OMR outperforms Legato 2 on Camera String Quartets and both Lieder conditions, with a four-condition OpenScore macro normalised edit distance of 0.2232 against 0.2998. Separate evaluations of lyrics, notation trees and rendered layout reveal complementary aspects of reconstruction and quantify the contribution of layout instructions. Training-stage, reward and candidate-selection studies further examine how recognition changes across model adaptation and decoding.
title: Cecilia: Towards Layout-Inclusive Optical Music Recognition

summary: Abstract This integrative research synthesis develops a candidate relational architecture across quantum foundations, physical history, persistent organization, relational time, and the recovery problem for spacetime. Its method is unification by decomposition : constraint, weighting, singular factualization, and retention are treated as distinct operations with distinct evidential burdens. Key Analyses & Framework Quantum Foundations & Entanglement: The double slit separates coherent alternatives, receiver-defined effects, Born weighting, and the $n = 1$ record. The Sorkin hierarchy and reconstruction literature delimit what is already formally known and leave open the physical motivation for second-order weighting. Entanglement is analyzed through a missing-loss audit: spatial routing, operational differentiation, and dynamical decoupling do not by themselves demonstrate ontological severance of a nonfactorizable joint state. Ontology & Event-Factualization: Primitive factualization is treated as a technical event-ontology posit, with fundamental agency as a stronger interpretive hypothesis (alongside objective stochasticity, Bohmian completion, Everettian branching, and collapse dynamics as comparison classes). A present-state coherence veto prevents absolute factualization while coherence-bearing degrees of freedom remain causally accessible to future interactions in which their phase relation can again matter. Retained factual consequences provide the bridge to physical history, memory, differential persistence, and increasingly organized agency. Downstream Physics & Empirical Testing: Transition and stabilization are treated as relational roles of one field-energy reality rather than new substances. The synthesis incorporates a fully exposed prospective transition-stabilization kill test in a driven liquid-to-vapor system and preserves planetary, gravitational, and spacetime extensions as explicitly conditional research branches. Methodological Stance: No universal master equation is claimed. The program is a structured ontology, audit, and research architecture whose modules must earn mathematical or empirical closure independently. Philosophical Extensions (Dual-Aspect Hypothesis): A further dual-aspect factualist hypothesis, with a panexperiential extension, distinguishes the publicly accessible objective face of factual processes from a minimally subjective first-person-like aspect associated with irreducible factual resolution. This is presented as a stronger ontological interpretation, not as an experimentally established consequence. It does not identify an elementary subjective aspect with a subject, mind, or consciousness. Complex biological agency is treated as potentially nested and hierarchically integrated, while the combination of elementary subjective loci into a unified subject is left as an explicit unresolved problem.
title: Unification by Decomposition: The Dualverse — From Quantum Factualization and Physical Memory to Hierarchical Individuality and Spacetime

summary: This repository provides the complete replication package for the paper "The Impact of Change Scope on Incremental Software Delivery: A Multi-Host Comparison of Monolithic and Microservice Architectures", accepted for presentation at the Lean and Agile Software Development (LASD) track of the 42nd ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC 2027). The study investigates how the scope of incremental software changes relates to local build-and-redeployment time in monolithic and microservice architectures. Two functionally equivalent applications implemented in Python and FastAPI were evaluated using six change scenarios involving one, two, or three services. The experiment was conducted on two Windows 11 hosts using Docker Desktop and WSL2, producing 240 observations. Repository contents: Complete benchmark source code and Docker Compose configurations. PowerShell scripts for experiment execution. Original measurement datasets from both experimental hosts. Python scripts for statistical analysis and result reproduction. Reproducible figures and descriptive statistics. Additional interaction analysis, bootstrap confidence intervals, and sensitivity checks. Supplementary material documenting the experimental environment, measurement procedure, results, and threats to validity. The repository includes instructions for reproducing the analyses and verifying the reported results. Scope and limitations: The measurements cover local application building and redeployment rather than the complete CI/CD pipeline. The experimental design does not fully separate architectural effects from container-management overhead or scenario-specific characteristics. Additional statistical analyses should therefore be interpreted as exploratory and conditional on the tested scenarios. Version: 1.0.0 License: MIT License.

summary: This repository provides supporting research code for the manuscript "LoRA-Based Diffusion Data Augmentation for Underwater Garbage Detection: An Empirical Study with YOLOv8s", submitted to Scientific Reports. The study investigates whether class-specific Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides additional benefits over ControlNet-conditioned synthetic data augmentation for underwater garbage detection using YOLOv8s. The archive includes selected Python source code for paired synthetic-image generation workflows, data and annotation quality assurance, detector-training controls, validation procedures, and exploratory Kernel Inception Distance (KID) analysis. The experiments use a frozen grouped dataset partition with 3,566 training images, 997 validation images, 471 test images, and 96 excluded images. The full-data comparison evaluates real-only training (A), ControlNet-only augmentation (E), and ControlNet-plus-LoRA augmentation (F) using five matched detector seeds. A separate 50%-training-data sensitivity analysis is evaluated on the validation set only. The released archive contains supporting code, configuration information, integrity checksums, and selected aggregate results. Original datasets, model checkpoints, and some historical execution records are not redistributed. Certain historical code versions have unresolved provenance, and the archive does not constitute a fully verified, one-command reproduction of the complete experiments. The experimental findings do not establish a consistent incremental detection benefit from LoRA over matched ControlNet-only augmentation.

summary: This dataset brings together five open data sources to study how users of Indonesian mobile telemedicine apps infer whether a human doctor or an automated agent is answering them, and how that perceived source attribution relates to trust and to the place of human care. It combines Google Play reviews of four telemedicine apps (Alodokter, Halodoc, KlikDokter, YesDok), expert-labelled doctor answers from Alodokter, interview quotes from generative-AI users, national context indicators from the World Bank, and generative-AI-era app reviews. No data were collected from scratch: every row is a coded extract of an openly licensed source, and the provenance of each row is recorded. The sources are kept in separate sheets by design: user reviews, doctors' messages and AI-user interviews offer three vantage points on the same phenomenon, and interpretation should remain tied to each source (comparison at the level of constructs, not pooled records). The sources also cover different periods, so differences between them may reflect time as well as vantage point. The workbook contains a README sheet, a source register with SHA-256 checksums, five coded data sheets, a codebook, value labels and a reliability record. Six sheets document the researchers' validation codes, recoding checks and reconciliation decisions, and seven further sheets report the blind post-revision holdout, the explicit or implicit classification of human attributions, agreement per category with bootstrap intervals, confusion matrices, the trust tables with and without platform-related reviews, and the coding of message cues that links the reviews to the doctor answers. Each sheet is also provided as a UTF-8 CSV file, together with five Python analysis scripts and the JASP 0.99.0 outputs that replicate the main estimates. The researchers set the codebook, categories, and keyword rules from the study's theoretical framework. An AI tool (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) was used only to apply that codebook in an initial labelling pass over Sources A and E. Reliability was examined in three steps. First, two researchers independently coded a stratified random sample of 100 Source A reviews without seeing the initial labels; before reconciliation they agreed on relevance for 98 reviews (κ = .79, bootstrap 95% CI .38 to 1.00, a prevalence effect; PABAK = .96) and, on the 94 reviews both judged relevant, κ = .93 for source attribution, .90 for trust basis and 1.00 for trust direction. The initial AI-assisted labels agreed poorly with the researchers (κ = .12 to .53) because two definitions had been read more narrowly, so the researchers' judgement was taken as the reference standard and the codebook was revised (relevance now covers platform communication; HUMAN_AFFIRMED now covers implicit attribution to the app's doctor). Second, all 1,248 Source A reviews were recoded under the revised rules and every changed row was checked by a researcher (352 rows on relevance, 7 corrected; 245 rows on attribution, 18 corrected); this check was not blind. Third, both researchers coded a fresh stratified holdout of 113 Source A reviews blind to the final codes and to each other, with rare categories oversampled: κ = .83 (.73 to .91) for source attribution, .86 (.78 to .93) for trust basis, .87 (.78 to .94) for trust direction and .78 for explicit versus implicit human attribution. Every human attribution is classified as explicit or implicit (HUMAN_EXPLICIT_IMPLICIT) so that analyses can exclude attribution inferred from praise. For Source E, one researcher coded 20 relevant reviews without seeing the initial labels (κ = .82 for generative AI attribution; κ = .45 for trust direction, so Source E trust is for descriptive use only). summary: NeoN is a next generation implementation of a CFD core. It leverages the features of modern C++ to implement core routines to efficiently solve PDEs required by CFD frameworks like OpenFOAM, and thus helps to catch up with the rapidly evolving HPC ecosystem. Our design goals are: Platform portable for all CPU and GPU hardware vendors Modular design leveraging the existing simulation software ecosystem like Kokkos, sundials, PETSc, or Ginkgo A domain specific language that encodes complex partial differential equations in a concise yet powerful form Simple adoption within OpenFOAM Target multiphysics simulations and enable simple integration of coupling software like preCICE The v0.3 release adds experimental distributed support, so NeoN runs across multiple MPI ranks and GPUs: processor boundaries with exact processor-face geometry, distributed linear system assembly through Ginkgo, mesh partitioning and GPU-aware halo exchange. NeoN is now usable from Python through nanobind bindings, published as pre-built wheels on PyPI ( pip install neon-pde ) and as conda packages for CPU and CUDA on prefix.dev. It also extends the numerics, with slip and inletOutlet boundary conditions, corrected and limited-corrected face-normal gradients, linearUpwind and backward schemes, tensor primitives, and an expression optimizer that fuses DSL operators. The linear algebra layer gains COO and CSR matrices, cell-based assembly, an L1-norm stopping criterion, merged-Pgm multigrid coarsening with setup reuse, and Umpire memory pools. Integration into OpenFOAM applications is demonstrated in our NeoFOAM repository. A full list of changes can be found in the CHANGELOG.md . Thank you to everyone who contributed to NeoN.
title: NeoN: a modern CFD core

summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed

summary: This dataset provides time-domain OpenFAST simulation results for the NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine mounted on the OC4-DeepCwind semisubmersible floating platform. Version 2.0.1 is a documentation, packaging and reproducibility-evidence correction. The numerical dataset is unchanged from version 2.0.0: it contains 256 Sea-State Groups and 1,280 simulation realisations, comprising the original population of 123 groups / 615 realisations and an extension of 133 groups / 665 realisations. Every group contains five wind-speed cases at 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 m/s. The 32 ZIP archives containing the raw OpenFAST time histories are unchanged. Qualification follows explicit and orthogonal criteria for physical-domain membership and numerical-record integrity. The combined inventory contains 175 Class A groups, 16 Class B groups and 65 Class C groups. Of the 1,280 realisations, 1,279 pass all mandatory C3 checks. The retained realisation G0013-V08 is shorter than the project-specific full-record completeness threshold of 300 Tp; its parent group also independently lies outside the adopted physical domain. The duration criterion is evaluated on the available record from t=0 and does not imply that an initial transient was removed. Version 2.0.1: synchronises the repository documentation with the complete 256-group version-2.0 domain described by the revised Data in Brief article; documents that the archived first-order wave-frequency band is 0.314159–1.570796 rad/s and supplies an explicit table of the 48 groups with nominal Tp <= 4 s, whose requested spectral peak lies above or at the upper cutoff; distinguishes the ROSCO 2.10.1 run-time banner from the ROSCO 2.7.0 tuning-file header; stages byte-identical controller input and rotor-performance-table copies in the worked OpenFAST case directory so that the archived relative paths resolve without changing any controller value; adds the completed representative replay and time-step-sensitivity workflow for Class A case G0195-V07, including scripts, compact evidence, hashes and a reviewed assessment; adds a deterministic finite-record sensitivity analysis over all 27 eligible Class A, C3-valid groups and 81 runs at Tp = 2, 3, 4, 7 or 9 s and V = 7, 9 and 11 m/s. Relative to the 300 Tp mean generated power, the complete-population median absolute differences are 0.1352% at 200 Tp and 0.0662% at 250 Tp; maxima are 0.8091% and 0.3195%, with all runs below 1% and 0.5%, respectively; reconciles all 665 extension manifest paths against the central directories of the 16 unchanged extension archives: 648 exact matches, 16 decimal wind-suffix corrections and one documented G0181 seed-truncation filename match, with zero unresolved paths. summary: The application of the FAIR Principles to digital research objects is near ubiquitous with endorsement by funders, publishers, and research organizations worldwide. At the national level in the UK, this is demonstrated by the draft UKRI Research Data Policy which puts an increased emphasis on FAIR compliance; the latest version of the UKRIO Code of Practice which strengthens expectations around data management and sharing, aligned with the FAIR Principles; the UKRI AI Research and Innovation Strategic Framework , and the UK DSIT AI for Science Strategy policy paper, which emphasise the importance of ensuring that data generated through UKRI-funded research aligns with FAIR to support a modernised, AI-ready data environment. Across the research landscape, statements such as “our repository enables FAIR data” or “this dataset meets the FAIR principles” are increasingly common. Yet, these claims are often difficult to interpret or trust, despite numerous tools having been implemented in the decade since the FAIR principles were launched. As this EOSC report has highlighted, the diversity of assessment approaches, many of them opaque or tool-specific, makes it hard to know what is really being measured, how rigorously, and against which definition(s) of FAIR. The FAIR Institutional Repository Metrics (FIRM) project was established in response to this challenge, with the first phase running from March to August 2026. Led by FAIRsharing and the Oxford University Research Archive (ORA) in collaboration with the UK Reproducibility Network (UKRN) , FIRM is a collaborative initiative to define and test a common FAIR compliance process for institutional repositories participating in the UKRN Open Research Programme. The participating repositories were generalist institutional repositories, supporting research datasets across a wide range of disciplines and research contexts. FIRM builds on the FAIR assessment work undertaken at the University of Oxford for ORA, moving from a single-repository interpretation towards a shared community benchmark. The resulting FAIR Benchmark for Institutional Repository Datasets provides a structured, transparent and reusable framework for assessing dataset metadata against the FAIR Principles. It covers both datasets deposited within an institutional repository and datasets held in external repositories but referenced or catalogued through it.  The FAIR compliance enabled by this benchmark uses a transparent procedure that shifts the focus from assessment to assistance, initially developed by the EOSC OSTrails project, of which the FAIRsharing team is a part. Targeted at developers and technical research support staff, this OSTrails Assessment Interoperability Framework (Assess-IF) provides ‘components’ that enable the definition of what FAIR means in a given context, how it should be measured, and how results should be weighted, interpreted, and potentially improved. FAIRsharing’s rich, manually curated metadata on standards, databases, and policies provide supporting context for the compliance and assistance process. The benchmark translates the high-level FAIR Principles into a set of concrete interpretations for institutional repository datasets covering identifiers, discovery metadata, links between metadata and data, searchability, access protocols, machine-readable metadata, FAIR vocabularies, relationships among research objects, licensing, provenance and recognised standards. The benchmark distinguishes between characteristics delivered through repository infrastructure or policy and those dependent on the metadata supplied for an individual record. This makes it possible to identify where FAIR compliance is effectively provided by the repository and where researchers or repository submission workflows have a role to play. summary: Software and reproducibility archive accompanying the author-review manuscript “Beyond Prediction Accuracy: Local-Slope Robustness in Takagi–Sugeno Fuzzy Models of Airfoil Self-Noise.” The IEEE Access manuscript has not been accepted or published; this DOI will identify the research archive, not the article. The NASA/UCI coefficient-sign certificate uses 1,503 airfoil self-noise observations in 106 operating groups. Selected TSK ridge has 4.166475 dB equal-configuration RMSE and Extra Trees has 2.381 dB. With a 0.1 dB maximum training-prediction change and 1% ridge-objective allowance, 403 of 510 local slope signs are protected and 107 admit strict reversal. A separate 1 dB plus 1% contextual sensitivity gives 135 protected and 375 strict reversals. Neither threshold is a calibrated per-row prediction interval. The R19 Southampton leave-one-geometry-out evaluation has 343 source-normalized rows, 38 spectra and seven geometries; equal-geometry normalized RMSE is 0.059396 for TSK and 0.047839 for Extra Trees. It does not establish absolute-SPL transfer. The UCI concrete source/split sensitivity is exploratory and supports no causal physical conclusion. This deposit contains the two previously SHA-verified EP10 public research ZIPs, 40 task ZIPs of newly reconstructed bootstrap states and audit journals, a SHA-256 manifest, standalone integrity verifier, completion certificate, independent QA record, environment specification and rights/provenance notices. The 40 task archives total 773,361,055 bytes and document 28,000 attempts, 27,998 newly replayed fitted states and two reproduced FCM fitting failures. The original historical fitted-state bytes and first October 2026 UCI download bytes remain unavailable. The new state files must not be described as recovered originals. A full historical-array numerical comparison requires reference arrays outside this public bundle; the included verifier checks all released state hashes, journals, CRCs and failure identities using public files alone. summary: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers

summary: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.
title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids

summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can improve pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies through imagined experiences. However, existing VLA-MBRL methods primarily rely on large-scale image or video generation world models, incurring large computational overhead. Latent world models offer a more efficient alternative but face two challenges: compounding errors during recursive prediction and incompatibility with VLAs' visual input interfaces. In this work, we propose LS-MBPO, a lightweight residual MBRL framework that leverages latent world models to improve upon pretrained VLAs. LS-MBPO introduces two key techniques: (1) Hierarchical Forcing, which combines dense causal supervision with autoregressive feedback to mitigate compounding prediction errors; and (2) Latent Subchunk Rollouts, which leverage action chunks from a frozen VLA policy and a latent residual policy for successive subchunk refinement, bridging the gap between latent imagination and VLA policy execution. We further introduce a Progress-Conditioned Branch-Start Curriculum that progressively shifts rollout starting points from later to earlier task stages, enabling effective policy learning from short imagined rollouts. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and a real-world ALOHA robot show that LS-MBPO achieves superior task performance and training efficiency compared to existing methods.
title: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Subchunk Rollouts in Latent World Models

summary: Data, derived results, and reservoir training code underlying the article "Photo-induced currents and short-term memory for reservoir computing in a ferroelectric semiconductor". The record is organised by figure. It contains: current-voltage characteristics, photocurrent relaxation traces for Ohmic and Schottky contacts, paired-pulse facilitation measurements, the full measured photocurrent response to a 400-pulse light sequence, the light-pulse input sequence, averaged pulse responses grouped by "past" pulse level, recognition accuracy as a function of training-set size for the reservoir / no-reservoir / simulated configurations, a baseline-drift correction, an accuracy-versus- node-count scan, and a double-exponential fit to the photocurrent decay. Both the as-measured data (in physical units) and the plotted/normalized traces are provided, together with the recipes needed to go from one to the other. The reservoir training code (fig3/reservoir_readout.py) is standalone and reproduces the published recognition accuracies from the data in this record. See README.md for the full figure-to-file map, data dictionary, and processing recipes.

summary: This article analyzes the philosophical implications of Alpöge's November 2026 Lean formalization of the Riemann hypothesis, a proof co-developed with AI assistance. While formal verification is established, conceptual understanding remains incomplete. The article introduces "hybrid conceptual authority" to describe how conceptual contribution and justificatory authority diverge in AI-assisted mathematics. Drawing on philosophy of chemistry's model of explanatory autonomy, it proposes a four-dimensional framework verification, reconstruction, attribution, and interpretation for evaluating epistemic practice in proof production.
title: Hybrid Conceptual Authority in AI-Assisted Mathematics

summary: Description This dataset documents the participation of female musicians in European concert life between 1750 and 1800. It records individual performers alongside detailed information on their appearances in public concerts, enabling the reconstruction of collaborative performance networks. By cross-referencing musicians and shared concert events, the dataset captures patterns of co-performance and professional interaction within Europe's musical scene.   Developed as part of a broader doctoral research project on women’s roles in eighteenth-century European music, the dataset integrates biographical data with performance records. The data is structured as an Excel database partitioned into functional sheets, including Nodes, Interactions, and Edges, which are optimized for direct import into Gephi network visualization software. Each node entry includes detailed attribute columns such as names, nationalities, roles, musical competencies (e.g., composer, singer, instrument, teacher), and documented travel corridors.   The database forms the direct foundation for network visualizations, in which musicians and associated entities are represented as nodes and their shared performances are represented as edges. These structured sheets allow for the direct analysis of the density, mobility, and structure of professional relationships, with data pre-formatted to easily reflect the frequency of collaboration.   Methodology The dataset was constructed through systematic analysis of primary sources and historical concert records, supplemented by secondary literature. Musicians were included based on the availability of sufficient biographical and performance data to support meaningful analysis. Relationships were established through documented co-appearances in concerts.   Limitations The dataset reflects the uneven survival of historical records and prioritizes musicians with sufficiently documented careers. As such, it does not represent a complete census of performers active in London during this period.   Data Integrity and Usage: This record contains original Excel databases developed as part of a doctoral dissertation. summary: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity

summary: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,μ\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control

summary: Continual learning requires a model to learn multiple new tasks sequentially while retaining performance on previous tasks. Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.
title: Dually Constrained Parameter Projection for Continual Learning

Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.

summary: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.
title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.
title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.
title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM

summary: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.
title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation

summary: Students may have access to a convincing mathematical explanation without being able to reconstruct or adapt it. A course must provide opportunities to develop that understanding while keeping the work sustainable for students and teachers. This article develops a methodology for service mathematics in which a question ledger guides both course authoring and classroom decisions. Course-relative didactic units organise explanatory purposes, prerequisites and connections, initially calibrated by a five-to-seven-minute expert account. Teaching combines preparation, student exposition and supported repair with substantial teacher exposition and synthesis. Their allocation changes with the topic, audience and conditions of teaching. Compression and recovery explain how developed constructions become reusable while their grounds remain accessible. Three analyses from mathematics for computing-full Sudoku encoding, grayscale projection and a software failure contract-show how contrasting cases guide explanation and revision. The practice-informed contribution connects coherent course design with adaptable teaching and manageable preparation, and identifies questions for evaluating learning, participation and sustained teacher effort.
title: Questions, Explanation and Synthesis in Service Mathematics: Course Design with Didactic Units and Hybrid Teaching
