summary: Abstract Abstract The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. summary: Background: Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) are valuable models for cancer research and precision medicine, but variable establishment efficiency limits their utility. The tissue characteristics that may help identify suitable specimens before culture remain insufficiently defined. We aimed to characterize tissue features associated with gastric cancer PDO establishment and develop an integrated pre-culture predictive model. Results: We analyzed 59 treatment-naive gastric cancer specimens cultured under a standardized protocol, comprising a training cohort (n = 31) and an independent validation cohort (n = 28). PDOs were successfully established, defined as stable expansion for at least three passages, from 48.4% and 53.6% of specimens, respectively. In the training cohort, all five specimens with a tumor area proportion ≤20% failed to establish PDOs. A collagen fiber-to-tumor area ratio ≥1 was associated with establishment failure in both cohorts (training, P = 0.043; validation, P = 0.013). Bulk RNA sequencing of 26 histologically eligible training specimens identified reduced immune-effector programs in the success group, consistent with immune-cell deconvolution and CD8 immunohistochemistry. An integrated model combining qPCR expression of LINC00886, TP63, UTS2, and ZBED2 with the collagen fiber-to-tumor area ratio and CD8-positive cell infiltration achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.916 in the training cohort and 0.840 in the independent validation cohort. Signature-based analysis of TCGA-STAD further supported the reproducibility of the success-associated immune-low molecular phenotype. Conclusions: Gastric cancer PDO establishment was associated with the histological, molecular, and immune characteristics of the starting tissue. An integrated model combining a four-gene qPCR signature with stromal collagen burden and CD8-positive cell infiltration showed discriminatory performance in an independent cohort. These findings provide a practical framework for pre-culture specimen assessment using accessible laboratory and pathology assays, pending prospective and multicenter validation.
title: Stromal, immune and molecular features predict gastric cancer organoid establishment

summary: This paper focused on the efficiency of Education Resource Centres  (ERC) as a vital educational ingredient to teaching-learning process anywhere in the  world especially in Nigeria. ERC helps in the training of in-service teachers as well  as professionals. Taking students to ERC for practical purpose reduces verbalism and  abstraction making discovered facts stick firmly to the memory of audience.  However, there is an outcry in the state of ERCs in Nigeria as teaching-learning  machines, tools, gadgets and equipments in the country’s ERCs today is no longer  supporting theories and research due to their deficiencies to measure accurately what  they purport to measure in accordance to the standard metric unit (SI unit) where it  claims to exist. The purpose of this study therefore, was to examine the efficiency of  ERC in improving quality education towards sustainable national development in  Nigeria. The paper is therefore discussed under the following headings: the concept  of ERC, education for sustainable national development, quality education, goals and  objectives in Education, the place of ERC in sustainable national development,  present status of ERC in Nigeria, the taxonomy of ERCs and their potent functions,  the factors affecting the establishment of ERC in Nigeria which include fund for the  acquisition of modern teaching-learning machines that supports modern day theories  and practices, poor policy or lack of policy implementation and practice were  exermined. Five solutions were suggested which includes: Positive educational  policies should be fully implemented and Government at all levels in partnership with  hosting communities should set up proactive monitoring team that will supervise and  evaluate the procurement and daily operational routine of the centre. The paper  concludes by making six recommendations which include; the Government should  make adequate funds available for the day-to-day running of ERC Centres and also,  ensures that the funds are judiciously utilized on what it was funded.
title: EDUCATION RESOURCE CENTRE (ERC): FOR IMPROVING QUALITY EDUCATION AND SUSTAINABLE NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT IN NIGERIA

summary: This fifth volume in the KSCCN Series advances from architectural resolution of the Palimpsestic Security Trilemma to operational closure of residual risk and contestable institutional deployment of Dual-Core Governed Palimpsest (DC-GP) systems. Three residual risks left open by Volume IV are addressed: post-quantum harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure on multi-decade Residual Track payloads, authorized-action residual risk inside legitimate tool scopes, and the empirical validation of topological and out-of-band controls under adaptive adversaries. Formal extensions quantify post-quantum key-migration thresholds, authorized-action Pareto frontiers, and sheaf-restriction calibration on real agent trajectories. PalimpsestSec-Bench results, leave-one-out ablations, and institutional Dual-Core deployment dossiers (extending Bangladesh and Estonia analyses) demonstrate measurable reduction in Expected Free Energy paralysis windows and switching costs. The volume supplies the practical baseline for contestable Dual-Core statecraft across the 2026–2035 bifurcation. KSCCN Working Paper, Volume V, Series on Critical AI & Digital Sovereignty Studies, November 2026 (5 pages). Continues Volume IV, Palimpsestic Sovereignty: The Security Trilemma, Data Warfare, and Data Security in the Long-Horizon Agentic Era (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24486850), and builds on Governing Palimpsestic Memory (Volume III, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24477507), Palimpsestic Memory for Long-Horizon Agents (Volume II, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24477488), Epistemic Architectures of Agent Memory (Volume I, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24471183) and Data Marauders and Organised Data Warriors for Hire in the Liquid Order (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24425707).

summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.
title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries

summary: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.
title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models

summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models

summary: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.
title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning

summary: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.
title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines

summary: Speech brain-computer interfaces aim to restore communication by translating neural activity into text, yet end-to-end decoders have historically trailed cascaded systems in accuracy. We introduce a Multi-Agent System for BraIn-to-Text (MAS-BIT), the first multi-agent framework for end-to-end brain-to-text decoding from intracortical recordings. MAS-BIT coordinates three specialized agents: a neural agent that interprets continuous neural representations, a phonetic agent that decodes soft phoneme posteriors, and an arbitration agent that integrates their complementary evidence with direct access to neural representations to generate the final transcription. The expert agents communicate with the arbiter through token-embedding-based latent communication, constructing continuous messages as probability-weighted combinations of token embeddings. These messages retain alternative token hypotheses and provide a differentiable interface through which sentence-level supervision jointly trains the neural encoders and specialized agents across participants. MAS-BIT achieves state-of-the-art end-to-end decoding performance on the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, with word error rates of 6.929% on '24 and 3.606% on the '25 public test set (3.892% on the private test set). These results surpass the published BIT cascade on the '25 public set and narrow the gap on '24, without ensembling independently trained models or using external language-model rescoring.
title: MAS-BIT: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-End BraIn-to-Text Decoding

summary: Semantic occupancy perception has emerged as a promising paradigm for jointly modeling 3D scene geometry and semantic information. However, this unified representation cannot compensate for missing information caused by occlusion and sensor coverage. Multi-agent cooperation alleviates this limitation, but information from different agents is not equally useful across spatial regions. Meanwhile, feature representations from each agent form the basis of reliable multi-agent fusion. Cross?modal fusion constructs such representations by integrating complementary semantic and geometric information. Despite this complementarity, jointly establishing reliable 3D correspondence across agents and preserving modality-specific structures remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose CoopOcc, which performs cooperative 3D semantic occupancy perception through multi-agent and cross-modal fusion. CoopOcc uses ego?query cross-agent attention (EQCA) to selectively aggregate aligned features across agents, and anchor-based bidirectional feature interaction (ABFI) for cross-modal exchange at matched coordinates. We further construct SemanticVVSim, a simulation dataset, and establish a unified benchmark. For simulation-to-real transfer, we propose confidence-aware hierarchical occupancy and relational distillation (CHORD). CoopOcc performs best overall among ten evaluated methods on SemanticVVSim. On Occ3D-nuScenes, CHORD improves performance using knowledge from SemanticVVSim. The code is available at https://github.com/LOTEAT/CoopOcc.
title: CoopOcc: Cooperative 3D Semantic Occupancy Perception via Multi-Agent and Cross-Modal Fusion

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming recommender systems from conventional preference matching toward reasoning-driven and explainable decision-making. Multi-agent collaboration further advances this paradigm by distributing recommendation reasoning across specialized agents. However, existing frameworks rarely assess the reliability of intermediate reasoning during collaboration, allowing erroneous judgments to propagate across agents and ultimately degrade recommendation quality. To address this issue, we propose Multi-Agent Debate-based Recommendation (MADRec), an evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning. MADRec consists of three coordinated modules. First, the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) module enables an Interaction Agent and a Semantic Agent to analyze interaction signals and content-level semantic signals from complementary perspectives, generating diverse recommendation judgments through structured debate. Second, the Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning (EG-RAR) module grounds the Semantic Agent's reasoning in item-level evidence and refines candidate scores by assessing how well the evidence supports the corresponding semantic claims. Third, the Judge-based Ranking Calibration (JRC) module leverages debate-derived reliability cues to adaptively calibrate interaction-based and semantic ranking results for the final recommendation. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MADRec consistently outperforms competitive baselines and enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning.
title: MADRec: Reliable Multi-Agent Reasoning with Evidence-Grounded Debate for Recommendation

summary: Multimodal Person Re-Identification (ReID) exploits complementary identity cues from different sensing modalities to mitigate the performance degradation caused by challenging imaging conditions. Existing methods typically estimate Modality Reliability at the query level, making it difficult to identify conflicting inputs that retain normal visual quality but correspond to an incorrect identity. Such inputs may receive high confidence, promote irrelevant gallery candidates, and lead to negative fusion. To address this issue, we propose SafeRank-ReID, a candidate-conditioned safe re-ranking framework for Multimodal Person Re-Identification (ReID). To capture the varying support of the same modality for different candidates, we introduce a candidate-conditioned evidence arbitration mechanism that integrates unimodal retrieval evidence, input quality, and cross-modal consistency to estimate trust and conflict logits for each modality-candidate pair. Together, these logits contribute to the normalized modality weights, allowing support strength to vary across modalities and candidates while reducing the contribution of potentially unreliable evidence. A candidate-set refinement module subsequently applies self-attention to jointly model candidate representations and predicts residual scores from their competitive relations, thereby refining the initial fused ranking. For fusion results that remain uncertain after refinement, a query-level fallback gate estimates an interpolation coefficient from the overall conflict level and cross-modal uncertainty, adaptively combining the fused scores with those of the most reliable unimodal branch. Experiments on RGBNT201 and MSVR310 show that SafeRank-ReID maintains competitive clean-input retrieval while improving robustness to Identity Conflicts across person and vehicle benchmarks.
title: SafeRank-ReID: Candidate-Conditioned Re-Ranking under Identity Conflicts for Multimodal Person Re-Identification

summary: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.
title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction

summary: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
title: Skill-Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion Policies

summary: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models

summary: The string-averaging (SA) method is a versatile algorithmic scheme for solving feasibility-seeking problems. It partitions the index set of all constraints into subsets of indices, called strings, allowing the user to apply operators successively along each string separately, and thus in parallel. The end-points of all such string operations are convexly combined to create the next iterate. Due to its flexible framework, SA is not restricted solely to this procedure; however, this characteristic applies only to the simultaneous step, while the sequential one is restricted to operator compositions. To permit alternative strategies in the latter, a novel algorithmic structure termed the Skeletal SA is introduced. Although its convergence is not established, it serves as a foundational "parent" structure that unveils unexamined SA algorithmic structures, as well as other known methods, obscured by standard compositions. To demonstrate the benefit of adopting the Skeletal SA framework over the standard SA scheme, we investigate a new approach, where instead of passing sequentially over each string via compositions, we employ a remotest-set-control-like strategy on every string by identifying the index of the operator farthest from the current iterate, and invoking it. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. However, remotest operator control SA (ROC-SA) methods have remained unexamined in this context.
title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking

title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking

summary: Persistent object maps must incorporate new surfaces while retaining valid identities and correcting earlier associations. We present a map-revision module that separates historical identity changes from new-surface admission. Proposed merges are tested against shared and separate mask explanations across views; a merge is allowed only if its evidence margin remains positive after removing any one observed frame. New measured points are assigned through local identity competition, with a mask witness and a seed-frame stability check. On two preselected KITTI-360 windows, the fixed method increases mean building/car instance AP50:90 from 17.259 to 18.762 under a local evaluation protocol. Controlled output interventions attribute the gains to fragment consolidation, protection against harmful overwrites, and local assignment of new points. Four additional spatial holdouts increase mean AP from 20.263 to 23.171, although unconditional revision is slightly higher at 23.251. The extra seed-frame check yields no AP gain over nearest-seed assignment in either set. A 330-frame garage recording demonstrates offline integration with LiDAR--inertial--visual odometry. These results identify where observation-supported revision improves object maps and where conservative decisions still limit recovery.

summary: Abstract Abstract The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. We follow this one synthetic data stream through the whole construction and back to the decision (Studies 83–90, held-out seeds, every check pre-registered and frozen with SHA-256). The data give a credal fibre and its probability bands; the margins give toric chambers and walls; the margins also set the mirror potential of the degree-six del Pezzo surface, whose thimbles form an exceptional collection in its Fukaya–Seidel category. The experiment is a carrier for a realistic decision problem, not a claim about seeding. What the example verifies. Each layer is tested on held-out data: (i) credal walls lie on the chamber walls, while Stokes events are mutations; (ii) margin-order ties are collision walls where two orthogonal objects swap, confirmed at the Floer level on 10 of 12 brackets (the other two, one not audited and one with a non-minimal representative, stay in the record); (iii) a full twist of the potential acts as the Serre functor; (iv) the support region of a vector-valued hypothesis is cut out by Markov moves on the table; (v) poisoning that preserves the margins cannot move a credal decision, though it flips conventional ones (6 flips against 0); (vi) caustics, where two critical points merge, are A2 folds acting by σ±3. What it does not verify. Nothing here concerns real data or whether seeding works. Three problems remain open after a registered repair, with their checks recorded as failed: chamber reuse after one Stokes event, the control bracket of Study 83 (and the held-out bracket with the same defect), and coherence of the lift on a full slice. Every failed check is kept in the record. Categorical status. In Seidel’s framework the thimbles generate and the identification of their category with the derived category of the surface is proved (lemma 262, corollary 263). Only 1 the wrapped version in the sense of Ganatra–Pardon–Shende still rests on two steps that are argued, not certified. The rest of the note. Part I identifies the state selected by a toric potential as the lexico- graphic max–min point, up to O(1/ log(1/T )), and writes the K¨ahler dictionary in probabilistic language. Part II reads it on contingency tables, where one count of data can cross a wall. Part III treats composition, contextuality, the value of information and poisone
title: Conditioned States as Toric K¨ahler Data A companion note to "Probability, Context and Differentiation: The Layers"

summary: Data, codebook, prompt, model outputs and code for a study of Chile's General Rule (NCG) No. 461 and corporate climate risk disclosure. The package contains a 20-item Climate Risk Disclosure Index (CRDI) aligned with IFRS S2 for 370 annual reports of 54 non-financial firms listed in Santiago (fiscal years 2019–2025), coded by a large language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) in three independent runs with page-level quotations; a human audit of the model's evidence for 20 reports (400 report-items); a blind manual recoding of 10 of those reports (200 report-items) and the adjudication of the disagreements; the firm-year panel with market and accounting variables; and the scripts that collect the reports, code them and estimate all difference-in-differences, event-study and fixed-effects models. Version 1.2.0 adds the blind recoding and adjudication (coding/blind_validation), with a script that reproduces the agreement statistics reported in the article.
title: Replication package for: Does Mandatory Integrated Reporting Improve Climate Risk Disclosure? Evidence from Chile's Staggered Mandate

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation over book-length documents must locate a small, coherent set of passages inside tens of thousands of tokens. Flat dense retrieval ignores document structure; RAPTOR instead builds a hierarchy by recursively clustering and summarizing with a language model. We study a complementary design that exploits the native structure of a document: a two-level retriever that (i) selects chapters with a hybrid BM25+dense match over chapter recaps, (ii) runs a chapter-filtered dense search, and (iii) expands top passages into contiguous, section-aware spans under a token budget, plus content-hash-gated delta ingestion to keep the index cheap to update. We evaluate on five public-domain books (113 chapter-localization queries) and on QuALITY and NovelQA (200K+ token novels). In-house, we find a seed-stable precision/ranking tradeoff: with section expansion off, hierarchical retrieval returns a higher fraction of chunks from the correct chapter (+3.3pp, Wilcoxon p=0.014); with expansion on, ranking improves (MRR, p=0.040). Accuracy differences are not significant. On QuALITY, hierarchical retrieval beats flat top-k (81.0% vs 70.4%, p=0.0019) and matches the full article (p=0.74). On NovelQA, hierarchical and flat retrieval are statistically tied (55.7% vs 56.8%, p=0.24); hierarchy helps aggregation questions while flat wins on localized facts. Against a faithful RAPTOR baseline we find a complementary tradeoff, not superiority. Delta ingestion reuses 94 to 99.7% of embeddings on incremental edits. We make no claim of semantic chapter-boundary inference and scope claims to English narrative prose.
title: Structure-Exploiting Hierarchical Retrieval for Long Narrative Documents: A Precision-Oriented Alternative to Learned Abstraction Trees

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.
title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever

summary: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG

summary: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. summary: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.
title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve

summary: Q-FORCE reproducibility archive for an exploratory benchmark of fixed four-qubit feature maps across eight observational time series and three direct forecasting horizons. summary: Differentially private zeroth-order optimization (DPZO) is a promising approach for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning, offering exceptional memory efficiency. However, its utility is highly sensitive to the clipping threshold $C$, a key DP-specific hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between noise injection and clipping bias. Existing DPZO methods typically tune $C$ by repeatedly evaluating candidate values and reporting the best result, which is computationally expensive and incurs additional privacy cost that must be accounted for under DP. Designing a practical DP procedure for selecting $C$ in DPZO is challenging because no fixed choice performs well across settings, straightforward search-based strategies suffer from poor utility and efficiency, and existing clipping-selection methods for DPSGD do not transfer well to DPZO due to its fundamentally different error regime. In this paper, we propose AutoClip-DPZO, a practical DP method that automatically and efficiently selects $C$ for DPZO. Our key idea is to avoid fine-tuning-based search by reducing clipping selection to a private quantile estimation problem, where the target quantile depends only on public privacy and training parameters. To derive this selection rule, we develop a novel characterization of DPZO error as a function of $C$ that captures both noise variance and clipping bias while remaining accurate and easy to optimize. Experiments show that AutoClip-DPZO achieves utility comparable to that obtained with the optimal $C$, while avoiding repeated fine-tuning-based search and incurring negligible additional overhead. Moreover, AutoClip-DPZO does not rely on sensitive hyperparameters.
title: AutoClip-DPZO: Practical Private Clipping Selection for Differentially Private Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

summary: We propose the Flow Matching Surface Neural Operator (FMSNO), which combines learning a shared map from irregular surface meshes to a regular two-dimensional grid on the sphere and training a neural operator on the regular grid. Constructing a separate map for each new geometry can dominate inference time on large meshes. We initially pretrain the mapping by flow matching using precomputed optimal transport maps as targets and then continue its training using combined geometry and CFD objectives. We apply it to unseen geometries in a single forward pass. The learned flow deforms the surface points, and we project its endpoints onto the sphere. We then splat geometric features onto the spherical grid, apply a neural operator (we tested both Fourier and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and interpolate its output back to the surface. For a mesh with $N$ points, evaluating the map costs O(N), and the full prediction costs O(NlogN) with the FNO backbone. We evaluate surface pressure prediction on ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, and drag coefficient prediction on DrivAerNet++. Across the three pressure benchmarks, our accuracy is on par with that of the most accurate baseline. On a surface with one million points, our method achieves a 354x end-to-end inference speedup over that baseline while keeping the same memory usage asymptotics of O(N).
title: FMSNO: Scaling Surface Neural Operators by Learned Flow Matching Reparametrisation

summary: Node affinity prediction in the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) asks how a node's future interactions will be distributed over other nodes. On this task, methods that reuse past ground-truth labels often outperform temporal graph neural networks, and the state of the art builds on them. Such comparisons assume a point-in-time correct evaluation, in which a model receives only information available at prediction time. Drawing on as-of joins and bitemporal databases, we formalize this requirement by distinguishing when a label must be predicted, its query time, from when it is fully determined, its availability time, and we audit the four TGB node affinity datasets and their evaluation loop with model-agnostic tools. None of the four meets it. On three datasets, each label summarizes a single day about five days after its timestamp, not the documented following week, yet the loop feeds it back right after that timestamp; on the fourth, the loop processes the edges from which each label is computed before predicting it. Under a drop-in leakage-free protocol, every method whose inputs leak loses up to 17% of its NDCG@10, the advantage of past labels over the interaction stream nearly vanishes or reverses, and both the best configuration of the state of the art and the rankings change; a blend of training-free long-memory statistics, with weights fit on validation data, matches or exceeds the state of the art under both protocols. Point-in-time correctness should therefore be built into benchmarks, and our tools carry over to other benchmarks whose labels aggregate event streams over time windows.
title: Temporal Leakage Distorts the TGB Node Affinity Leaderboard: A Point-in-Time Audit

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation

title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation

summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.
title: Composing Independently Distilled Memory and Retrieval Policies for Long-Term Agents

summary: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.
title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models

summary: Robot agents built on frontier vision-language models now solve most robot memory benchmarks. Does this mean they can remember what they need in a home, where people and machines keep moving things? Existing memory benchmarks cannot answer this question, because they pause the simulator while the model thinks: nothing can change during a decision, so whatever the robot remembers is still true when it acts. We introduce RoboLiveMem, a benchmark that runs the same memory tasks twice, once with the world paused while the model thinks and once with the world running. It contains 29 task families in three tiers, from 16 realistic BEHAVIOR-1K scenes of homes, workshops and a restaurant to controlled ManiSkill tasks. Every task mixes real changes with harmless look-alikes and runs without any change, so that no fixed strategy succeeds, and most tasks have a twin that keeps the change in view, which separates forgetting from acting too late. Testing 16 models on 34,176 episodes, we find three surprises. (1) Paused results hide the problem: when a remembered object changes in a realistic scene, the 8 Claude and GPT models succeed in 97% of episodes on average with the world paused, but in only 50% with the world running, and their ranking changes: Claude Opus 5.5, which never fails when paused, succeeds in 44%. (2) Speed is not the fix: slower models do no worse, and models given only 2 s per decision still fall at least 36 points below their paused success. (3) Models see the change but act on camera frames from before it ended. Looking again just before acting closes most of the realistic gap, yet when identical objects are swapped several times, all nine models we test still lose points to memory.
title: RoboLiveMem: Is Robot Memory Solved When the World Does Not Wait?

summary: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.
title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning

summary: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.
title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming

summary: We study how observed many-body system size affects the number of state copies needed to estimate a zero-temperature first-order transition point. The unknown Hamiltonian has bounded, translation-invariant on-site and nearest-neighbour interactions on a 3D cubic lattice with local dimension three. The field coupling is known, and all models share a known boundary field penalizing one local level. The limiting order parameter is uniformly separated across the transition. Each query returns an independently prepared Gibbs or ground state at an adaptive field and system size. For error $ε$ and fixed confidence, we prove an exponential separation between two size caps at the same temperature. There are absolute constants $0<c_0<C$ and $c_1>0$ such that, at inverse temperature $β=c_1/ε$, restricting side lengths to $L\le c_0/ε$ requires $\exp(Ω(1/ε))$ copies in worst-case expectation, even with collective measurements. Allowing $L\le C/ε$ permits $O(\log^2(1/ε))$ copies and $O(ε^{-3})$ total spins, using local measurements and polynomial classical postprocessing. The minimax expected total spin count is $Θ(ε^{-3})$ uniformly for $β\ge c_1/ε$. At fixed positive temperature it is $Θ_β(ε^{-2})$, attained from one- and eight-site Gibbs states followed by exponential classical computation. For ground-state copies it is $Θ(ε^{-3})$. The lower bound uses a three-state ferromagnet whose boundary suppresses the sector carrying transition information. A spanning-forest argument and edge-boundary counting control its Gibbs weight uniformly over fields and allowed sizes, and a trace-distance hybrid argument handles adaptive learners with quantum memory. The upper bound combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, concavity and local order-parameter measurements.
title: Estimating a Transition Point from Gibbs and Ground States

summary: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.
title: What Should World Models Plan Over? Learning Geometry-Aligned Representations of Body Motion

summary: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding

In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding

summary: Modern astronomical workflows require the coordinated use of specialised software, scientific archives, heterogeneous data, and domain-specific knowledge. Advances in large language models and multimodal foundation models enable natural-language interaction with scientific data and tools. Realising this potential requires integrating these models with established scientific capabilities. We present MAASAI (Multi-agent Astronomy Assistant for Scientific Analysis and Inference), a modular multi-agent system combining foundation-model reasoning, retrieval-augmented knowledge, and specialised astronomical tools within a graph-based execution framework. MAASAI coordinates request preparation, planning, execution, and response synthesis via specialised workers. Its architecture supports native and external applications, artefact and provenance management, optional human approval, and configurable inference backends, including fully local deployment with open-weight models. Motivated by SKA-era data-analysis challenges, MAASAI is also designed to support other astronomical domains. We evaluate MAASAI through radio-image benchmarks, single- and multi-step workflow demonstrations, and literature-grounded reasoning. Compared with a commercial-model baseline, MAASAI improves macro-averaged F1 scores from 0.53 to 0.72 for extended/diffuse emission classification and from 0.37 to 0.88 for source morphology classification. Workflow demonstrations show the coordination of measurements, source extraction, archive queries, and catalogue processing. A 94-question literature benchmark yielded generally favourable automated assessments, with comparable ratings from a pilot expert evaluation of 59 answers. These results highlight how tool-augmented multi-agent systems extend foundation-model reasoning to specialised astronomical analyses through established scientific software.
title: MAASAI: A Tool-Augmented Multi-Agent System for Astronomical Data Analysis

summary: During multi-agent video reasoning, model weights and per-agent key-value caches can exceed high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity. High-bandwidth flash (HBF) adds capacity, but agents still wait for GPU execution. Synapse, an HBM-coordinated near-memory computing architecture, overlaps HBF attention and expert execution with GPU computation across agents. It also reduces dispatch delays and unnecessary refreshes. Across three models, Synapse achieves 48.92-66.60% lower end-to-end latency, up to $2.98\times$ throughput, and up to 64.48% lower modeled energy per output token than GPU execution with passive HBF. Wear simulations project 46% longer HBF lifetime than block-wide refresh at equal workload rates.
title: Synapse: An HBM-Coordinated HBF Near-Memory Computing Architecture for Pipelined Agentic AI Execution

summary: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.
title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging

summary: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.
title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning

summary: We present CART, a computational pipeline for extracting political narratives from parliamentary discourse and organizing them into a data-driven taxonomy without relying on predefined narrative categories. It encodes parliamentary discourse using semantic representations, filters relevant and reliable content through unsupervised confidence estimation, extracts narrative statements using LLMs, and uses narrative clustering and cluster analysis to construct a narrative taxonomy. Applied to Greek Parliament proceedings surrounding the 2023 Tempi train crash, it identifies ten recurring narrative families concerning responsibility attribution, institutional failure, railway safety, accountability, privatization, and the political interpretation of the tragedy. Our results demonstrate how combining unsupervised learning with LLM narrative extraction enables large parliamentary corpora to be transformed into interpretable, data-driven taxonomies of political narratives.
title: CART: Clustering-based Analysis of Recurring narratives for Taxonomy construction

summary: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.
title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?

summary: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.
title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
