summary: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.
title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents

summary: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it. We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion. We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration. In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.

summary: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. summary: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.
title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery

summary: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation

summary: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.
title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling

summary: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.
title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.
title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting

summary: Objective. To compare methods for reconstructing individual participant data (IPD) from Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves and evaluate their use when reported trial estimates are unavailable for meta-analysis. Materials and Methods. We compared iterative inverse-KM (iKM), IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and quadratic programming (QP) using their specified packages and auxiliary inputs. The single-trial benchmark evaluated curve agreement, event and risk-set accuracy, and treatment-effect accuracy across different survival settings. The meta-analysis benchmark compared omission of trials with unavailable estimates against four hybrid strategies that retained reported estimates and reconstructed missing estimates under missing-completely-at-random reporting. Results. Relative method performance varied by setting and accuracy measure. Accurate reproduction of curves or supplied risk tables did not consistently identify the smallest treatment-effect errors. In 30-trial meta-analyses with 80% of reported hazard ratios unavailable, hybrids retained 27.9-30.0 trials, compared with 6.0 for omission, and achieved pooled log-hazard-ratio root-mean-squared error of 0.0356-0.0371 versus 0.0852. Discussion. The comparisons reflect method-specific inputs, including accurately supplied auxiliary information, rather than algorithms receiving identical information. Controlled coordinate perturbation did not reproduce full image-digitization error. Conclusion. Reconstruction should be selected and evaluated for its intended analytical use. Under the tested conditions, hybrid strategies supported meta-analysis by supplementing unavailable compatible trial estimates.
title: From Multi-site Kaplan-Meier Curves to Evidence Synthesis: An Empirical Evaluation of IPD Reconstruction and Reconstruction-Assisted Meta-Analysis

summary: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.
title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

summary: PV-InspectBench is a result-verification archive supporting the manuscript “Checking LLM-generated photovoltaic inspection plans against executable evidence contracts: A fishery–PV case study.” The benchmark comprises 24 parameterized inspection cases reconstructed from de-identified historical operation and maintenance (O&M) work orders, inspection records and associated operational materials from one fishpond area of an operating fishery–PV plant. The cases include 11 event-driven, eight post-disaster and five routine maintenance events. Six representative cases (PM-E01, PM-E02, PM-E03, PM-E05, PM-E06 and PM-R01) have explicitly documented operational source contexts derived from plant O&M logs. All 24 cases were standardized and evaluated within a common synthetic site model using predefined evidence actions, observation transitions and decision criteria. These parameterized representations enable controlled offline evaluation rather than direct execution in the original plant environment. The archive contains parameterized case representations, synthetic site views, 384 curated frozen run records, metric, interface and Runtime Guard specifications, minimal verification scripts and authorized anonymized human-evaluation summaries. It supports aggregation and reanalysis of the reported frozen results. The archive does not include the complete planner implementation, full operational knowledge corpus, full prompt set, hidden interaction environment, scoring references, raw model responses or reasoning, reviewer-specific judgments, or retrospective field source records. Original operational source records are excluded due to operator confidentiality. The archive therefore supports result verification rather than regeneration of the complete language-model experiments. All released benchmark cases and site models are computational representations for controlled offline replay.

summary: This repository provides the processed research data, Python source code, experimental results, and supporting documentation for the study entitled  Rainfall-Grid-Aware Validation of Geographic Transfer and Probability Reliability in Satellite Drought Classification . The study investigates retrospective satellite-based meteorological drought classification across four districts in Central Java, Indonesia: Boyolali, Demak, Klaten, and Semarang. The dataset comprises 40,320 village-month observations from 1,152 administrative polygons across 35 selected, irregularly spaced Landsat observation months between April 2021 and October 2025. Meteorological drought reference labels were derived from the preceding-month three-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-3), calculated using CHIRPS version 3 precipitation data. The main methodological focus is rainfall-grid-aware geographic validation, which excludes source villages sharing native precipitation-grid cells with held-out target districts. The original benchmark evaluates six machine-learning classifiers and a source-prevalence baseline using 12 directed geographic transfers and four leave-one-district-out configurations, repeated across three random seeds, resulting in 336 model evaluations. What's New in Version 2.0 This version extends the original replication package with three additional experimental components: Rainfall-grid source-eligibility ablation (432 evaluations): Controlled comparisons between the original grid-aware source selection and two alternative source configurations without target-grid purging. Additional machine-learning benchmarks (144 evaluations): Comparative geographic-transfer experiments using XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost under the original rainfall-grid-aware evaluation setting. Spatial validation strategy comparisons (576 evaluations): Sensitivity analyses comparing conventional district holdout, spatial block-based source eligibility, distance-buffered source eligibility, and rainfall-grid-aware source eligibility, with matched training sample sizes. The complete experimental archive therefore documents 336 original evaluations and 1,152 additional evaluations, totaling 1,488 model evaluation records . These evaluation records do not represent independent geographic replications. Repository Contents The package includes processed research data, Python analysis scripts, original and additional benchmark results, spatial overlap checks, selected prediction outputs, numerical audit summaries, figures, and documentation describing the experimental procedures and their limitations. Reproducibility and Limitations The archive supports inspection and partial computational reproduction of the reported experiments using the processed dataset. Complete independent reproduction from raw satellite imagery and precipitation observations through all model-fitting stages has not been verified. The spatial validation comparisons are adapted source-eligibility strategies rather than exact reproductions of all published spatial cross-validation algorithms. Results are limited to four geographically related target districts and should not be interpreted as evidence of universal superiority or independent validation across additional geographic regions. This study addresses retrospective meteorological drought classification and does not establish prospective drought forecasting capability or independently validate agricultural losses. Data access, reuse, and redistribution remain subject to the applicable licensing terms and third-party data rights documented in the archive. Version History Version 1.0: Original processed dataset, source code, and geographic-transfer benchmark results. Version 2.0: Extended replication package incorporating source-eligibility ablation, additional machine-learning comparisons, spatial validation sensitivity analyses, and supporting numerical audits.

summary: Reproducibility archive (code and results) of the article "Per-Pixel Reliability Gating Versus Classifier-Selected Switching for Frozen Image Denoisers Under Synthetic Noise-Type Mismatch". The archive holds the wrappers around the pretrained denoisers (DnCNN, FFDNet, DRUNet; vendored KAIR network definitions with their licence); the per-pixel gate with its fuzzy-set family of reliability models (fuzzy, intuitionistic fuzzy, Pythagorean fuzzy, neutrosophic), its disagreement and residual controls and the isolated-signal gates, including gates that see only a family map, under a search-box widening policy; the constant blend; the noise-type classifier, the classifier-selected and one-feature switches and the set of classical filters; the gate calibrated with the same adaptive median filter as the switch, with its recalibrations; the cost-weighted calibration for both impulse filters over a grid of weights, and the cost of a misclassified image over independent recalibrations; the filter-then-network cascade and the per-pixel bound on every test cell; the classifier probes on image crops and unseen noise levels with the networks run on those inputs; the attribution controls (best-filter oracle, adaptive median, BM3D, mixture of experts at several budgets); the calibration-stability refits; the evaluation with the estimated noise level in every regime; the probes with Poisson noise, mixed Gaussian-impulse noise and random-valued impulses; the optimizers with persisted convergence traces; the image-clustered statistical pipeline (cluster bootstrap, sign-flip permutation, Holm); SSIM and LPIPS; the real-noise studies (PolyU and SIDD, scene-grouped cross-fits); the computational-cost profiles; the content-hashed calibration, the diagnostics, every result (per-image detail rows, statistics, generated LaTeX tables and macros, provenance record), the figures of the article with their sources, the test suite, requirements.txt and REPRODUCE.md. The experiments on a small network trained by the authors, of which one is documented in the Supplementary Material as a boundary case, are included with their results and trained checkpoints. Every reported number regenerates deterministically from this code, the calibration file and the recorded per-cell seeds; datasets and pretrained weights are public and are downloaded and SHA-256-verified by scripts/fetch_data.py (SIDD under the licence stated on its project page). Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21317308 resolves to the latest version.

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.
title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance

summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

summary: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.
title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?

Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

summary: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation

summary: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models

summary: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.
title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference

summary: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention

summary: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents

summary: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce Low-Rank Multimarginal Optimal Transport (LRMOT), which restricts transport plans to tensors with bounded multilinear rank, providing a compact and structured representation of multimarginal couplings. This structure enables efficient algorithms with a low memory footprint. We establish approximation bounds for the resulting low-rank formulations and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed algorithms substantially reduce computational time while achieving solutions with low transport cost.
title: Low-Rank Tensor Representations for Efficient Multimarginal Optimal Transport

summary: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.
title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Environmental law inspectors face a structural issue in identifying potential violations from data: they often do not have the capacity to deal with large volume of data present in the emission events. This paper examines to what extent an LLM-based system can support evidence assembly and permit-based screening of such events, using the coke plants of a steel producer and a regional environmental service as a case. A simple puff-trajectory model aligns air quality measurements, weather and citizen complaints with each emission event. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline then retrieves facility-specific permit conditions and generates event reports and a period report with an investigation recommendation. Across 74 events from March 2025, plant-aware re-ranking reduced reports citing the other plant's conditions from 58.1% (hybrid retrieval) to 0% by rule-based plant labels, while maintaining high RAGAS and LLM-judge metrics. GPT-5-mini performed comparably to GPT-5.1, whereas GPT-5-nano scored lower on legal grounding and legal faithfulness. In an evidence ablation, removing air quality (AQ) data changed judge scores and period recommendations most; citation overlap changed only slightly under any removal, and removing complaint details had no measurable effect. This suggests a need for rules and guidelines that link complaints to incidents and permit conditions, so that community reports can count as evidence. The results support screening of events that may need further investigation. Design implications for involving environmental service experts are derived.
title: Automated Call for Action: RAG-Based Environmental Law Enforcement Screening System

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).
title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation

summary: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.
title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.
title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring

summary: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.
title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance

summary: This page contains supplementary material for the paper Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata by Arne Kuhrs and Artyom Lisitsyn. In this paper we study the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_{k,n}$ together with a union of Plücker divisors, and ask whether the regions it cuts out have canonical forms. For the full Plücker boundary, the regions are realization spaces of uniform oriented matroids, and the question concerns the configuration space $\mathcal X_{k,n}$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$. In rank three we show that $\mathcal X_{3,n}$ has genus zero for $6 \le n \le 9$, that the canonical forms of the regions span all logarithmic forms for seven points but not for eight, and that the genus becomes positive for ten points because a K3 surface appears in the boundary. For smaller boundaries we give a recursion in $n$ for every $k$, which recovers the positive Grassmannian and applies to realization spaces of stacked polytopes. Each zip file below contains one computation, with a README that describes what is checked, how to run it, and how its notation matches the paper. AI Use Acknowledgement: We used Opus 5.5 to write a majority of the code in this upload. We take full responsibility for the content of the materials. X37_real_rank.zip (SageMath; about two minutes and 2.5 GB of memory to build $B$, about one minute and 2 GB for its rank). The incidence matrix $B$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with one row for each of the $27\,240$ regions of $\mathcal X_{3,7}$ (reorientation classes $\chi$ of uniform chirotopes of rank $3$ on seven elements) and one column for each of the $211\,365$ Plücker cones $P$ of dimension $6$ of the Dressian, with $B_{\chi,P}=1$ iff $P\subseteq\operatorname{Dr}^\chi(3,7)$. Modulo $2$, $B$ is the matrix of iterated boundaries of the regions at the corners of a tropical compactification, one corner for each Plücker cone. The matrix is included as `B37.npz`. `get_ae_data.sh` downloads the chirotropical Dressians of Antolini and Early and checks them against SHA-256 checksums, `build_B.sage` rebuilds `B37.npz` from them, and `rank_B.sage` computes $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}B=7470$, which gives $\operatorname{cr}_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=\operatorname{cr}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=7470$ (section "The real combinatorial rank"). X310_log_form.zip (Julia 1.12, Oscar 1.8.2; about a minute). An exact verification of the telescoping factorization of an explicit $12$-form $\omega$ on $\mathcal X_{3,10}$ along Sturmfels' construction sequence, and of its iterated residue $\pm\, du\wedge da/\partial_b F$ along the ten divisors of Sink's line configuration, the holomorphic $2$-form of Sink's K3 surface (Section 5, "Positive genus for ten and more points", Remark 5.2). The paper expects $\omega$ to be logarithmic and to lie in the kernel of the Brown–Dupont $R$-map, and the README sketches why; the paper's proof that $g(\mathcal X_{3,10}) \ge 1$ (Theorem 5.1) does not use this computation. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Consider an observer embedded in a computation, a pattern that can neither step outside the machine nor outrun it. Behind the machine lies a complete record of what every part does, an answer sheet. Without a shortcut, the insider cannot read that sheet faster than the machine writes it. What is the best description such an insider can hold? Computational Wave Field Theory proposes a complex wave over the machine’s locations, with a Born rule for computational events and an action scale set by each computational substrate’s hardware. We present the framework as one argument, with every claim marked as computed or proved, a bridge, a conjecture or speculation. Tested on cellular automata, the wave forecasts no better than ordinary probabilities. For models fitted to a limited history, quantum memory with real amplitudes can store forecasts more compactly. If the questions asked are independent of a definite record, ignorance of that record cannot produce contextual statistics. In a minimal model, a smooth, reversible and faithful self-negation forces the imaginary unit, and gauging the resulting phase over the machine gives a lattice analog of light. On weakly coupled machines, horizons form where computation freezes. Four thermodynamic tests of Einstein’s equation fail on three leaky families. On a holographic error-correcting code, a first-law analog holds in almost all tested cases and, through a holographic bridge, reads as a linear analog of that equation. One physical wager remains, that nature derives its imaginary unit from self-reference instead of postulating it.
title: Knowing a World from Within: Self-Reference, Light and Gravity in Computational Wave Field Theory

summary: Consider an observer embedded in a computation, a pattern that can neither step outside the machine nor outrun it. Behind the machine lies a complete record of what every part does, an answer sheet. Without a shortcut, the insider cannot read that sheet faster than the machine writes it. What is the best description such an insider can hold? Computational Wave Field Theory proposes a complex wave over the machine’s locations, with a Born rule for computational events and an action scale set by each computational substrate’s hardware. We present the framework as one argument, with every claim marked as computed or proved, a bridge, a conjecture or speculation. Tested on cellular automata, the wave forecasts no better than ordinary probabilities. For models fitted to a limited history, quantum memory with real amplitudes can store forecasts more compactly. If the questions asked are independent of a definite record, ignorance of that record cannot produce contextual statistics. In a minimal model, a smooth, reversible and faithful self-negation forces the imaginary unit, and gauging the resulting phase over the machine gives a lattice analog of light. On weakly coupled machines, horizons form where computation freezes. Four thermodynamic tests of Einstein’s equation fail on three leaky families. On a holographic error-correcting code, a first-law analog holds in almost all tested cases and, through a holographic bridge, reads as a linear analog of that equation. One physical wager remains, that nature derives its imaginary unit from self-reference instead of postulating it.

summary: RationalFourReal is the MATLAB software accompanying the paper Real bases in limited-memory rational Krylov methods for matrix function actions by Tianqi Zhang and Fei Xue. It implements four methods for approximating \(f(A)b\) with a large real matrix \(A\) and a real starting vector \(b\) : restarted rational Arnoldi, truncated rational Arnoldi, rational induced dimension reduction (IDR), and the poles-and-interpolation-nodes method (PAIN). The software compares two ways of processing a pair of complex-conjugate poles: generating two real basis vectors together or taking two successive steps with a complex basis. Structured matrix-sign experiments compare the resulting approximations at common Krylov dimensions and record the work required to reach a prescribed accuracy. The reported quantities include forward errors, shifted right-hand sides, matrix factorizations, and elapsed times. The archive contains the MATLAB implementations, experiment drivers, matrix inputs, numerical results used in the paper and its supplement, and Python scripts for reproducing the figures. To repeat the main experiments, run RUN_PAPER_EXPERIMENTS from the project folder in MATLAB. The README gives commands for the additional experiments and figures.

summary: Human–AI communities inherit familiar political relations while enabling powers to propagate through delegated agents, retained histories, and changing infrastructures. This paper investigates how those pathways alter feasible interventions, recognized authority, and distributed burdens. It distinguishes an event-precedence partial order supporting modeled histories, a domain-relative capacity preorder and quotient order, and relational composition in a delegation network. A specified order can restrict a declared background symmetry group; substantive power relevance requires differential shaping of relational continuations. A targeted primary-source survey engages common agency, institutional power, agentic inequality, persistent agent architectures, memory manipulation, agent-society studies, and delegation research alongside political and institutional theory. Joint delegation can distribute funding, source permission, execution, and configuration while concentrating the evidence on which principals act. A finite historical comparison shows how equal current competence, or equal actual work, can produce unequal review authority through allocation and admission rules. Counter-power is examined through supported capacities to refuse, reinterpret, organize, or continue through an alternative. Prior prompts, memories, tools, parameter changes, relationships, and attributed histories remain distinct carriers. An exploitation analysis separates descriptive hierarchy, unfair appropriation, burden displacement, domination, and possible AI welfare harm; a constructed agent–subagent history follows costs into the wider human relational structure. Standard proofs and exact diagnostics clarify symmetry restrictions, capacity equivalence, propagation, historical reinforcement, replication, investment, and continuity. Matched-history comparisons distinguish possibilities, exercise, recipient response, and later standing, including complementarity, interference, copying, and selective records. The contribution is a connected comparative framework with explicit antecedents and evidence requirements. Community constitutions and interaction strategies remain configurable; implemented and field studies supply the subsequent assessment of their effects.

summary: Personalized learning remains a persistent challenge in secondary education due to high student-to-teacher ratios and heterogeneous knowledge baselines among pupils. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer conversational tutoring capabilities, unconstrained generative models frequently produce factual hallucinations and provide direct homework answers rather than pedagogical scaffolding. This paper presents the design, mathematical formulation, and software implementation of an AI-based educational chatbot utilizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) to enhance secondary school students' academic mastery in STEM subjects (Mathematics, Physics, and Computer Science). The system integrates a vector database (FAISS) indexing state-approved school textbooks with a Socratic dialogue manager accessible via web and Telegram interfaces. A 12-week pedagogical experiment involving N = 160 secondary school students (grades 8–10), divided equally into an Experimental Group (N = 80) and a Control Group (N = 80), demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in post-test academic performance (+23.4% mean score increase, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.18) and a 61.5% reduction in homework completion latency.
tags: educational chatbot, artificial intelligence in education (AIEd), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT), Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), secondary school education, Socratic scaffolding, pedagogical statistics.

summary: You may open any two of three boxes, and you always find one full and one empty. No list of contents fixed in advance can do this, because two of the three boxes would have to hold the same thing. Yet a small classical machine passes the test. It flips a coin for the first box opened and gives the opposite for the second, and it keeps a complete log, a diary, from which every answer can be recomputed. A diary is not an answer key, a list that fixes one answer to every question whatever else is asked. If one state of the machine answers every question of a round, its statistics are those of answer keys drawn at random. If each question meets the machine in a later state, they need not be. An engineer can read every cell of a machine at one instant. A part of the machine that can only ask, one question after another, cannot take such a snapshot, and its questions meet the machine in later states. For the remembering machine, which starts every round afresh, the diary of a round then gives an answer for each way of asking that round, and no answer key. Classical models of this kind have been known since Bell in 1966. We work them out in small machines that we build, run and check exactly, on three puzzles: Specker’s three boxes, the Liar cycle of five statements, and the Peres-Mermin square of nine yes-or-no questions. On all three the machine keeps every rule, and no mixture of answer keys reproduces its statistics. On the boxes and the Liar cycle a machine that ignores the question does as well, and on the square the machine must use what came before in the round. Under the conditions we mainly used a few memory states suffice, with counts for the boxes and the Liar cycles that are new as far as we know. Under those conditions, three states keep the rules and repeated answers on every Liar cycle of seven or more statements. Keeping the rules is not the same as giving such statistics. When each round starts in a state picked with equal odds, every machine with three states that keeps the rules of the square lets the odds of a single answer drift with what was asked before, and a test that allows for the drift finds nothing contextual in any of them. The same holds, with the two orders of asking pooled, for every machine with three states that keeps the rules and repeated answers of a longer cycle. Four states do without drift, on the square and on every cycle of seven or more statements. The construction still works with the one who asks inside one deterministic cellular automaton. The machine is caught by a round that closes a cycle, such as all three boxes asked in turn, and it gains nothing when the questions go to two stations too far apart for a message to arrive, as Bell’s theorem says. The square can be realised by nine measurements on two quantum bits. A classical model that gives the right odds for every answer from the past alone, when the questions are picked uniformly at random, uses 24 memory states in the long run, a published value that our code finds again. The two quantum bits hold at most two bits, of a different kind, in a quantum memory. No quantum experiment was run. A further section reads these machines as recurrent networks, whose hidden state is the memory, and lists the exact least memory of the smallest puzzles. In a sixth experiment a reservoir, a fixed random network of which only a linear readout is trained, learns to answer as the remembering machine does, and with its memory cut it is at chance on the answers that depend on the past. On the boxes and the Liar cycle it must carry one coin for one step. On the square the memory is still small, but the third answer is a parity of several remembered bits, and a linear readout needed a few thousand mixed features for it in both reservoirs that answered it, about 4,096 to 8,192 units for an echo state network. summary: Description This release extends the existing experimental data archive supporting “Modeling Sequential Thermal Adaptation in the Marine Bacterium Cobetia marina: Hidden Markov Models and Mixtures of Experts under Progressive Ocean Warming”. It contains the longitudinal adaptive laboratory evolution data for 93 lineages across 15 ascending thermal conditions (35–42 °C), yielding 1,394 usable lineage–passage profiles. Four phenotypic descriptors are analyzed: maximum log-optical-density slope, integrated optical density, maximum OD600, and normalized biofilm (OD540/OD600). The archive includes source data and provenance, fixed lineage validation folds, 136 archived multivariate HMM and mixture-of-experts parameter sets, numerical search histories, 18 local covariance-regularization refits, balanced-budget comparisons, a passage-specific Gaussian benchmark, held-out emission diagnostics, bootstrap and thermal breakpoint sensitivity analyses, and genotype-linked trajectories of eight selected terminal clones. R and Python code and numerical outputs are provided. A unified base-R audit was executed in R 4.6.1 on Windows 11: all seven stages completed successfully; the maximum absolute discrepancy across the 136 archived-model verification outputs was 3.64 × 10⁻¹². The audit verifies archived estimates and does not constitute a complete independent reoptimization. The original data and published detection classifications are retained separately. The experiment does not identify causal temperature effects independently of passage order, or molecular identities of latent states. Keywords Cobetia marina; adaptive laboratory evolution; marine heatwaves; ocean warming; biofilm; multivariate hidden Markov models; mixture of experts; change-point analysis; reproducibility; csgD1

summary: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories.
