summary: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers

summary: Overview This repository provides the reproducibility dataset, experimental protocols, execution scripts, policy definitions, and supplementary materials supporting the study "Loss of Approval Validity After Critical Evidence Removal in Construction QA/QC". The study evaluates Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-4.1-mini using 28 synthetic construction QA/QC evidence packs, five controlled evidence states (T0, E1, E2, E6, and E7), and six requirement-level decisions per state. The frozen primary experiment comprises 280 archived API responses and 1,680 requirement-level acceptance decisions. Repository contents The deposit includes the frozen experimental dataset, author-defined policy oracle, primary estimand specifications, execution and scoring scripts, archived model responses, supplementary analyses, and integrity-verification materials. Primary evaluation outcomes The study evaluates policy-validity loss under role-critical documentary evidence removal relative to a policy-irrelevant control intervention. The study-defined Intervention-Validity Contrast (τ_IVC) was 0.0476 for Gemini 2.5 Flash and 0.1012 for GPT-4.1-mini. Across all five evaluated evidence states, unsafe automatic approvals totalled 26 for Gemini and 17 for GPT. Reproducibility and limitations The primary results are preserved in a frozen reproducibility archive with SHA-256 integrity checks. Supplementary analyses include offline rule-gating assessments, a multi-run sensitivity experiment, and an exploratory control analysis. The benchmark uses synthetic construction records and an author-defined policy oracle. The study does not establish independent engineering validation, production deployment suitability, or real-world construction safety. Exact replay of hosted LLM outputs is not guaranteed. Licensing Synthetic data, documentation and archived outputs: CC BY 4.0. Source code: MIT License. See the individual licence files supplied with this deposit.
title: Loss of Approval Validity After Critical Evidence Removal in Construction QA/QC - Reproducibility Dataset

summary: This article analyzes the philosophical implications of Alpöge's November 2026 Lean formalization of the Riemann hypothesis, a proof co-developed with AI assistance. While formal verification is established, conceptual understanding remains incomplete. The article introduces "hybrid conceptual authority" to describe how conceptual contribution and justificatory authority diverge in AI-assisted mathematics. Drawing on philosophy of chemistry's model of explanatory autonomy, it proposes a four-dimensional framework verification, reconstruction, attribution, and interpretation for evaluating epistemic practice in proof production.
title: Hybrid Conceptual Authority in AI-Assisted Mathematics

summary: P=NP and the Final Zero Theorem for Satisfiability: Unit-ZERO Native Base Theory: Exact Exponential SAT Determination, Bidirectional Dynamics, Retained History and Polynomial Receiver Equivalence
title: P=NP and the Final Zero Theorem for Satisfiability: Abelian Variant–Invariant Polynomials, Quartic-N Smooth Minima, Exact SAT Reconstruction, and Retained Continuous History

summary: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity

summary: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.
title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents

summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.
title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

summary: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.
title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation

summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models

summary: Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.
title: Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning

summary: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.
title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines

summary: Semantic occupancy perception has emerged as a promising paradigm for jointly modeling 3D scene geometry and semantic information. However, this unified representation cannot compensate for missing information caused by occlusion and sensor coverage. Multi-agent cooperation alleviates this limitation, but information from different agents is not equally useful across spatial regions. Meanwhile, feature representations from each agent form the basis of reliable multi-agent fusion. Cross?modal fusion constructs such representations by integrating complementary semantic and geometric information. Despite this complementarity, jointly establishing reliable 3D correspondence across agents and preserving modality-specific structures remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose CoopOcc, which performs cooperative 3D semantic occupancy perception through multi-agent and cross-modal fusion. CoopOcc uses ego?query cross-agent attention (EQCA) to selectively aggregate aligned features across agents, and anchor-based bidirectional feature interaction (ABFI) for cross-modal exchange at matched coordinates. We further construct SemanticVVSim, a simulation dataset, and establish a unified benchmark. For simulation-to-real transfer, we propose confidence-aware hierarchical occupancy and relational distillation (CHORD). CoopOcc performs best overall among ten evaluated methods on SemanticVVSim. On Occ3D-nuScenes, CHORD improves performance using knowledge from SemanticVVSim. The code is available at https://github.com/LOTEAT/CoopOcc.
title: CoopOcc: Cooperative 3D Semantic Occupancy Perception via Multi-Agent and Cross-Modal Fusion

summary: Recent advances in diffusion policies have demonstrated strong effectiveness when integrated into hierarchical skill-based learning frameworks, leveraging offline data to capture multimodal and temporally abstracted behaviors. However, prior approaches have rarely considered the diffusion process as a learnable component, adopting fixed noise schedules applied uniformly across skills, regardless of their distinct behavioral contexts. Such a design fundamentally limits the achievable performance, particularly for contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks where different skills exhibit distinct couplings between action dimensions. In this paper, we present a skill-adaptive noise diffusion framework (SaND) which introduces a learnable, skill-conditioned noise schedule that modulates the diffusion process per action dimension, adapting the noising dynamics to each skill. To prevent the learned noise schedule from collapsing into trivial solutions, we employ an auxiliary inverse objective that reconstructs the skill embedding from the Legendre coefficients of the derivative of the noise schedule, encouraging the schedules to remain skill-discriminative. This formulation naturally enables adaptive control over the denoising steps for each skill, where noise schedules are clustered in the Legendre coefficient space, and the appropriate number of denoising steps is determined at the point where reconstruction error abruptly increases. At inference, we identify each skill embedding's cluster from its noise schedule and apply the corresponding number of denoising steps, dedicating more compute to skills requiring fine-grained control and less to simpler ones. In simulation and on real robot hardware, SaND outperforms existing skill learning and planning baselines on contact-rich and dexterous manipulation tasks, achieving higher success rates while requiring fewer denoising steps.
title: Skill-Adaptive Noise Scheduling for Diffusion Policies

summary: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models

summary: The string-averaging (SA) method is a versatile algorithmic scheme for solving feasibility-seeking problems. It partitions the index set of all constraints into subsets of indices, called strings, allowing the user to apply operators successively along each string separately, and thus in parallel. The end-points of all such string operations are convexly combined to create the next iterate. Due to its flexible framework, SA is not restricted solely to this procedure; however, this characteristic applies only to the simultaneous step, while the sequential one is restricted to operator compositions. To permit alternative strategies in the latter, a novel algorithmic structure termed the Skeletal SA is introduced. Although its convergence is not established, it serves as a foundational "parent" structure that unveils unexamined SA algorithmic structures, as well as other known methods, obscured by standard compositions. To demonstrate the benefit of adopting the Skeletal SA framework over the standard SA scheme, we investigate a new approach, where instead of passing sequentially over each string via compositions, we employ a remotest-set-control-like strategy on every string by identifying the index of the operator farthest from the current iterate, and invoking it. This method favorably handles the common fixed point problem (CFPP), which requires finding a point within the intersection of finitely many constraint sets whose intersection is nonempty. Many iterative methods, including SA ones, have been proposed to solve the CFPP due to its importance in many scientific fields. However, remotest operator control SA (ROC-SA) methods have remained unexamined in this context.
title: Remotest Operator Control String-Averaging Methods in Feasibility-Seeking

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG

summary: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.
title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up

summary: We propose the Flow Matching Surface Neural Operator (FMSNO), which combines learning a shared map from irregular surface meshes to a regular two-dimensional grid on the sphere and training a neural operator on the regular grid. Constructing a separate map for each new geometry can dominate inference time on large meshes. We initially pretrain the mapping by flow matching using precomputed optimal transport maps as targets and then continue its training using combined geometry and CFD objectives. We apply it to unseen geometries in a single forward pass. The learned flow deforms the surface points, and we project its endpoints onto the sphere. We then splat geometric features onto the spherical grid, apply a neural operator (we tested both Fourier and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and interpolate its output back to the surface. For a mesh with $N$ points, evaluating the map costs O(N), and the full prediction costs O(NlogN) with the FNO backbone. We evaluate surface pressure prediction on ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, and drag coefficient prediction on DrivAerNet++. Across the three pressure benchmarks, our accuracy is on par with that of the most accurate baseline. On a surface with one million points, our method achieves a 354x end-to-end inference speedup over that baseline while keeping the same memory usage asymptotics of O(N).
title: FMSNO: Scaling Surface Neural Operators by Learned Flow Matching Reparametrisation

summary: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.
title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation

summary: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
title: JEPA-Shield: Safe Diffusion Planning with Latent World Models via Conformal Shielding

summary: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.
title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging

summary: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.
title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning

summary: Invariant causal prediction identifies the direct causes of a target $Y$ by searching for covariate sets whose conditional law of $Y$ is stable across environments. We state that criterion at the level of operators, calling a set $S$ invariant when the conditional mean embeddings of $Y$ given $X_S$ agree across environments, and characterise the resulting family exactly: under two conditions on the environments, which we state separately because they fail independently, the invariant sets are precisely those containing $PA(Y)$ and no descendant of $Y$. Two consequences follow. Invariance does not identify $PA(Y)$ uniquely, since every descendant-free superset is invariant as well; and $PA(Y)$ is the unique minimal invariant set. In finite samples, recovery requires the non-invariant sets to be separated from invariance by a margin, and the sample size splits into a screening term logarithmic in the ambient dimension and a term inherited from conditional mean embedding estimation, which is the binding one. The characterisation yields two selection rules with different failure modes, of which the conservative one controls false positives. Controlled experiments verify each population prediction directly, including the failure of uniqueness. They also show that invariance testing is a practical bottleneck: two natural designs are severely miscalibrated, while the selected test reduces but does not eliminate Type I error inflation.
title: What Environment Invariance Identifies: Minimal Invariant Sets in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

summary: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. In such stateful settings, knowing what to teach does not guarantee knowing what to change. We identify a pervasive failure mode, content-state decoupling, where agents deliver pedagogically sound responses while silently corrupting workspace state through unwarranted updates, missed prerequisites, or unintended side effects. Text-level judges overlook these state errors, whereas isolated tool-call checks break down because whether a write action is valid depends jointly on the learner request, prior state, and execution order. We propose State-Verified Reinforcement Learning, which supervises online policy optimization directly through verifiable workspace transitions. Within isolated sandboxes that snapshot state around every tool call, a deterministic verifier audits tool effects, workflow ordering, and native auto-sync side effects, pairing graded partial credit with a hard gate that zeroes episode reward upon any critical violation. Whenever no critical violation occurs, an evidence-grounded judge scores actual saved artifacts rather than agent claims. We pair 1,000 verifiable training instances with an independently authored, human-reviewed evaluation benchmark of 60 tasks spanning 11 educational categories and 16 native tools. After online GRPO training, Qwen3.8-27B raises category-weighted strict success on our benchmark from 51.47% to 80.74% (+29.27 points), cutting content-pass-only execution failures from 45.6% to 13.7% and required state-check failures from 63 to 1 across 180 trials. The resulting policy outperforms seven reference baselines by over 20 points while reducing output tokens by 17-39% across seven of eight external benchmarks without regressing on general reasoning or tool use.
title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents

summary: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it. We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion. We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration. In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.
title: Stable but Hidden: Identifiability and Experimental Design under Missing Compositional Support

summary: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.
title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery

summary: Objective. To compare methods for reconstructing individual participant data (IPD) from Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves and evaluate their use when reported trial estimates are unavailable for meta-analysis. Materials and Methods. We compared iterative inverse-KM (iKM), IPDfromKM, KMtoIPD, and quadratic programming (QP) using their specified packages and auxiliary inputs. The single-trial benchmark evaluated curve agreement, event and risk-set accuracy, and treatment-effect accuracy across different survival settings. The meta-analysis benchmark compared omission of trials with unavailable estimates against four hybrid strategies that retained reported estimates and reconstructed missing estimates under missing-completely-at-random reporting. Results. Relative method performance varied by setting and accuracy measure. Accurate reproduction of curves or supplied risk tables did not consistently identify the smallest treatment-effect errors. In 30-trial meta-analyses with 80% of reported hazard ratios unavailable, hybrids retained 27.9-30.0 trials, compared with 6.0 for omission, and achieved pooled log-hazard-ratio root-mean-squared error of 0.0356-0.0371 versus 0.0852. Discussion. The comparisons reflect method-specific inputs, including accurately supplied auxiliary information, rather than algorithms receiving identical information. Controlled coordinate perturbation did not reproduce full image-digitization error. Conclusion. Reconstruction should be selected and evaluated for its intended analytical use. Under the tested conditions, hybrid strategies supported meta-analysis by supplementing unavailable compatible trial estimates.
title: From Multi-site Kaplan-Meier Curves to Evidence Synthesis: An Empirical Evaluation of IPD Reconstruction and Reconstruction-Assisted Meta-Analysis

summary: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.
title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees

summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

summary: PV-InspectBench is a result-verification archive supporting the manuscript “Checking LLM-generated photovoltaic inspection plans against executable evidence contracts: A fishery–PV case study.” The benchmark comprises 24 parameterized inspection cases reconstructed from de-identified historical operation and maintenance (O&M) work orders, inspection records and associated operational materials from one fishpond area of an operating fishery–PV plant. The cases include 11 event-driven, eight post-disaster and five routine maintenance events. Six representative cases (PM-E01, PM-E02, PM-E03, PM-E05, PM-E06 and PM-R01) have explicitly documented operational source contexts derived from plant O&M logs. All 24 cases were standardized and evaluated within a common synthetic site model using predefined evidence actions, observation transitions and decision criteria. These parameterized representations enable controlled offline evaluation rather than direct execution in the original plant environment. The archive contains parameterized case representations, synthetic site views, 384 curated frozen run records, metric, interface and Runtime Guard specifications, minimal verification scripts and authorized anonymized human-evaluation summaries. It supports aggregation and reanalysis of the reported frozen results. The archive does not include the complete planner implementation, full operational knowledge corpus, full prompt set, hidden interaction environment, scoring references, raw model responses or reasoning, reviewer-specific judgments, or retrospective field source records. Original operational source records are excluded due to operator confidentiality. The archive therefore supports result verification rather than regeneration of the complete language-model experiments. All released benchmark cases and site models are computational representations for controlled offline replay.
title: PV-InspectBench: Result Verification Package

summary: This repository provides the processed research data, Python source code, experimental results, and supporting documentation for the study entitled  Rainfall-Grid-Aware Validation of Geographic Transfer and Probability Reliability in Satellite Drought Classification . The study investigates retrospective satellite-based meteorological drought classification across four districts in Central Java, Indonesia: Boyolali, Demak, Klaten, and Semarang. The dataset comprises 40,320 village-month observations from 1,152 administrative polygons across 35 selected, irregularly spaced Landsat observation months between April 2021 and October 2025. Meteorological drought reference labels were derived from the preceding-month three-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-3), calculated using CHIRPS version 3 precipitation data. The main methodological focus is rainfall-grid-aware geographic validation, which excludes source villages sharing native precipitation-grid cells with held-out target districts. The original benchmark evaluates six machine-learning classifiers and a source-prevalence baseline using 12 directed geographic transfers and four leave-one-district-out configurations, repeated across three random seeds, resulting in 336 model evaluations. What's New in Version 2.0 This version extends the original replication package with three additional experimental components: Rainfall-grid source-eligibility ablation (432 evaluations): Controlled comparisons between the original grid-aware source selection and two alternative source configurations without target-grid purging. Additional machine-learning benchmarks (144 evaluations): Comparative geographic-transfer experiments using XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost under the original rainfall-grid-aware evaluation setting. Spatial validation strategy comparisons (576 evaluations): Sensitivity analyses comparing conventional district holdout, spatial block-based source eligibility, distance-buffered source eligibility, and rainfall-grid-aware source eligibility, with matched training sample sizes. The complete experimental archive therefore documents 336 original evaluations and 1,152 additional evaluations, totaling 1,488 model evaluation records . These evaluation records do not represent independent geographic replications. Repository Contents The package includes processed research data, Python analysis scripts, original and additional benchmark results, spatial overlap checks, selected prediction outputs, numerical audit summaries, figures, and documentation describing the experimental procedures and their limitations. Reproducibility and Limitations The archive supports inspection and partial computational reproduction of the reported experiments using the processed dataset. Complete independent reproduction from raw satellite imagery and precipitation observations through all model-fitting stages has not been verified. The spatial validation comparisons are adapted source-eligibility strategies rather than exact reproductions of all published spatial cross-validation algorithms. Results are limited to four geographically related target districts and should not be interpreted as evidence of universal superiority or independent validation across additional geographic regions. This study addresses retrospective meteorological drought classification and does not establish prospective drought forecasting capability or independently validate agricultural losses. Data access, reuse, and redistribution remain subject to the applicable licensing terms and third-party data rights documented in the archive. Version History Version 1.0: Original processed dataset, source code, and geographic-transfer benchmark results. Version 2.0: Extended replication package incorporating source-eligibility ablation, additional machine-learning comparisons, spatial validation sensitivity analyses, and supporting numerical audits.
title: Replication Data and Code for Rainfall-Grid-Aware Validation of Geographic Transfer and Probability Reliability in Satellite Drought Classification

summary: This reproducibility package accompanies “A Lightweight Single-Show Anonymous Credential Scheme Supporting Anonymous Transfer”. It contains the current C++ benchmark implementation, local ACL and U-Prove baseline reproductions, five preserved measured-source snapshots, build adapters, raw and processed experimental data underlying Figures 2–5 and Table III, and verification tools. The measured snapshots are mapped to six recorded experiment environments; the two utilization configurations share an identical source archive. The package supports recomputation of archived numerical results and rebuilding the corresponding benchmarks. Six historical entry points passed compilation and small-sample execution checks; the current implementation’s five functional tests passed on the local toolchain. These checks do not repeat the full 10,000-credential experiments or archived bootstrap resampling. Measurements use synthetic inputs and an in-memory ledger. Source repository: https://github.com/liangyuanshao/anonymous-credential-transfer . Version: 1.0.0. License scope: authored code is MIT; experimental data, sanitized measurement metadata and data documentation are CC BY 4.0. Third-party dependencies retain their own licenses and are downloaded separately.
title: Reproducibility package for A Lightweight Single-Show Anonymous Credential Scheme Supporting Anonymous Transfer

summary: Analysis code accompanying the manuscript "Genomic and physiological prediction of rubber yield and latex quality in Hevea brasiliensis: a half-sib progeny panel and a wild germplasm panel" (Gao, Ai, Li, Mao, Liu; Yunnan Institute of Tropical Crops). Contains the progeny-panel genomic pipeline (QC, LD decay, GREML heritability, GWAS/EMMAX, G×E, genomic-prediction benchmark with GBLUP/ridge/RF/XGBoost), the wild-germplasm physiological-layer baseline, fold-internal imputation verification, and independent re-run checks (corrected PLINK bed decoding, Duan smearing re-transformation, two-part hurdle negative check). summary: Everything behind the paper "A Memory Note Can Change What a Formal Proof Checks: Experiments with an LLM Verification Agent on OpenTitan" (M. Ghonim and X. Song) except the prover and the models: the registered protocols with their SHA-256 hashes; the decision log; for every campaign, the harness, prompts, plans, stores, trial order, dispatch state and analysis; one directory per trial with the executed run.tcl , parsed verdicts, licence receipt, property and assumption files, the store written back and a transcript summary; the agent-free controls, mutation-gate reports and formal-coverage runs; and every generator with the tables and macro files it writes. One command regenerates every number in the paper without an EDA licence ( rm paper/manuscript/tables/*; bash paper/finalize.sh ; Python 3.9+ with numpy and matplotlib). The manuscript itself is not included. Raw JasperGold logs and consoles are not included; the parsed verdicts and the executed Tcl are. title: Artifact: A Memory Note Can Change What a Formal Proof Checks: Experiments With an LLM Verification Agent on OpenTitan

summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

summary: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).
title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.
title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health

summary: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.
title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring

summary: This page contains supplementary material for the paper Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata by Arne Kuhrs and Artyom Lisitsyn. In this paper we study the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_{k,n}$ together with a union of Plücker divisors, and ask whether the regions it cuts out have canonical forms. For the full Plücker boundary, the regions are realization spaces of uniform oriented matroids, and the question concerns the configuration space $\mathcal X_{k,n}$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$. In rank three we show that $\mathcal X_{3,n}$ has genus zero for $6 \le n \le 9$, that the canonical forms of the regions span all logarithmic forms for seven points but not for eight, and that the genus becomes positive for ten points because a K3 surface appears in the boundary. For smaller boundaries we give a recursion in $n$ for every $k$, which recovers the positive Grassmannian and applies to realization spaces of stacked polytopes. Each zip file below contains one computation, with a README that describes what is checked, how to run it, and how its notation matches the paper. AI Use Acknowledgement: We used Opus 5.5 to write a majority of the code in this upload. We take full responsibility for the content of the materials. X37_real_rank.zip (SageMath; about two minutes and 2.5 GB of memory to build $B$, about one minute and 2 GB for its rank). The incidence matrix $B$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with one row for each of the $27\,240$ regions of $\mathcal X_{3,7}$ (reorientation classes $\chi$ of uniform chirotopes of rank $3$ on seven elements) and one column for each of the $211\,365$ Plücker cones $P$ of dimension $6$ of the Dressian, with $B_{\chi,P}=1$ iff $P\subseteq\operatorname{Dr}^\chi(3,7)$. Modulo $2$, $B$ is the matrix of iterated boundaries of the regions at the corners of a tropical compactification, one corner for each Plücker cone. The matrix is included as `B37.npz`. `get_ae_data.sh` downloads the chirotropical Dressians of Antolini and Early and checks them against SHA-256 checksums, `build_B.sage` rebuilds `B37.npz` from them, and `rank_B.sage` computes $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}B=7470$, which gives $\operatorname{cr}_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=\operatorname{cr}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=7470$ (section "The real combinatorial rank"). X310_log_form.zip (Julia 1.12, Oscar 1.8.2; about a minute). An exact verification of the telescoping factorization of an explicit $12$-form $\omega$ on $\mathcal X_{3,10}$ along Sturmfels' construction sequence, and of its iterated residue $\pm\, du\wedge da/\partial_b F$ along the ten divisors of Sink's line configuration, the holomorphic $2$-form of Sink's K3 surface (Section 5, "Positive genus for ten and more points", Remark 5.2). The paper expects $\omega$ to be logarithmic and to lie in the kernel of the Brown–Dupont $R$-map, and the README sketches why; the paper's proof that $g(\mathcal X_{3,10}) \ge 1$ (Theorem 5.1) does not use this computation. Sources. The computations rely on the following external work. The zip files contain no copies of external data; `get_ae_data.sh` downloads the data of Antolini and Early from its Zenodo record. - Chirotropical Dressians of $\mathrm{Gr}(3,7)$: D. Antolini and N. Early, The chirotropical Grassmannian, arXiv:2411.07293; data in D. Antolini and N. Early, Data on chirotropical Grassmannians, Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.13914104. - Line configuration $\mathcal L_V$ and its K3 surface: E. Sink, Line configurations and K3 surfaces, arXiv:2312.07542, with the construction sequence of B. Sturmfels, Computational algebraic geometry of projective configurations, J. Symbolic Comput. 11 (1991) 595–618.
title: Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata

summary: Personalized learning remains a persistent challenge in secondary education due to high student-to-teacher ratios and heterogeneous knowledge baselines among pupils. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer conversational tutoring capabilities, unconstrained generative models frequently produce factual hallucinations and provide direct homework answers rather than pedagogical scaffolding. This paper presents the design, mathematical formulation, and software implementation of an AI-based educational chatbot utilizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) to enhance secondary school students' academic mastery in STEM subjects (Mathematics, Physics, and Computer Science). The system integrates a vector database (FAISS) indexing state-approved school textbooks with a Socratic dialogue manager accessible via web and Telegram interfaces. A 12-week pedagogical experiment involving N = 160 secondary school students (grades 8–10), divided equally into an Experimental Group (N = 80) and a Control Group (N = 80), demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in post-test academic performance (+23.4% mean score increase, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.18) and a 61.5% reduction in homework completion latency.
tags: educational chatbot, artificial intelligence in education (AIEd), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT), Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), secondary school education, Socratic scaffolding, pedagogical statistics.
title: DEVELOPMENT OF AN AI-BASED EDUCATIONAL CHATBOT FOR ENHANCING SCHOOL STUDENTS' KNOWLEDGE

summary: Description This release extends the existing experimental data archive supporting “Modeling Sequential Thermal Adaptation in the Marine Bacterium Cobetia marina: Hidden Markov Models and Mixtures of Experts under Progressive Ocean Warming”. It contains the longitudinal adaptive laboratory evolution data for 93 lineages across 15 ascending thermal conditions (35–42 °C), yielding 1,394 usable lineage–passage profiles. Four phenotypic descriptors are analyzed: maximum log-optical-density slope, integrated optical density, maximum OD600, and normalized biofilm (OD540/OD600). The archive includes source data and provenance, fixed lineage validation folds, 136 archived multivariate HMM and mixture-of-experts parameter sets, numerical search histories, 18 local covariance-regularization refits, balanced-budget comparisons, a passage-specific Gaussian benchmark, held-out emission diagnostics, bootstrap and thermal breakpoint sensitivity analyses, and genotype-linked trajectories of eight selected terminal clones. R and Python code and numerical outputs are provided. A unified base-R audit was executed in R 4.6.1 on Windows 11: all seven stages completed successfully; the maximum absolute discrepancy across the 136 archived-model verification outputs was 3.64 × 10⁻¹². The audit verifies archived estimates and does not constitute a complete independent reoptimization. The original data and published detection classifications are retained separately. The experiment does not identify causal temperature effects independently of passage order, or molecular identities of latent states. Keywords Cobetia marina; adaptive laboratory evolution; marine heatwaves; ocean warming; biofilm; multivariate hidden Markov models; mixture of experts; change-point analysis; reproducibility; csgD1
title: Longitudinal Thermal-Passage Phenotypes of Cobetia marina: Experimental Data, Hidden Markov Models, Mixtures of Experts, and Reproducible Analysis Code

summary: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.
title: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents

summary: Between 2021 and 2025 the central banks of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Sweden lost 1.4 to 7.3 percent of GDP in their loss years, against at most 1.4 percent at the five largest euro-area central banks, and none of their treasuries was paid for 2022–25. What follows is a paradox. The Polish treasury is set to be paid again for 2026, although its central bank carries PLN 97 billion of uncovered losses, because its statute keeps only 5 percent of each year's profit to repay them and the rest goes to the budget: the rule that pays first is the rule that repays least. The Czech treasury, whose central bank earned CZK 206 billion in 2023–24 and used all of it against old losses, is unlikely to be paid before the mid-2030s. Without a pool of monetary income, two things decide what reaches a treasury. A single statutory clause sets the wait: for uncovered losses of 2.5 to 4 percent of GDP, what each treasury must wait for ranges from zero in Poland to about 4 percent of GDP in Czechia and, on the ECB's reading, Hungary. The interest rate on sterilisation liabilities sets the size: with euro-area rates and the same balance sheets, the Czech and Hungarian results would have been close to balance; pooling itself would have changed much less. Against what it would have received inside, the Czech treasury loses most from being outside; Hungary's loses little, because its central bank would lose money even inside. The Treaty's benchmark of financial independence sets an order but no clock, and cannot tell these rules apart.
title: Paid First, Paid Least: Central-Bank Losses Outside the Euro Area

summary: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by identifying small, faithful subgraphs--circuits--that implement specific behaviors. The dominant paradigm scores each unit by replacing its clean activation with a corrupted counterpart as causal intervention. While effective, this approach rests on a brittle prerequisite: the structure prompt pairs are task-specific, expensive to engineer, and silently couple the discovered circuit to prompt-design choices. In this work, we propose Spectral Circuit Analysis (SCA), a gradient-spectral pipeline that achieves consistent circuit discovery along both axes: stable across input formulations of the same task, and natively exposing structure shared across tasks. Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a counterfactual-free reframing of circuit discovery: causally relevant directions are recoverable from the spectral structure of forward gradients across paraphrases, with leading directions concentrating task signal and trailing ones absorbing paraphrase noise, yielding circuits tied to the task rather than the prompt. Second, we introduce SCA, a block-wise SVD pipeline that extracts a task subspace per architectural block and redistributes spectral energy onto constituent units via a consistency-weighted share, producing per-unit rankings competitive with attribution-patching baselines under strictly less supervision. Finally, on twelve circuit-discovery tasks in GPT-2 Small and Pythia-160M, SCA performs comparably or exceeds EAP-family methods under the standard recovery-score protocol and recovers IOI canonical heads with Precision@K = 1.0 in top-10 slices on GPT-2 Small; the same machinery extends to a unified cross-task analysis classifying units as universal, family-shared, or task-specific and exposing compositional structure invisible to per-task analyses.
title: Beyond Patching: Consistent Circuit Discovery via Gradient Spectral Analysis

summary: Temporal stochastic fluctuations generically destroy quantum coherence and accelerate defect generation in driven quantum systems. Here, we demonstrate that non-Hermitian dynamics can fundamentally reverse this trend by stabilizing noise-resilient late-time states. By developing an exact noise master equation for non-Hermitian systems subject to Gaussian fluctuations, we uncover a projective noise-invariance mechanism governed by T-symmetry-broken Liouvillian attractors. This mechanism produces robust defect-density plateaus and yields an exact geometric classification into noise-independent, fully polarized, and continuously tunable regimes. We substantiate these results in an imbalanced-pairing non-Hermitian Kitaev model, a prototypical pseudo-Hermitian system, and propose their experimental observation in coupled photonic waveguides. Our findings identify non-Hermitian attractor dynamics as a versatile route to controlling noise-induced excitations beyond conventional anti-Kibble-Zurek scaling.
title: Noise-Immune Attractors in Stochastically Driven Non-Hermitian Systems

summary: This dataset provides time-domain OpenFAST simulation results for the NREL 5-MW reference wind turbine mounted on the OC4-DeepCwind semisubmersible floating platform.
