summary: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,μ\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control

summary: Continual learning requires a model to learn multiple new tasks sequentially while retaining performance on previous tasks. Projecting model parameters onto the Jacobian null space of previous tasks after unconstrained training on a new task has emerged as an effective paradigm. However, unidirectional projection merely minimizes the parameter distance to the new-task optimum, overlooking the new-task loss landscape. To address this limitation, we propose DUET, a bidirectional projection algorithm that imposes Jacobian null-space constraints from both previous and new tasks during post-training projection. Specifically, DUET formulates the post-training adjustment as a dually constrained optimization problem. It minimizes the distance between parameters before and after training on a new task, subject to loss preserving constraints on both tasks. To solve the optimization problem, we develop an alternating bidirectional projection algorithm, whose convergence is guaranteed by the contraction mapping theorem. For reliable multi-step projection, we rectify existing step size selection criteria via an effective-rank aware formulation, overcoming their failure under rank-deficient Jacobians. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DUET consistently outperforms existing unidirectional projection methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.
title: Dually Constrained Parameter Projection for Continual Learning

summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.
title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.
title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM

summary: Abstract Abstract The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. We follow this one synthetic data stream through the whole construction and back to the decision (Studies 83–90, held-out seeds, every check pre-registered and frozen with SHA-256). The data give a credal fibre and its probability bands; the margins give toric chambers and walls; the margins also set the mirror potential of the degree-six del Pezzo surface, whose thimbles form an exceptional collection in its Fukaya–Seidel category. The experiment is a carrier for a realistic decision problem, not a claim about seeding. What the example verifies. Each layer is tested on held-out data: (i) credal walls lie on the chamber walls, while Stokes events are mutations; (ii) margin-order ties are collision walls where two orthogonal objects swap, confirmed at the Floer level on 10 of 12 brackets (the other two, one not audited and one with a non-minimal representative, stay in the record); (iii) a full twist of the potential acts as the Serre functor; (iv) the support region of a vector-valued hypothesis is cut out by Markov moves on the table; (v) poisoning that preserves the margins cannot move a credal decision, though it flips conventional ones (6 flips against 0); (vi) caustics, where two critical points merge, are A2 folds acting by σ±3. What it does not verify. Nothing here concerns real data or whether seeding works. Three problems remain open after a registered repair, with their checks recorded as failed: chamber reuse after one Stokes event, the control bracket of Study 83 (and the held-out bracket with the same defect), and coherence of the lift on a full slice. Every failed check is kept in the record. Categorical status. In Seidel’s framework the thimbles generate and the identification of their category with the derived category of the surface is proved (lemma 262, corollary 263). Only 1 the wrapped version in the sense of Ganatra–Pardon–Shende still rests on two steps that are argued, not certified. The rest of the note. Part I identifies the state selected by a toric potential as the lexico- graphic max–min point, up to O(1/ log(1/T )), and writes the K¨ahler dictionary in probabilistic language. Part II reads it on contingency tables, where one count of data can cross a wall. Part III treats composition, contextuality, the value of information and poisone
title: Conditioned States as Toric K¨ahler Data A companion note to "Probability, Context and Differentiation: The Layers"

summary: Semantic occupancy perception has emerged as a promising paradigm for jointly modeling 3D scene geometry and semantic information. However, this unified representation cannot compensate for missing information caused by occlusion and sensor coverage. Multi-agent cooperation alleviates this limitation, but information from different agents is not equally useful across spatial regions. Meanwhile, feature representations from each agent form the basis of reliable multi-agent fusion. Cross?modal fusion constructs such representations by integrating complementary semantic and geometric information. Despite this complementarity, jointly establishing reliable 3D correspondence across agents and preserving modality-specific structures remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose CoopOcc, which performs cooperative 3D semantic occupancy perception through multi-agent and cross-modal fusion. CoopOcc uses ego?query cross-agent attention (EQCA) to selectively aggregate aligned features across agents, and anchor-based bidirectional feature interaction (ABFI) for cross-modal exchange at matched coordinates. We further construct SemanticVVSim, a simulation dataset, and establish a unified benchmark. For simulation-to-real transfer, we propose confidence-aware hierarchical occupancy and relational distillation (CHORD). CoopOcc performs best overall among ten evaluated methods on SemanticVVSim. On Occ3D-nuScenes, CHORD improves performance using knowledge from SemanticVVSim. The code is available at https://github.com/LOTEAT/CoopOcc.
title: CoopOcc: Cooperative 3D Semantic Occupancy Perception via Multi-Agent and Cross-Modal Fusion

summary: Predicting the transient nonlinear responses of complex engineering structures remains challenging due to large finite element meshes, heterogeneous structural components, and history-dependent mechanical behavior. This study proposes a topology-prior-guided regional latent dynamics (TPLD) surrogate model that combines physically structured regional representations with dynamics-aware latent learning for full-field time-history prediction. Based on mesh topology and engineering priors, structural responses are encoded into spatially coupled regional latent variables through region-aware feature extraction and topology-constrained interactions. An auxiliary one-step prediction task enhances latent-space dynamical predictability by introducing state-transition supervision. A load-conditioned spatiotemporal Mamba model then predicts regional latent trajectories by integrating temporal causal scanning and bidirectional spatial scanning, while a shared coordinate-conditioned decoder reconstructs full-field nodal responses. The framework is evaluated on three finite element datasets: a parametric stiffened panel, a partitioned pressure impact plate, and a Toyota Yaris full-vehicle crash model. The relative L2 errors for the three displacement components range from 4.00% to 8.21% on the stiffened panel and from 1.41% to 12.22% on the approximately 1.49-million-node vehicle model. On the BIW crash benchmark, TPLD achieves a relative L2 position error of 0.620%, representing a 30.7% reduction compared with the best-performing GeoTransolver configuration. Ablation studies demonstrate the advantages of topology-guided regional representations over global latent and learnable soft-slice alternatives, while auxiliary one-step prediction particularly improves the prediction of accumulated plastic strain.
title: Topology-Prior-Guided Regional Latent Dynamics for Transient Structural Response Prediction

summary: Abstract Abstract The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. summary: Node affinity prediction in the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) asks how a node's future interactions will be distributed over other nodes. On this task, methods that reuse past ground-truth labels often outperform temporal graph neural networks, and the state of the art builds on them. Such comparisons assume a point-in-time correct evaluation, in which a model receives only information available at prediction time. Drawing on as-of joins and bitemporal databases, we formalize this requirement by distinguishing when a label must be predicted, its query time, from when it is fully determined, its availability time, and we audit the four TGB node affinity datasets and their evaluation loop with model-agnostic tools. None of the four meets it. On three datasets, each label summarizes a single day about five days after its timestamp, not the documented following week, yet the loop feeds it back right after that timestamp; on the fourth, the loop processes the edges from which each label is computed before predicting it. Under a drop-in leakage-free protocol, every method whose inputs leak loses up to 17% of its NDCG@10, the advantage of past labels over the interaction stream nearly vanishes or reverses, and both the best configuration of the state of the art and the rankings change; a blend of training-free long-memory statistics, with weights fit on validation data, matches or exceeds the state of the art under both protocols. Point-in-time correctness should therefore be built into benchmarks, and our tools carry over to other benchmarks whose labels aggregate event streams over time windows.
title: Temporal Leakage Distorts the TGB Node Affinity Leaderboard: A Point-in-Time Audit

summary: Modern astronomical workflows require the coordinated use of specialised software, scientific archives, heterogeneous data, and domain-specific knowledge. Advances in large language models and multimodal foundation models enable natural-language interaction with scientific data and tools. Realising this potential requires integrating these models with established scientific capabilities. We present MAASAI (Multi-agent Astronomy Assistant for Scientific Analysis and Inference), a modular multi-agent system combining foundation-model reasoning, retrieval-augmented knowledge, and specialised astronomical tools within a graph-based execution framework. MAASAI coordinates request preparation, planning, execution, and response synthesis via specialised workers. Its architecture supports native and external applications, artefact and provenance management, optional human approval, and configurable inference backends, including fully local deployment with open-weight models. Motivated by SKA-era data-analysis challenges, MAASAI is also designed to support other astronomical domains. We evaluate MAASAI through radio-image benchmarks, single- and multi-step workflow demonstrations, and literature-grounded reasoning. Compared with a commercial-model baseline, MAASAI improves macro-averaged F1 scores from 0.53 to 0.72 for extended/diffuse emission classification and from 0.37 to 0.88 for source morphology classification. Workflow demonstrations show the coordination of measurements, source extraction, archive queries, and catalogue processing. A 94-question literature benchmark yielded generally favourable automated assessments, with comparable ratings from a pilot expert evaluation of 59 answers. These results highlight how tool-augmented multi-agent systems extend foundation-model reasoning to specialised astronomical analyses through established scientific software.
title: MAASAI: A Tool-Augmented Multi-Agent System for Astronomical Data Analysis

summary: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.
title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?

summary: AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it. We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion. We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration. In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.
title: Stable but Hidden: Identifiability and Experimental Design under Missing Compositional Support

summary: Version 1.25.0. Code, a dated analysis log and statistics files for a study of verbatim uptake of chatbot text in students' graded project proposals (FLoRA Open Data IPS, 275 students). v1.1.0 added log entry R1: time-aware echo correction, third-source filter, clock check from chat-box keystrokes, validation against logged paste events, and extended analyses of grades and detection. v1.2.0 adds log entry R2: three open zero-shot AI-text detectors (log-likelihood, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars on Qwen2.5 models) evaluated against logged provenance at paragraph level, by first language, and sensitivity of the third-source threshold. All analyses are exploratory. No third-party data are redistributed. v1.3.0 adds log entry R3: attribution of each token of the submitted artefact to five provenance classes (chatbot-first, echo, shared source, typed, untraced insertion), applied to FLoRA and to the RelianceScope programming dataset with validation against human response-use codes and an unaided post-test; FLoRA detector reanalysis on typed vs untraced text (post hoc). Third-party data are not redistributed. v1.4.0 adds log entry R4: entry mode by edit size, validation of typed and untraced classes against logged pastes, chance baseline and conservative bounds for chatbot-first code, length-controlled validation against human codes, and a censored model of the post-test. v1.4.1 records the RelianceScope authors' permission to use the dataset with citation; no analyses changed. v1.5.0 adds log entry R5: within-document moves in the untraced class, token-level projection, clock distribution, segment-local entry rule, origin of echo text, timing baseline by class, code-aware tokenisation for the programming data, robustness of the grade model (multiple imputation, censoring, transformations, class shares) and of the post-test models (chance-corrected and reference-excluded uptake, task progress), detector thresholds, and a size-matched and semantic paraphrase check. v1.6.0 adds log entry R6, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: attribution with degraded logs (dialogue only, thinned editor snapshots), effect of every parameter choice on the main quantities, chance baseline by n-gram length, descriptive subdivision of the untraced class, origin of logged pastes, minimum detectable effects and simulated power of the outcome models, and a self-contained end-to-end demonstration on synthetic logs (demo/). No measure or class definition changed. v1.7.0 adds log entry R7, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: comparison of students with and without logged paste events, agreement of segment uptake with each human response-use code, a diagram of the routes by which text reaches the editor, and the class figure recomputed with the edit-size entry rule. No measure or class definition changed. v1.8.0 adds log entry R8, committed before its analyses ran, after earlier results were known: sensitivity of the grade analysis to misclassification of untraced text, equivalence tests, order of the echo and shared-source rules, agreement with retyped code, a label-noise ceiling for the human codes, a comparison with the LLM classifiers released with RelianceScope, post-test models with pre-activity covariates, numerical-Hessian standard errors for the censored models, and token-level five-class labels produced by the attribution of the 275 FLoRA proposals (CC BY 4.0). No measure or class definition changed. v1.9.0 renames the analysis files from PREREG_* to ANALYSIS_LOG_* (file names cited inside them updated, content otherwise unchanged; the entries record decisions made as the analysis proceeded and are not pre-registrations) and adds log entry R9: accuracy against simulated logs with known routes under clock offsets, snapshot thinning and paraphrase; an audit of sampled passages against keystrokes and chatbot-panel selections that the attribution does not use; echo split by entry mode and route
title: Bidirectional provenance attribution of chatbot text in writing and programming logs (FLoRA, RelianceScope): code, analysis log, benchmark, statistics

summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.
title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains

summary: Reproducibility archive (code and results) of the article "Per-Pixel Reliability Gating Versus Classifier-Selected Switching for Frozen Image Denoisers Under Synthetic Noise-Type Mismatch". The archive holds the wrappers around the pretrained denoisers (DnCNN, FFDNet, DRUNet; vendored KAIR network definitions with their licence); the per-pixel gate with its fuzzy-set family of reliability models (fuzzy, intuitionistic fuzzy, Pythagorean fuzzy, neutrosophic), its disagreement and residual controls and the isolated-signal gates, including gates that see only a family map, under a search-box widening policy; the constant blend; the noise-type classifier, the classifier-selected and one-feature switches and the set of classical filters; the gate calibrated with the same adaptive median filter as the switch, with its recalibrations; the cost-weighted calibration for both impulse filters over a grid of weights, and the cost of a misclassified image over independent recalibrations; the filter-then-network cascade and the per-pixel bound on every test cell; the classifier probes on image crops and unseen noise levels with the networks run on those inputs; the attribution controls (best-filter oracle, adaptive median, BM3D, mixture of experts at several budgets); the calibration-stability refits; the evaluation with the estimated noise level in every regime; the probes with Poisson noise, mixed Gaussian-impulse noise and random-valued impulses; the optimizers with persisted convergence traces; the image-clustered statistical pipeline (cluster bootstrap, sign-flip permutation, Holm); SSIM and LPIPS; the real-noise studies (PolyU and SIDD, scene-grouped cross-fits); the computational-cost profiles; the content-hashed calibration, the diagnostics, every result (per-image detail rows, statistics, generated LaTeX tables and macros, provenance record), the figures of the article with their sources, the test suite, requirements.txt and REPRODUCE.md. The experiments on a small network trained by the authors, of which one is documented in the Supplementary Material as a boundary case, are included with their results and trained checkpoints. Every reported number regenerates deterministically from this code, the calibration file and the recorded per-cell seeds; datasets and pretrained weights are public and are downloaded and SHA-256-verified by scripts/fetch_data.py (SIDD under the licence stated on its project page). Concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21317308 resolves to the latest version.
title: Reproducibility archive: Per-Pixel Reliability Gating Versus Classifier-Selected Switching for Frozen Image Denoisers Under Synthetic Noise-Type Mismatch

summary: Human–AI communities inherit familiar political relations while enabling powers to propagate through delegated agents, retained histories, and changing infrastructures. This paper investigates how those pathways alter feasible interventions, recognized authority, and distributed burdens. It distinguishes an event-precedence partial order supporting modeled histories, a domain-relative capacity preorder and quotient order, and relational composition in a delegation network. A specified order can restrict a declared background symmetry group; substantive power relevance requires differential shaping of relational continuations. A targeted primary-source survey engages common agency, institutional power, agentic inequality, persistent agent architectures, memory manipulation, agent-society studies, and delegation research alongside political and institutional theory. Joint delegation can distribute funding, source permission, execution, and configuration while concentrating the evidence on which principals act. A finite historical comparison shows how equal current competence, or equal actual work, can produce unequal review authority through allocation and admission rules. Counter-power is examined through supported capacities to refuse, reinterpret, organize, or continue through an alternative. Prior prompts, memories, tools, parameter changes, relationships, and attributed histories remain distinct carriers. An exploitation analysis separates descriptive hierarchy, unfair appropriation, burden displacement, domination, and possible AI welfare harm; a constructed agent–subagent history follows costs into the wider human relational structure. Standard proofs and exact diagnostics clarify symmetry restrictions, capacity equivalence, propagation, historical reinforcement, replication, investment, and continuity. Matched-history comparisons distinguish possibilities, exercise, recipient response, and later standing, including complementarity, interference, copying, and selective records. The contribution is a connected comparative framework with explicit antecedents and evidence requirements. Community constitutions and interaction strategies remain configurable; implemented and field studies supply the subsequent assessment of their effects.
title: A Discussion of Political Authority and Infrastructural Power in Human–AI Communities

summary: Description This release extends the existing experimental data archive supporting “Modeling Sequential Thermal Adaptation in the Marine Bacterium Cobetia marina: Hidden Markov Models and Mixtures of Experts under Progressive Ocean Warming”. It contains the longitudinal adaptive laboratory evolution data for 93 lineages across 15 ascending thermal conditions (35–42 °C), yielding 1,394 usable lineage–passage profiles. Four phenotypic descriptors are analyzed: maximum log-optical-density slope, integrated optical density, maximum OD600, and normalized biofilm (OD540/OD600). The archive includes source data and provenance, fixed lineage validation folds, 136 archived multivariate HMM and mixture-of-experts parameter sets, numerical search histories, 18 local covariance-regularization refits, balanced-budget comparisons, a passage-specific Gaussian benchmark, held-out emission diagnostics, bootstrap and thermal breakpoint sensitivity analyses, and genotype-linked trajectories of eight selected terminal clones. R and Python code and numerical outputs are provided. A unified base-R audit was executed in R 4.6.1 on Windows 11: all seven stages completed successfully; the maximum absolute discrepancy across the 136 archived-model verification outputs was 3.64 × 10⁻¹². The audit verifies archived estimates and does not constitute a complete independent reoptimization. The original data and published detection classifications are retained separately. The experiment does not identify causal temperature effects independently of passage order, or molecular identities of latent states. Keywords Cobetia marina; adaptive laboratory evolution; marine heatwaves; ocean warming; biofilm; multivariate hidden Markov models; mixture of experts; change-point analysis; reproducibility; csgD1
title: Longitudinal Thermal-Passage Phenotypes of Cobetia marina: Experimental Data, Hidden Markov Models, Mixtures of Experts, and Reproducible Analysis Code

summary: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.
title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems

summary: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation

summary: Data curation---the process of collecting, cleaning, and joining raw datasets for unified analysis---is a time-consuming yet crucial part of any data science project. With the emergence of powerful agentic coding tools, it is tempting to "vibe curate"---i.e., to prompt AI agents to perform data curation operations and blindly trust their outputs in order to finish work more quickly. However, this can exacerbate two key challenges that already plague manual data curation workflows: reproducibility---the ability to trace the exact set of modifications applied to raw datasets---and verifiability---the ability to audit changes and confirm that data is processed properly. To address these issues, we introduce Scrub Data, a framework that enables the use of AI agents in data curation workflows while transparently maintaining both reproducibility and verifiability. The framework involves an interactive data curation loop between a user and an AI agent, backed by a data provenance graph that tracks and versions all dataset updates. The data graph requires that all updates are formatted as self-contained executable steps, allowing any version of a dataset to be reconstructed from raw data by playing forward the transformations stored in the graph. This workflow takes place within a lightweight web application that is designed to be modified by users and agents in real-time to create custom visualization tools for identifying data curation needs and verifying outcomes. We demonstrate the usefulness of the framework with a real data curation use case from animal movement ecology. Starting with 89M raw GPS coordinates, we use the framework to curate a benchmark dataset of 2.5M coordinates to be used for machine learning or statistical analysis. The framework is available for use and extension at https://github.com/justinkay/scrubdata.
title: Scrub Data: A Framework for Reproducible Data Curation with AI Coding Agents

summary: A latent diffusion model's output has already passed through its autoencoder, so a second round trip changes it very little. This "déjà vu" underlies reconstruction-based detectors of generated images; we analyse when it reveals a generated image and when it does not. Read by a frozen vision foundation model without training, the trace is strongest in intermediate layers, and, unlike pixel-level reconstruction error, it treats blur as a sign of a real image. It belongs to the generator's exact decoder: on Synthbuster, the exact decoders of Stable Diffusion 1.3, 1.4, 2 and XL are the strongest of eight autoencoders and catch 94-100% of their generators' images at a 5% false-alarm rate (SDXL's version identified post hoc), while near-identical versions catch 7-42%. A detector trained only on real photographs and their autoencoder copies matches one trained on 162k generated images on GenImage (+2.3 points, 95% CI [0.9, 3.7]) and complements it in fusion, but one resize with JPEG re-save, or a mild blur, costs it 19-27 points. Two lessons concern benchmarks. The in-the-wild benchmark Chameleon can be solved from image width alone. And on Synthbuster, how the real photographs are matched to the generated images' size decides whether our detector leads or trails (+4.4 or -9.7 points): the matching protocol alone can reverse a detector comparison. Code and per-image scores: https://github.com/iamsaugatpandey/deja-vae
title: Déjà VAE: When Do Autoencoder Traces Reveal Generated Images?

summary: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural networks by identifying small, faithful subgraphs--circuits--that implement specific behaviors. The dominant paradigm scores each unit by replacing its clean activation with a corrupted counterpart as causal intervention. While effective, this approach rests on a brittle prerequisite: the structure prompt pairs are task-specific, expensive to engineer, and silently couple the discovered circuit to prompt-design choices. In this work, we propose Spectral Circuit Analysis (SCA), a gradient-spectral pipeline that achieves consistent circuit discovery along both axes: stable across input formulations of the same task, and natively exposing structure shared across tasks. Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a counterfactual-free reframing of circuit discovery: causally relevant directions are recoverable from the spectral structure of forward gradients across paraphrases, with leading directions concentrating task signal and trailing ones absorbing paraphrase noise, yielding circuits tied to the task rather than the prompt. Second, we introduce SCA, a block-wise SVD pipeline that extracts a task subspace per architectural block and redistributes spectral energy onto constituent units via a consistency-weighted share, producing per-unit rankings competitive with attribution-patching baselines under strictly less supervision. Finally, on twelve circuit-discovery tasks in GPT-2 Small and Pythia-160M, SCA performs comparably or exceeds EAP-family methods under the standard recovery-score protocol and recovers IOI canonical heads with Precision@K = 1.0 in top-10 slices on GPT-2 Small; the same machinery extends to a unified cross-task analysis classifying units as universal, family-shared, or task-specific and exposing compositional structure invisible to per-task analyses.
title: Beyond Patching: Consistent Circuit Discovery via Gradient Spectral Analysis

summary: Based on symmetry analysis, the Pna2_1 wurtzite-based crystal structure with Mn as a magnetic group-II element, MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 belong to the class of altermagnets because spin-up and spin-down Mn in the unit cell are related by rotation or mirror plane type operations rather than inversion or translation. Spin polarized density functional theory calculations and quasiparticle self-consistent (QS) GW calculations support the symmetry analysis and identify the lowest-energy spin configuration as Pna'2_1' in agreement with neutron diffraction data. The altermagnetic band splittings allowed for the three different antiferromagnetic ordering patterns are reported and symmetry analyzed. Additionally, spin wave dispersions, chiral magnon spltting, and Neel temperature estimates from the mean-field and random-phase approximations are provided, as well as calculations of the optical dielectric function using the Bethe-Salpeter Equation method. MnSiN2 exhibits both Wannier-type excitons with N-p to Si-s transition character and charge-transfer Frenkel-type excitons with hole on N-p and electron on Mn-d orbital character.
title: Altermagnetism of MnSiN2 and MnGeN2 in a wurtzite-based crystal structure

summary: Temporal stochastic fluctuations generically destroy quantum coherence and accelerate defect generation in driven quantum systems. Here, we demonstrate that non-Hermitian dynamics can fundamentally reverse this trend by stabilizing noise-resilient late-time states. By developing an exact noise master equation for non-Hermitian systems subject to Gaussian fluctuations, we uncover a projective noise-invariance mechanism governed by T-symmetry-broken Liouvillian attractors. This mechanism produces robust defect-density plateaus and yields an exact geometric classification into noise-independent, fully polarized, and continuously tunable regimes. We substantiate these results in an imbalanced-pairing non-Hermitian Kitaev model, a prototypical pseudo-Hermitian system, and propose their experimental observation in coupled photonic waveguides. Our findings identify non-Hermitian attractor dynamics as a versatile route to controlling noise-induced excitations beyond conventional anti-Kibble-Zurek scaling.
title: Noise-Immune Attractors in Stochastically Driven Non-Hermitian Systems

summary: Multi-View Stereo (MVS) and Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) provide complementary cues for dense 3D reconstruction. While MVS leverages explicit geometry for metric depth, it struggles in challenging regions where feature matching is unreliable. Conversely, MDE provides robust structural priors but typically yields scale-ambiguous results. Existing hybrid methods mainly exploit monocular cues in a unidirectional manner, leaving the mutual enhancement between MDE and MVS insufficiently explored. To address this limitation, we propose BridgeMVS, a unified cascaded multi-stage MVS framework that bridges monocular depth features and multi-view cost volume representations through Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF). At each stage, BDF performs dynamic mono-to-cost and cost-to-mono updates, where monocular structural features guide cost volume refinement for more robust MVS depth estimation, while multi-view geometric evidence recalibrates monocular representations to improve their metric-scale consistency. Furthermore, the fused monocular and multi-view representations are progressively propagated from coarse to fine stages and constrained by stage-wise relative-scale MDE supervision and metric-scale MVS supervision, enabling cross-branch interactions to benefit subsequent high-resolution depth estimation. In addition, BDF is designed as a plug-and-play module that can be conveniently integrated into existing cascaded MVS frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BridgeMVS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D benchmarks, while simultaneously boosting the accuracy of monocular depth estimation. Notably, BridgeMVS ranks first on both the Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced benchmarks. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}.
title: BridgeMVS: Bridging Multi-View Stereo and Monodepth via Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion

summary: Abstract Abstract The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. We follow this one synthetic data stream through the whole construction and back to the decision (Studies 83–90, held-out seeds, every check pre-registered and frozen with SHA-256). The data give a credal fibre and its probability bands; the margins give toric chambers and walls; the margins also set the mirror potential of the degree-six del Pezzo surface, whose thimbles form an exceptional collection in its Fukaya–Seidel category. The experiment is a carrier for a realistic decision problem, not a claim about seeding. What the example verifies. Each layer is tested on held-out data: (i) credal walls lie on the chamber walls, while Stokes events are mutations; (ii) margin-order ties are collision walls where two orthogonal objects swap, confirmed at the Floer level on 10 of 12 brackets (the other two, one not audited and one with a non-minimal representative, stay in the record); (iii) a full twist of the potential acts as the Serre functor; (iv) the support region of a vector-valued hypothesis is cut out by Markov moves on the table; (v) poisoning that preserves the margins cannot move a credal decision, though it flips conventional ones (6 flips against 0); (vi) caustics, where two critical points merge, are A2 folds acting by σ±3. What it does not verify. Nothing here concerns real data or whether seeding works. Three problems remain open after a registered repair, with their checks recorded as failed: chamber reuse after one Stokes event, the control bracket of Study 83 (and the held-out bracket with the same defect), and coherence of the lift on a full slice. Every failed check is kept in the record. Categorical status. In Seidel’s framework the thimbles generate and the identification of their category with the derived category of the surface is proved (lemma 262, corollary 263). Only 1 the wrapped version in the sense of Ganatra–Pardon–Shende still rests on two steps that are argued, not certified. The rest of the note. Part I identifies the state selected by a toric potential as the lexico- graphic max–min point, up to O(1/ log(1/T )), and writes the K¨ahler dictionary in probabilistic language. Part II reads it on contingency tables, where one count of data can cross a wall. Part III treats composition, contextuality, the value of information and poisone
title: Conditioned States as Toric K¨ahler Data A companion note to "Probability, Context and Differentiation: The Layers"

summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.
title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence

summary: A multi-agent group-generation system, as operated here, spends test-time compute uniformly across tasks. That a single agent's own vote distribution can gate its test-time compute is already reported by CATTS; we ask the multi-agent question: whether the distribution of stated confidences and critiques across a group of role-specialised agents predicts how hard a task is, which would let the group's compute be allocated adaptively. Taking as testbed a five-agent orchestrator for Perturb-seq response prediction inspired by CellForge and operated via MassGen, we define four trace metrics — Agent Confidence Entropy (ACE), Critique Severity Dispersion (CSD), a convergence signal (ΔC), and a Winner Flip Rate (WFR) — and their composite, the Task Difficulty Index (TDI). We pre-register five hypotheses with criteria: attainable error on Adamson 2016 (CRISPR interference) and Norman 2019 (CRISPR activation), the Architect agent's backbone-choice entropy, the rank correlation of each TDI component with held-out error, and cross-dataset transfer of a calibrated TDI. The design is 41 held-out K562 tasks (21 Adamson, 15 Norman singletons, 5 Norman doublets) drawn deterministically, a trainer sweep of 27 records per task and three fixed-length agentic lifecycle runs per task, all in one process. The agents are large language models (LLMs) from a pinned roster of Anthropic Claude models (Haiku 4.5 for the four proposer roles, Sonnet 5.5 for the Validator) whose served model is recorded and asserted per call; a run with any rule-based fallback step is invalid. Every run records its git revision, resolved configuration, library versions, dataset SHA-256 digests, task plan and label contract. We find that four of the five pre-registered hypotheses are supported and the cross-dataset transfer hypothesis is not; every hypothesis could be evaluated. The trainer sweep reaches the pre-registered error on both screens, and the Architect's choice of backbone varies above the pre-registered entropy floor. Within each screen, the drop in the agents' confidence across rounds, and the composite that inherits it, rank tasks by held-out error. From the second round on, however, every agent's prompt carries the previous round's held-out error, so that drop is stated after an error has been shown. In an exploratory analysis, the mean confidence stated before any feedback does not rank tasks by error (ρ = 0.003 on Adamson and 0.214 on Norman, both intervals including zero). Read with the design and that analysis, the pre-registered pass is consistent with stated confidence falling further where a larger error was shown; it is not evidence that the group's confidence anticipates difficulty. The composite fitted on Adamson did not meet the pre-registered transfer criterion on Norman (ρ = 0.286 against a criterion of > 0.4). The point estimates for confidence entropy, an evenness index over the agents, run against the pre-registered direction in both screens; this is exploratory, and no claim is made. The preflight probe and recommender are specified but not evaluated. The values reported in the earlier release of this work are superseded in full; the defects behind each are listed in the appendix.
title: Does Multi-Agent Confidence Predict Task Difficulty, or Only React to It? A Pre-registered Test on Perturb-seq

Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The library that did not own its readers In the imagined city of Meridian, the librarian inherited three copies of an ancient atlas. One could be read on the eastern terminal, one on the western terminal, and one in the shelter beneath the school. When the reader software was retired, all three became unreadable on the same morning. There was no fire, no lost disk, and no malicious visitor. The collection had survived in a form that nobody could open. Letter to the future: A letter to a librarian not yet born Build a library whose continued operation does not depend upon loyalty to its first librarian. Give later caretakers the authority to replace the catalog, repair the software, correct the record, and create new routes through the collection. Keep the old record when its lawful preservation matters; keep the correction equally visible. In a faraway city, the most valuable inheritance might not be an indestructible monument. It might be a modest institution that knows how to repair itself without silencing its readers. Research Gate 001: Replica independence — Mechanism contrast Origin: Replica independence begins with a question: what would remain unexplained if researchers could separate archive replicas by failure domain? An archive object is usable only when its bytes, format, provenance and rights survive together. A manifest is not itself a reconstruction, and geographically separated disks may share one decoder. The unit of analysis is a requested licensed record, not a file count or a storage device. The mechanism contrast is a distinct experiment on that question, not a claim that the intervention has succeeded. At first the school judged the tutor by the beauty of the notebooks that returned from its lessons. The notebooks became magnificent. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The library that did not own its readers In the imagined city of Meridian, the librarian inherited three copies of an ancient atlas. One could be read on the eastern terminal, one on the western terminal, and one in the shelter beneath the school. When the reader software was retired, all three became unreadable on the same morning. There was no fire, no lost disk, and no malicious visitor. The collection had survived in a form that nobody could open. Letter to the future: A letter to a librarian not yet born Build a library whose continued operation does not depend upon loyalty to its first librarian. At first the school judged the tutor by the beauty of the notebooks that returned from its lessons. The notebooks became magnificent. One could be read on the eastern terminal, one on the western terminal, and one in the shelter beneath the school. When the reader software was retired, all three became unreadable on the same morning. There was no fire, no lost disk, and no malicious visitor. The collection had survived in a form that nobody could open. Letter to the future: A letter to a librarian not yet born Build a library whose continued operation does not depend upon loyalty to its first librarian. Give later caretakers the authority to replace the catalog, repair the software, correct the record, and create new routes through the collection. It might be a modest institution that knows how to repair itself without silencing its readers. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The machine that learned to be quiet The school in Meridian received a tutor that could speak in more languages than any citizen. It could finish a proof before a learner found the first line, and write a polished argument before the learner decided what the question meant. At first the school judged the tutor by the beauty of the notebooks that returned from its lessons. The notebooks became magnificent. Then, during a planned offline afternoon, some of the students discovered that they could not explain the work attributed to them. Letter to the future: A letter to the teacher of another sky If our methods become part of your school, you are free to abandon them wherever they do not help. We do not need every child to call a research question a Research Gate. We need children to discover that a question can belong to them, that an explanation may be tested, and that changing their minds can be a sign of intellectual strength. direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [REVERSE]
summary: Este trabalho relata a experiência de desenvolvimento e implantação do RIF, sistema web de controle de refeições estudantis do Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia de Rondônia (IFRO) – Campus Porto Velho Calama. O sistema surgiu da necessidade do Departamento de Assistência ao Educando (DEPAE) de superar o gerenciamento baseado na importação recorrente de planilhas e de ampliar o acompanhamento da utilização das refeições. A aplicação foi construída de forma incremental, a partir de requisitos levantados junto ao DEPAE e ao restaurante institucional, com PHP, CodeIgniter 4, MySQL e arquitetura MVC, e integra o cadastro de estudantes e usuários, a solicitação, a análise e o agendamento das refeições, a confirmação por mensagem e o registro de retirada por QR Code. Entre 3 e 31 de agosto de 2026, o RIF registrou 18.882 refeições liberadas, das quais 13.337 foram confirmadas (70,63%) e 10.464 tiveram retirada registrada, além de 2.873 confirmações sem retirada e 86 inativações, envolvendo 80 estudantes que ignoraram as mensagens de confirmação. Os resultados indicam que o sistema fornece ao DEPAE indicadores e históricos para o acompanhamento do benefício. A experiência evidenciou, ainda, as dificuldades formativas da equipe e o impacto da mudança de requisitos, e apontou a necessidade de um manual de procedimentos para orientar os novos integrantes.
title: RIF: SISTEMA DE CONTROLE DE REFEIÇÕES ESTUDANTIS DO IFRO – CAMPUS PORTO VELHO CALAMA

summary: This is a leakage-controlled active-learning benchmark archive evaluating diversity-, uncertainty-, committee-, Gaussian-process-, and D-optimal acquisition policies on molecular adsorption free-energy prediction under cold- and warm-start replay regimes. The release includes identity-level learning-curve metrics, family-locked inferential comparisons, operational threshold sensitivity analyses, machine-readable figure datasets, formatted reference tables, and reproducible Python verification scripts tied to protocol SHA-256 e3729ec2ec9d1df5d6e3f57121e4596a8e33454125d5210e2a6631e591f2f059. Raw upstream descriptor matrices and adsorption free-energy tables from an ongoing companion study are withheld pending publication, with their SHA-256 provenance digests retained in data/protocol_config.json.

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/
title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models

summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.
title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories

summary: The work continues the geometric model of the distribution of primes [2] and the work “The Number Arrow and the Line 1/2” [1]. The geometric formula for the number of odd composites up to p², N(p) = 1 + 3(p − 1)(p − 3)/8, is treated as the first level of a ladder in which the scale is squared at each step: 5² → 5⁴ → 5⁸ → 5¹⁶. It is shown that this formula is the best quadratic formula for the level up to 5⁴: it is exact everywhere except for one compensating pair of misses (p = 15 and p = 17). The quadratic lattice of a level holds up to the basis 7 inclusive and breaks down right after it. The error of the formula splits into two superimposed tables: a smooth level correction and an oscillation which, in the explicit formula, is a sum of cosines over the zeros of the zeta function. The main result is a law of levels, checked on exact values of π(x) up to 3³² ≈ 1.9 · 10¹⁵: when the scale is squared, the relative error of the prime count is squared, and the error itself is inverse to the linear scale p = √x obtained from the difference of squares: ε · p stays of order one at all checked steps. The law holding at all steps is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis (von Koch, 1901). The author puts forward the hypothesis that the self-similarity of the ladder may become a route to its proof: for this one must show that the step structure itself does not allow ε · p to grow faster than a power of the logarithm. This step is named but not taken. The method may become the basis for an exact count of prime density by levels without the exponential and the logarithm in the level formula. Section 7 gives a geometric reading for a reader without mathematical training: why the basis of the model is 2, 3, 5, 7, how the seam 8–9 links the linear and the quadratic levels, why the centres of the seam differ by exactly ¼ and how π arises from all the differences together, where zero is on the arrow and why the whole arrow projects into one circle. The similarity with the construction of the Birth of Dimensions model is shown. Section 8 shows that the accumulated mismatch over the seams is Euler's sine at one half (π), while accumulation over the primes gives γ (Mertens); that the error of the prime count at a step is of the order of the square root of the mismatch of the frame; and that the transfer of the observer changes nothing if and only if all zeros lie on the axis 1/2 — this is the Hilbert — Pólya programme. Each seam is a right triangle in a circle: the centre along the line is the radius, the centre on the circle the cosine, the hole the sine, and sin² + cos² = 1. The author believes that this work can become a proof of the Riemann hypothesis; the missing step is to show that the unity of the process makes the transfer of the observer a symmetry. The work is laid out as a programme of proof: the missing step is formulated as a target statement resting on the birth of the arrow — a pure projection from one unit, the product over the primes. The missing step is also written as a statement about positivity: from Mertens' square 2(1 + cos θ)², which pushes the zeros away from 1, to the square of Weil's energy, which must hold them on ½ and forbid pairs of zeros on opposite sides of the circle. The work rests on classical results — Pell–Lagrange, Legendre's sieve, the explicit formula of Riemann and von Mangoldt — and proposes a new linking of them: the geometry of the seam as a model of the process linking the primes. The author's answer to Riemann's question is geometric: on each range chosen in a definite way, the process of the link of the primes is seen as the unit circle and a sinusoid around it; for his work the author regards this answer as a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and what in it is accepted as an initial prin

summary: This release provides crystal structures, thermal-conductivity data, pretrained DANA-$\kappa$ models, and computational workflows for high-throughput discovery of low-conductivity materials. It includes DANA-$\kappa$ predictions for 1,953,259 structures from Materials Project and Crystoria, 4,724 GRACE-based thermal-conductivity results, and CIF files for the 1,712 GRACE records satisfying $0<\kappa_{\mathrm L}<2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The DFT dataset contains 60 completed calculations with corresponding relaxed structures, including 58 phases below $2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and 29 below $0.5~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The lowest DFT value is approximately $0.1826~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CsKAu_2}$. Conductivity values refer to 300 K and represent the diagonal average of the population-plus-coherence lattice thermal-conductivity tensor, excluding electronic conductivity. Additional resources include second- and third-order DFT force constants and reference transport outputs for the 58 low-conductivity phases, three split-specific DANA-$\kappa$ checkpoints, and scripts for inference, physical-property filtering, computational-cost estimation, structural deduplication, GRACE calculations, and VASP validation. Structure provenance, calculation settings, and quality annotations accompany the data to support reproducible analysis and subsequent model development.

summary: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.

summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used for medical image reconstruction and super-resolution, but their samples may contain plausible fine-scale hallucinations that are difficult to identify from the reconstructed image alone. We propose Med-PODiff, a patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) diffusion framework for brain MRI super-resolution that performs generative reconstruction in compact and interpretable local coefficient spaces. Unlike pixel-space or learned-latent diffusion models, Med-PODiff uses the POD structure to separate low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residual variation, enabling predictive uncertainty to be decomposed into total, coarse, and fine components. summary: This paper proposes a method for identifying a control-oriented model of a stable continuous-time linear system from aperiodically sampled input-output data. Rather than recovering the continuous-time matrices, the method directly identifies a discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) state-space model that depends affinely on the measured normalized sampling-interval variation, a structure obtained from the first-order expansion of the zero-order-hold discretization. The resulting model is directly usable in control design for aperiodic sampled-data systems. An initial LPV estimate, including approximate first-order terms, is derived from a standard LTI subspace model through sampled-data relations. The method then iteratively alternates state-sequence reconstruction and LPV parameter refitting. Numerical examples show that the identified model retains high validation accuracy over a wide range of sampling-interval variations where a fixed LTI model degrades. Already at initialization, the state-space LPV structure substantially outperforms an LPV-ARX regression with the same scheduling variable, and the iterative refinement brings the model close to a state-measured benchmark, a practical upper-bound reference.
title: Iterative Identification of Aperiodic Sampled-Data Systems via Affine LPV Models Scheduled by the Sampling Interval

summary: We study scalar-field models in 1+1 dimensions with field-dependent kinetic coefficients, motivated by self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory as a generator of integrable equations. We derive the Euler-Lagrange equation, traveling-wave reduction, and first integral, and solve the inverse problem: given a kinetic structure and a prescribed tanh kink, which potential makes it exact? A quadratic spatial deformation with a canonical temporal sector yields a sextic potential. We obtain: (i) a closed-form kink energy with a Bogomolny-type formulation, independent of the odd parameter, which nonetheless shapes the energy density asymmetrically; (ii) vacuum curvature relations tying the spectrum to the kinetic function at the vacua; (iii) two propositions on speed families, plus a lemma showing single-speed data probe only one combination of the kinetic functions; (iv) a unified admissibility analysis in which positivity of the spatial kinetic function controls hyperbolicity, the potential bound along the kink, and the vacuum masses; (v) a self-adjoint fluctuation operator with a closed-form potential whose asymptotes are the vacuum masses, an exact translation zero mode, and numerical spectra with no negative mode on the admissible region, evidence for spectral stability. Exact SDYM reductions yield integrable equations, whereas the deformed model is generically non-integrable and cannot be an exact reduction. The correct bridge is the moduli-space route: SDYM reduces to the Bogomolny equations, whose BPS monopole and dyon dynamics produce field-dependent kinetic terms; any smooth one-dimensional moduli metric expands, to second order, to the quadratic model studied here, and the Taub-NUT metric of well-separated dyons gives an explicit realization. Full identification of the sextic potential within a specific gauge-theory moduli dynamics remains open and is formulated as a research program.
title: Field-Dependent Kinetics, Exact Kinks, and a Moduli-Space Route from Self-Dual Yang-Mills Theory
