summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.
title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action

summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning

summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

summary: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation

summary: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models

summary: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.
title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?

summary: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.
title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference

summary: We propose loom attention, which allows a Transformer to dynamically rewire its circuits at every token by interweaving a head's vertical attention over the outputs of earlier heads (to obtain its query, key and value) with its horizontal attention over tokens. We instantiate vertical attention efficiently with normalized and gated linear attention over a per-token matrix memory, which stores the compressed head outputs and serves as a second residual stream. This yields LoomFormer, a dual-stream architecture that splits control and content between the vector and matrix streams. Across model sizes and training token budgets in language modeling and downstream tasks, LoomFormer matches Transformers trained with over 3x compute and recent residual-stream baselines (HC/mHC, MUDDFormer, AttnRes) trained with ~1.7-2.8x. For example, trained on the same 300B tokens with only 2% extra FLOPs, LoomPythia-2.8B achieves ~1.6x the average downstream gain of mHC-Pythia-2.8B over Pythia-2.8B, and matches (0-shot) or surpasses (5-shot) Pythia-12B. Code is available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/LoomFormer
title: Rewirable Circuits in Transformers with Loom Attention

summary: Long-horizon agents repeatedly feed an ever-growing interaction trajectory to a specialized agent model. Prefix caching reuses computation over repeated history, but cannot prevent context growth or remove information irrelevant to the current decision. This is especially costly when the specialized agent lacks the cached-input discounts available to general-purpose models, making trajectory compression a natural alternative. However, existing compression methods on selective context risk losing global information, recursively rewriting summary leads to semantic drift, while repeatedly recompressing the full history shifts the growing cost to the compressor. Therefore, we introduce DMC-5 (Dual-Model Collaboration with CaChe-aware Context Compression), an asymmetric framework that assigns full-history integration to a general compression model and action generation to a specialized agent model. DMC-5 maintains the raw trajectory as an Append-only Canonical View, preserving global access while allowing the compressor to reuse a stable historical prefix instead of recursively rewriting or recomputing prior context. The agent operates only on a compact Decision View with recent raw interactions, reducing repeated input while retaining the information needed for the next action. DMC-5 further incorporates YAMATO (integritY-Aware Memory Abstractions for Tool Operations) to preserve execution-critical information during lossy compression. Experiments on AppWorld, OfficeBench, and 8-objective QA show that DMC-5 reduces agent model input by 38.5-57.0% and end-to-end cost by 14.5-28.0% with 78.0-85.0% compressor cache-hit rates, while improving task performance by 1.0-5.8% over the uncompressed baseline.
title: DMC-5: Dual-Model Collaboration with Cache-aware Context Compression for Long-horizon Agents

summary: Multimarginal Optimal Transport (MOT) suffers from exponential computational and memory costs in the number of marginals, as transport plans are represented by high-dimensional tensors. We introduce Low-Rank Multimarginal Optimal Transport (LRMOT), which restricts transport plans to tensors with bounded multilinear rank, providing a compact and structured representation of multimarginal couplings. This structure enables efficient algorithms with a low memory footprint. We establish approximation bounds for the resulting low-rank formulations and demonstrate experimentally that the proposed algorithms substantially reduce computational time while achieving solutions with low transport cost.
title: Low-Rank Tensor Representations for Efficient Multimarginal Optimal Transport

summary: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.
title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

summary: Environmental law inspectors face a structural issue in identifying potential violations from data: they often do not have the capacity to deal with large volume of data present in the emission events. This paper examines to what extent an LLM-based system can support evidence assembly and permit-based screening of such events, using the coke plants of a steel producer and a regional environmental service as a case. A simple puff-trajectory model aligns air quality measurements, weather and citizen complaints with each emission event. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline then retrieves facility-specific permit conditions and generates event reports and a period report with an investigation recommendation. Across 74 events from March 2025, plant-aware re-ranking reduced reports citing the other plant's conditions from 58.1% (hybrid retrieval) to 0% by rule-based plant labels, while maintaining high RAGAS and LLM-judge metrics. GPT-5-mini performed comparably to GPT-5.1, whereas GPT-5-nano scored lower on legal grounding and legal faithfulness. In an evidence ablation, removing air quality (AQ) data changed judge scores and period recommendations most; citation overlap changed only slightly under any removal, and removing complaint details had no measurable effect. This suggests a need for rules and guidelines that link complaints to incidents and permit conditions, so that community reports can count as evidence. The results support screening of events that may need further investigation. Design implications for involving environmental service experts are derived.
title: Automated Call for Action: RAG-Based Environmental Law Enforcement Screening System

summary: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. We introduce MH-RAG-DIVE, a dynamic interactive user simulation framework designed to evaluate RAG systems in more complex multi-hop and multi-turn settings. The framework extends RAG-DIVE with a Context Discoverer, which identifies documents that can be combined to generate multi-hop questions within an ongoing conversation. To address the high computational cost of dynamic user simulation, we further introduce a Conversation Cacher, which reuses turns from previous evaluation runs while preserving the dynamic nature of the evaluation. We evaluate the framework across six distinct RAG configurations and compare its results with the original RAG-DIVE evaluation and the static, human-created CLAPNQ dataset. Our experiments show consistent performance trends across the evaluation approaches, while the more complex multi-hop and multi-turn setting exposes additional challenges for RAG systems. Furthermore, the Conversation Cacher substantially reduces token consumption, demonstrating its potential to make dynamic evaluation more cost-efficient. Finally, we apply MH-RAG-DIVE to an industrial RAG system with domain-specific data, demonstrating its applicability to real-world evaluation scenarios. Overall, our results show that the proposed approach provides a more complex and cost-efficient framework for evaluating RAG systems. All code and experimental data are publicly available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/Daniel-Innsbruck/MH-RAG-DIVE).
title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation

summary: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. We indexed 484,368,086 OpenAlex works, searched exactly on a GPU for evaluation (10,065 NFCorpus, BioASQ, SciFact and PubMedQA questions) and through a compressed 230-million-abstract index in deployment. On 1,000 stratified questions, we compared single-shot, multi-hop, corrective and deep-research retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with Claude Sonnet. SHAKTI adds conversational query rewriting, USDA FoodData Central lookups, source-link checks and online verification of quotes and numbers. It was tested in 36 scripted conversational turns, a 248-question memory-depth test and a 38-question load test. Claims were checked by a Claude Opus judge against exactly the text the system saw. MedCPT reranking of hybrid retrieval gave the best MRR (0.21) and MAP@100 (0.14). Across existing RAG methods, faithfulness was 0.95-0.96, claim hallucination 0.5-0.8% and context precision up to 0.98; the deep-research agent answered 73.2% of BioASQ questions correctly. In conversation, SHAKTI reached a context-awareness score of 97.1%, faithfulness 95.5%, 1.9% unsupported claims, no contradicted claims and 229/229 working source links; it resolved references to the first question after 16 unrelated questions. An answer cost 14,716 tokens (US$0.06) with a median latency of 24 s. Large-scale retrieval with agentic evidence selection and mechanical verification yields auditable, low-hallucination nutrition answers.
title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health

summary: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.
title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring

summary: This study investigates whether domain grounding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) can enhance the accuracy and reliability of pet care advice generated by large language models (LLMs). We curated a dataset of breed-specific dog care information and used it to develop two systems: a RAG pipeline based on TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B model adapted using LoRA. Both systems were evaluated on 15 dog care questions. The RAG model achieved a perfect average score of 2.0, outperforming the fine-tuned model (mean = 1.47). Statistical analyses, including Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney U, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (all p < 0.05), confirmed the significance of the performance gap. Our findings suggest that retrieval-based domain grounding leads to more accurate, consistent, and trustworthy responses than standalone fine-tuning in specialized LLM applications.
title: LLM-Based Assistant for Dog Care Guidance

summary: This page contains supplementary material for the paper Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata by Arne Kuhrs and Artyom Lisitsyn. In this paper we study the Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_{k,n}$ together with a union of Plücker divisors, and ask whether the regions it cuts out have canonical forms. For the full Plücker boundary, the regions are realization spaces of uniform oriented matroids, and the question concerns the configuration space $\mathcal X_{k,n}$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$. In rank three we show that $\mathcal X_{3,n}$ has genus zero for $6 \le n \le 9$, that the canonical forms of the regions span all logarithmic forms for seven points but not for eight, and that the genus becomes positive for ten points because a K3 surface appears in the boundary. For smaller boundaries we give a recursion in $n$ for every $k$, which recovers the positive Grassmannian and applies to realization spaces of stacked polytopes. Each zip file below contains one computation, with a README that describes what is checked, how to run it, and how its notation matches the paper. AI Use Acknowledgement: We used Opus 5.5 to write a majority of the code in this upload. We take full responsibility for the content of the materials. X37_real_rank.zip (SageMath; about two minutes and 2.5 GB of memory to build $B$, about one minute and 2 GB for its rank). The incidence matrix $B$ over $\mathbb F_2$ with one row for each of the $27\,240$ regions of $\mathcal X_{3,7}$ (reorientation classes $\chi$ of uniform chirotopes of rank $3$ on seven elements) and one column for each of the $211\,365$ Plücker cones $P$ of dimension $6$ of the Dressian, with $B_{\chi,P}=1$ iff $P\subseteq\operatorname{Dr}^\chi(3,7)$. Modulo $2$, $B$ is the matrix of iterated boundaries of the regions at the corners of a tropical compactification, one corner for each Plücker cone. The matrix is included as `B37.npz`. `get_ae_data.sh` downloads the chirotropical Dressians of Antolini and Early and checks them against SHA-256 checksums, `build_B.sage` rebuilds `B37.npz` from them, and `rank_B.sage` computes $\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb F_2}B=7470$, which gives $\operatorname{cr}_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=\operatorname{cr}(\mathcal X_{3,7})=7470$ (section "The real combinatorial rank"). X310_log_form.zip (Julia 1.12, Oscar 1.8.2; about a minute). An exact verification of the telescoping factorization of an explicit $12$-form $\omega$ on $\mathcal X_{3,10}$ along Sturmfels' construction sequence, and of its iterated residue $\pm\, du\wedge da/\partial_b F$ along the ten divisors of Sink's line configuration, the holomorphic $2$-form of Sink's K3 surface (Section 5, "Positive genus for ten and more points", Remark 5.2). The paper expects $\omega$ to be logarithmic and to lie in the kernel of the Brown–Dupont $R$-map, and the README sketches why; the paper's proof that $g(\mathcal X_{3,10}) \ge 1$ (Theorem 5.1) does not use this computation. Sources. The computations rely on the following external work. The zip files contain no copies of external data; `get_ae_data.sh` downloads the data of Antolini and Early from its Zenodo record. - Chirotropical Dressians of $\mathrm{Gr}(3,7)$: D. Antolini and N. Early, The chirotropical Grassmannian, arXiv:2411.07293; data in D. Antolini and N. Early, Data on chirotropical Grassmannians, Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.13914104. - Line configuration $\mathcal L_V$ and its K3 surface: E. Sink, Line configurations and K3 surfaces, arXiv:2312.07542, with the construction sequence of B. Sturmfels, Computational algebraic geometry of projective configurations, J. Symbolic Comput. 11 (1991) 595–618.
title: Positive Geometry of Oriented Matroid Strata

summary: Consider an observer embedded in a computation, a pattern that can neither step outside the machine nor outrun it. Behind the machine lies a complete record of what every part does, an answer sheet. Without a shortcut, the insider cannot read that sheet faster than the machine writes it. What is the best description such an insider can hold? Computational Wave Field Theory proposes a complex wave over the machine’s locations, with a Born rule for computational events and an action scale set by each computational substrate’s hardware. We present the framework as one argument, with every claim marked as computed or proved, a bridge, a conjecture or speculation. Tested on cellular automata, the wave forecasts no better than ordinary probabilities. For models fitted to a limited history, quantum memory with real amplitudes can store forecasts more compactly. If the questions asked are independent of a definite record, ignorance of that record cannot produce contextual statistics. In a minimal model, a smooth, reversible and faithful self-negation forces the imaginary unit, and gauging the resulting phase over the machine gives a lattice analog of light. On weakly coupled machines, horizons form where computation freezes. Four thermodynamic tests of Einstein’s equation fail on three leaky families. On a holographic error-correcting code, a first-law analog holds in almost all tested cases and, through a holographic bridge, reads as a linear analog of that equation. One physical wager remains, that nature derives its imaginary unit from self-reference instead of postulating it.
title: Knowing a World from Within: Self-Reference, Light and Gravity in Computational Wave Field Theory

summary: RationalFourReal is the MATLAB software accompanying the paper Real bases in limited-memory rational Krylov methods for matrix function actions by Tianqi Zhang and Fei Xue. It implements four methods for approximating \(f(A)b\) with a large real matrix \(A\) and a real starting vector \(b\) : restarted rational Arnoldi, truncated rational Arnoldi, rational induced dimension reduction (IDR), and the poles-and-interpolation-nodes method (PAIN). The software compares two ways of processing a pair of complex-conjugate poles: generating two real basis vectors together or taking two successive steps with a complex basis. Structured matrix-sign experiments compare the resulting approximations at common Krylov dimensions and record the work required to reach a prescribed accuracy. The reported quantities include forward errors, shifted right-hand sides, matrix factorizations, and elapsed times. The archive contains the MATLAB implementations, experiment drivers, matrix inputs, numerical results used in the paper and its supplement, and Python scripts for reproducing the figures. To repeat the main experiments, run RUN_PAPER_EXPERIMENTS from the project folder in MATLAB. The README gives commands for the additional experiments and figures.
title: RationalFourReal: MATLAB software for real bases in limited-memory rational Krylov methods for matrix function actions

summary: Human–AI communities inherit familiar political relations while enabling powers to propagate through delegated agents, retained histories, and changing infrastructures. This paper investigates how those pathways alter feasible interventions, recognized authority, and distributed burdens. It distinguishes an event-precedence partial order supporting modeled histories, a domain-relative capacity preorder and quotient order, and relational composition in a delegation network. A specified order can restrict a declared background symmetry group; substantive power relevance requires differential shaping of relational continuations. A targeted primary-source survey engages common agency, institutional power, agentic inequality, persistent agent architectures, memory manipulation, agent-society studies, and delegation research alongside political and institutional theory. Joint delegation can distribute funding, source permission, execution, and configuration while concentrating the evidence on which principals act. A finite historical comparison shows how equal current competence, or equal actual work, can produce unequal review authority through allocation and admission rules. Counter-power is examined through supported capacities to refuse, reinterpret, organize, or continue through an alternative. Prior prompts, memories, tools, parameter changes, relationships, and attributed histories remain distinct carriers. An exploitation analysis separates descriptive hierarchy, unfair appropriation, burden displacement, domination, and possible AI welfare harm; a constructed agent–subagent history follows costs into the wider human relational structure. Standard proofs and exact diagnostics clarify symmetry restrictions, capacity equivalence, propagation, historical reinforcement, replication, investment, and continuity. Matched-history comparisons distinguish possibilities, exercise, recipient response, and later standing, including complementarity, interference, copying, and selective records. The contribution is a connected comparative framework with explicit antecedents and evidence requirements. Community constitutions and interaction strategies remain configurable; implemented and field studies supply the subsequent assessment of their effects.
title: A Discussion of Political Authority and Infrastructural Power in Human–AI Communities

summary: Personalized learning remains a persistent challenge in secondary education due to high student-to-teacher ratios and heterogeneous knowledge baselines among pupils. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer conversational tutoring capabilities, unconstrained generative models frequently produce factual hallucinations and provide direct homework answers rather than pedagogical scaffolding. This paper presents the design, mathematical formulation, and software implementation of an AI-based educational chatbot utilizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) to enhance secondary school students' academic mastery in STEM subjects (Mathematics, Physics, and Computer Science). The system integrates a vector database (FAISS) indexing state-approved school textbooks with a Socratic dialogue manager accessible via web and Telegram interfaces. A 12-week pedagogical experiment involving N = 160 secondary school students (grades 8–10), divided equally into an Experimental Group (N = 80) and a Control Group (N = 80), demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in post-test academic performance (+23.4% mean score increase, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.18) and a 61.5% reduction in homework completion latency.
tags: educational chatbot, artificial intelligence in education (AIEd), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT), Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), secondary school education, Socratic scaffolding, pedagogical statistics.
title: DEVELOPMENT OF AN AI-BASED EDUCATIONAL CHATBOT FOR ENHANCING SCHOOL STUDENTS' KNOWLEDGE

summary: You may open any two of three boxes, and you always find one full and one empty. No list of contents fixed in advance can do this, because two of the three boxes would have to hold the same thing. Yet a small classical machine passes the test. It flips a coin for the first box opened and gives the opposite for the second, and it keeps a complete log, a diary, from which every answer can be recomputed. A diary is not an answer key, a list that fixes one answer to every question whatever else is asked. If one state of the machine answers every question of a round, its statistics are those of answer keys drawn at random. If each question meets the machine in a later state, they need not be. An engineer can read every cell of a machine at one instant. A part of the machine that can only ask, one question after another, cannot take such a snapshot, and its questions meet the machine in later states. For the remembering machine, which starts every round afresh, the diary of a round then gives an answer for each way of asking that round, and no answer key. Classical models of this kind have been known since Bell in 1966. We work them out in small machines that we build, run and check exactly, on three puzzles: Specker’s three boxes, the Liar cycle of five statements, and the Peres-Mermin square of nine yes-or-no questions. On all three the machine keeps every rule, and no mixture of answer keys reproduces its statistics. On the boxes and the Liar cycle a machine that ignores the question does as well, and on the square the machine must use what came before in the round. Under the conditions we mainly used a few memory states suffice, with counts for the boxes and the Liar cycles that are new as far as we know. Under those conditions, three states keep the rules and repeated answers on every Liar cycle of seven or more statements. Keeping the rules is not the same as giving such statistics. When each round starts in a state picked with equal odds, every machine with three states that keeps the rules of the square lets the odds of a single answer drift with what was asked before, and a test that allows for the drift finds nothing contextual in any of them. The same holds, with the two orders of asking pooled, for every machine with three states that keeps the rules and repeated answers of a longer cycle. Four states do without drift, on the square and on every cycle of seven or more statements. The construction still works with the one who asks inside one deterministic cellular automaton. The machine is caught by a round that closes a cycle, such as all three boxes asked in turn, and it gains nothing when the questions go to two stations too far apart for a message to arrive, as Bell’s theorem says. The square can be realised by nine measurements on two quantum bits. A classical model that gives the right odds for every answer from the past alone, when the questions are picked uniformly at random, uses 24 memory states in the long run, a published value that our code finds again. The two quantum bits hold at most two bits, of a different kind, in a quantum memory. No quantum experiment was run. A further section reads these machines as recurrent networks, whose hidden state is the memory, and lists the exact least memory of the smallest puzzles. In a sixth experiment a reservoir, a fixed random network of which only a linear readout is trained, learns to answer as the remembering machine does, and with its memory cut it is at chance on the answers that depend on the past. On the boxes and the Liar cycle it must carry one coin for one step. On the square the memory is still small, but the third answer is a parity of several remembered bits, and a linear readout needed a few thousand mixed features for it in both reservoirs that answered it, about 4,096 to 8,192 units for an echo state network. A square with no contextuality cost an echo state network about as much as the real square, another cost less but far more than the c
title: A Diary Is Not an Answer Key: Memory, Contextuality and the Insider of a Classical Machine

summary: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning

summary: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.
title: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents

summary: Generative priors are state-of-the-art for modeling medical images in image reconstruction tasks, but reconstruction with video priors takes tens of seconds to minutes per frame. Latent priors inherit the errors of their autoencoder, the memory of pixel-space whole-frame priors grows with the frame size, and pixel-space patch priors are slow for two reasons. First, their deep networks process every frame at full resolution at every sampling step, even though early steps resolve only low frequencies. Second, their samplers spend many network evaluations per sampling step on overlapping windows, multiple re-noising rounds, or backpropagation through the prior. We introduce TesseraFlow, a complex-valued pixel-space flow prior that reduces the first cost. A global encoder reads a low-resolution view of every frame once per sampling step. A single shallow decoder operates on this view during early steps and on full-resolution space-time tiles during later steps, so no network processes a whole frame at full resolution. Our sampler, ReTile, addresses the second reason. We use randomized grid shifting at every sampling step along with re-noising, which acts as a stochastic gradient instead of computing overlapping tiles, so a single network pass per sampling step suffices. On its own, ReTile speeds up an existing global-context patch prior by 6-9x, and our prior adds a further 3-5x speedup. TesseraFlow reconstructs about one 256x256 frame per second, 20-367x faster than patch and latent video priors, and can match or exceed the best generative baseline on cardiac, brain, and abdominal MRI and lung CT, at a fraction of its GPU time.
title: TesseraFlow: Scalable Video Diffusion for Dynamic Medical Imaging Inverse Problems

summary: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.
title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage

summary: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation

summary: Irregular time series are recorded at nonuniform times and are often queried at other times: between observations, after the last one, or on a regular grid. Continuous-time models answer such queries by integrating latent dynamics, and time-aware attention models answer them by revisiting the observation tokens. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), an attention operator that writes an irregular history into a rank-M function space with explicit time coordinates. Masked self-attention first exchanges content among the observations; the updated values are then contracted against kernel-smoothed HiPPO-Legendre features and solved through a regularized Gram matrix, so the retained coefficients define a function that is read at any time through the same features. The write and read have the form of an interdomain sparse Gaussian-process mean: every readout lies in an M-dimensional reproducing-kernel subspace, and a pointwise bound separates the approximation error of this subspace from the error of the learned memory. Removing the functional memory from the encoder raises Spiral reconstruction RMSE 18-fold. The full model has the lowest error in 11 of 12 Spiral settings, the highest overall accuracy and best average rank on 20 irregular UEA datasets, the highest event-type accuracy on all five multi-type event benchmarks, and a 21% lower extrapolation MSE than CRU on PhysioNet. Because the memory has fixed rank, the state retained after encoding keeps a fixed size as the history grows and is 102 times smaller than a token cache at 1,024 observations.
title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series

summary: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.
title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence

summary: Multi-View Stereo (MVS) and Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) provide complementary cues for dense 3D reconstruction. While MVS leverages explicit geometry for metric depth, it struggles in challenging regions where feature matching is unreliable. Conversely, MDE provides robust structural priors but typically yields scale-ambiguous results. Existing hybrid methods mainly exploit monocular cues in a unidirectional manner, leaving the mutual enhancement between MDE and MVS insufficiently explored. To address this limitation, we propose BridgeMVS, a unified cascaded multi-stage MVS framework that bridges monocular depth features and multi-view cost volume representations through Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion (BDF). At each stage, BDF performs dynamic mono-to-cost and cost-to-mono updates, where monocular structural features guide cost volume refinement for more robust MVS depth estimation, while multi-view geometric evidence recalibrates monocular representations to improve their metric-scale consistency. Furthermore, the fused monocular and multi-view representations are progressively propagated from coarse to fine stages and constrained by stage-wise relative-scale MDE supervision and metric-scale MVS supervision, enabling cross-branch interactions to benefit subsequent high-resolution depth estimation. In addition, BDF is designed as a plug-and-play module that can be conveniently integrated into existing cascaded MVS frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BridgeMVS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DTU, Tanks-and-Temples, and ETH3D benchmarks, while simultaneously boosting the accuracy of monocular depth estimation. Notably, BridgeMVS ranks first on both the Tanks-and-Temples Intermediate and Advanced benchmarks. The source code is available at \href{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}{https://github.com/JianfeiJ/BridgeMVS}.
title: BridgeMVS: Bridging Multi-View Stereo and Monodepth via Bidirectional Dynamic Fusion

summary: The web contains vast amounts of scattered quantitative evidence that is difficult to organize into comparable and verifiable structures. Yet its unstructured, sparse, and sometimes conflicting nature makes a systematic distillation costly and error-prone. Existing approaches force users to make a trade-off: search engines return document lists that require labor-intensive extraction and reconciliation, while generative AI systems produce fluent summaries that obscure data provenance, introduce reporting bias, and hide inconsistencies. We present DataRecycle, an interactive system that helps transform scattered web evidence into structured tables of comparable numerical facts. Given a user's query or statement, DataRecycle decomposes it into entities and attributes, retrieves candidate evidence, and organizes scattered, potentially conflicting records in a table-based evidence view. To address key challenges in automated data distillation (i.e., incomplete retrieval, untraceable generation, sparse data distribution, and multi-source inconsistency), DataRecycle adopts an ontology-guided, top-down data acquisition strategy, visualizes the recorded lineage from retrieved snippets to extracted values, and aligns heterogeneous data across dimensions such as time, definition, and scale. We evaluate DataRecycle through module-level experiments, a usage scenario, and a user study, showing that the system helps users organize numerical web evidence into provenance-linked tables and inspect uncertainty and conflicting sources.
title: DataRecycle: Trustworthy Distillation of Structured Data from Scattered Web Evidence

Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The library that did not own its readers In the imagined city of Meridian, the librarian inherited three copies of an ancient atlas. One could be read on the eastern terminal, one on the western terminal, and one in the shelter beneath the school. When the reader software was retired, all three became unreadable on the same morning. There was no fire, no lost disk, and no malicious visitor. The collection had survived in a form that nobody could open. Letter to the future: A letter to a librarian not yet born Build a library whose continued operation does not depend upon loyalty to its first librarian. Give later caretakers the authority to replace the catalog, repair the software, correct the record, and create new routes through the collection. Keep the old record when its lawful preservation matters; keep the correction equally visible. In a faraway city, the most valuable inheritance might not be an indestructible monument. It might be a modest institution that knows how to repair itself without silencing its readers. Research Gate 001: Replica independence — Mechanism contrast Origin: Replica independence begins with a question: what would remain unexplained if researchers could separate archive replicas by failure domain? An archive object is usable only when its bytes, format, provenance and rights survive together. A manifest is not itself a reconstruction, and geographically separated disks may share one decoder. The unit of analysis is a requested licensed record, not a file count or a storage device. The mechanism contrast is a distinct experiment on that question, not a claim that the intervention has succeeded. Extreme extrapolation: Imagine that shared power and software dependencies produces the same visible outcome in replica independence. Change the named lever while holding the task and resource allocation fixed. Compare with the strongest matched baseline; ask which observable changes before the terminal endpoint. In that world, blind restoration of a randomly requested record is the proposed independent witness. A distant settlement is a limiting scenario, not a source of observations; test the contrast in a bounded terrestrial or computational analog first. Same fixed score rubric; randomized assignment for causal interpretation. Novelty or unequal help time can mimic gain; mask scoring and hold instruction time constant. Measurement error of score change: SD = sqrt(2*s^2*(1-rho)). Equal error variance at pre/post; covariance rho*s^2. Raters may drift in a systematic direction; cross-score anchor responses. Two-arm standard error: SE = s*sqrt(2/n). Independent arms, equal group size and variance; integer n. Class-level correlation inflates variance; randomize or analyze clusters appropriately. Retention decay: G(t) = G0*exp(-k*t). Illustrative initial gain 10 points and exponential decay. Repeated tests can provide practice; use parallel unseen tasks and equal contact. Help dependence contrast: D = S_help-S_alone. Parallel matched rubric tasks; no claim that a gap is caused by AI. Item difficulty differences can create gaps; counterbalance task forms and order. Cluster design effect: DE = 1+(m-1)*rho. Equal cluster sizes and exchangeable within-cluster correlation. Unequal sizes and teacher effects require cluster-specific analysis, not naive participant counts. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The machine that learned to be quiet The school in Meridian received a tutor that could speak in more languages than any citizen. It could finish a proof before a learner found the first line, and write a polished argument before the learner decided what the question meant. At first the school judged the tutor by the beauty of the notebooks that returned from its lessons. The notebooks became magnificent. Then, during a planned offline afternoon, some of the students discovered that they could not explain the work attributed to them. Letter to the future: A letter to the teacher of another sky If our methods become part of your school, you are free to abandon them wherever they do not help. We do not need every child to call a research question a Research Gate. We need children to discover that a question can belong to them, that an explanation may be tested, and that changing their minds can be a sign of intellectual strength. The school should remember the student who quietly offered a counterexample as well as the student who won a competition. The future is not made solely by the fastest minds. It is also made by the space we give one another to think. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The pendulum of the little red school In an imagined Martian classroom a student hung a weight from a string. An old Earth lesson stated the period of a pendulum as though the word gravity needed no explanation. Her measurement disagreed. Some students blamed the clock; others blamed the length of the string. One proposed that the old lesson was simply wrong. Their teacher wrote each explanation on the board, leaving room beneath it for a test. Letter to the future: The notebook with a blank margin I hope the next school teaches not only the use of a ruler but the right to ask whether its markings are reliable. I hope it offers experiments whose outcome can surprise the teacher, and whose risks are small enough that curiosity is not punished with avoidable injury. A research notebook should not demand that its writer be present to defend it. Its quiet achievement is to let an unfamiliar person understand the question, reconstruct the observation and, if necessary, improve the answer. A good experiment makes a little of the world shareable without requiring everyone to agree about it. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The door whose descendants had different names In the library of Meridian, one shelf held books that ended with questions. The custom began when an early writer realized that the last sentence of a book could either close a conversation or invite another. He left a question in a notebook, together with the observations that had led to it and the assumptions he had not been able to establish. Years later a reader opened the notebook and refused the first suggested answer. She investigated a different mechanism. Her question belonged to the same lineage, but it was not a copy of the old one. Letter to the future: To the next first founder The educational award for which we might someday apply would be a welcome occasion to explain this design. Yet a medal cannot establish that it works, nor can the absence of a medal settle the value of the idea. The real study concerns what an independent learner can do after encountering a research gate. We can ask for a fair comparison and accept the answer. A living educational tradition is not one that protects its first answer from disagreement. It is one that gives its descendants the means to begin again. Part IX legend excerpt (fiction): The evening when the sky fell silent The fictional city lost its outside connection on an ordinary evening. The message board froze, the live tutors fell silent, and a student who had planned to study from a distant archive could not retrieve the next chapter. In the shelter there was a cabinet with a repairable reader and a collection of locally stored lessons. The cabinet was useful, but several lessons required a service that was no longer available. One contained a video without a transcript. Another asked a student to submit work to a server that could not be reached. Letter to the future: A letter that does not require a reply If you send a reply to another world, let the reply be yours. If you never send one, let your learning still matter. The point of an open archive is not to gather everyone into a single conversation under a central authority. It is to make many conversations possible, including ones whose participants may never meet. In this sense, the most precious thing that can travel across the stars may not be a perfectly preserved answer. It may be the permission to begin with a question. Behind them are methods that can be reconstructed, criticized, modified and sometimes rejected. There will be other doors we have not imagined. Let the next person find them. Let technology be powerful enough to help and humble enough to stop. Let a civilization that reaches toward the stars remember to create a place at its table for the person who has not yet found the words for their own question. summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/
title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models

summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.
title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories

summary: This release provides crystal structures, thermal-conductivity data, pretrained DANA-$\kappa$ models, and computational workflows for high-throughput discovery of low-conductivity materials. It includes DANA-$\kappa$ predictions for 1,953,259 structures from Materials Project and Crystoria, 4,724 GRACE-based thermal-conductivity results, and CIF files for the 1,712 GRACE records satisfying $0<\kappa_{\mathrm L}<2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The DFT dataset contains 60 completed calculations with corresponding relaxed structures, including 58 phases below $2~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and 29 below $0.5~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. The lowest DFT value is approximately $0.1826~\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{CsKAu_2}$. Conductivity values refer to 300 K and represent the diagonal average of the population-plus-coherence lattice thermal-conductivity tensor, excluding electronic conductivity. Additional resources include second- and third-order DFT force constants and reference transport outputs for the 58 low-conductivity phases, three split-specific DANA-$\kappa$ checkpoints, and scripts for inference, physical-property filtering, computational-cost estimation, structural deduplication, GRACE calculations, and VASP validation. Structure provenance, calculation settings, and quality annotations accompany the data to support reproducible analysis and subsequent model development.
title: Accelerated Discovery of Ultralow-Thermal-Conductivity Materials via Structure-to-Property and Machine-Learning Potential Models

summary: A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.
title: PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction

summary: Diffusion models are increasingly used for medical image reconstruction and super-resolution, but their samples may contain plausible fine-scale hallucinations that are difficult to identify from the reconstructed image alone. We propose Med-PODiff, a patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) diffusion framework for brain MRI super-resolution that performs generative reconstruction in compact and interpretable local coefficient spaces. Unlike pixel-space or learned-latent diffusion models, Med-PODiff uses the POD structure to separate low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residual variation, enabling predictive uncertainty to be decomposed into total, coarse, and fine components. Building on this decomposition, we define a pixel-wise hallucination-risk score, $H_p$, that emphasizes regions where fine-detail uncertainty dominates coarse structural uncertainty. On brain MRI, Med-PODiff outperforms representative diffusion baselines in reconstruction quality while producing well-calibrated predictive intervals, with total uncertainty detecting high-error regions at AUROC 0.954. More importantly, the decomposed uncertainty is scale-selective: coarse and fine uncertainty preferentially predict errors at the corresponding scales, with $H_p$ localizing fine error at AUROC $0.906$. Controlled injections and retrospective Cartesian $k$-space undersampling further support fine-detail localization and degradation robustness. The discarded POD tail is only $3.8\%$ of the retained fine-error magnitude, and Med-PODiff improves downstream segmentation consistency while requiring substantially less inference time than pixel-space diffusion.
title: Interpretable Orthogonal Latent Diffusion with Scale-Selective Uncertainty for Medical Image Super-Resolution

summary: This paper proposes a method for identifying a control-oriented model of a stable continuous-time linear system from aperiodically sampled input-output data. Rather than recovering the continuous-time matrices, the method directly identifies a discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) state-space model that depends affinely on the measured normalized sampling-interval variation, a structure obtained from the first-order expansion of the zero-order-hold discretization. The resulting model is directly usable in control design for aperiodic sampled-data systems. An initial LPV estimate, including approximate first-order terms, is derived from a standard LTI subspace model through sampled-data relations. The method then iteratively alternates state-sequence reconstruction and LPV parameter refitting. Numerical examples show that the identified model retains high validation accuracy over a wide range of sampling-interval variations where a fixed LTI model degrades. Already at initialization, the state-space LPV structure substantially outperforms an LPV-ARX regression with the same scheduling variable, and the iterative refinement brings the model close to a state-measured benchmark, a practical upper-bound reference.
title: Iterative Identification of Aperiodic Sampled-Data Systems via Affine LPV Models Scheduled by the Sampling Interval

summary: We study scalar-field models in 1+1 dimensions with field-dependent kinetic coefficients, motivated by self-dual Yang-Mills (SDYM) theory as a generator of integrable equations. We derive the Euler-Lagrange equation, traveling-wave reduction, and first integral, and solve the inverse problem: given a kinetic structure and a prescribed tanh kink, which potential makes it exact? A quadratic spatial deformation with a canonical temporal sector yields a sextic potential. We obtain: (i) a closed-form kink energy with a Bogomolny-type formulation, independent of the odd parameter, which nonetheless shapes the energy density asymmetrically; (ii) vacuum curvature relations tying the spectrum to the kinetic function at the vacua; (iii) two propositions on speed families, plus a lemma showing single-speed data probe only one combination of the kinetic functions; (iv) a unified admissibility analysis in which positivity of the spatial kinetic function controls hyperbolicity, the potential bound along the kink, and the vacuum masses; (v) a self-adjoint fluctuation operator with a closed-form potential whose asymptotes are the vacuum masses, an exact translation zero mode, and numerical spectra with no negative mode on the admissible region, evidence for spectral stability. Exact SDYM reductions yield integrable equations, whereas the deformed model is generically non-integrable and cannot be an exact reduction. The correct bridge is the moduli-space route: SDYM reduces to the Bogomolny equations, whose BPS monopole and dyon dynamics produce field-dependent kinetic terms; any smooth one-dimensional moduli metric expands, to second order, to the quadratic model studied here, and the Taub-NUT metric of well-separated dyons gives an explicit realization. Full identification of the sextic potential within a specific gauge-theory moduli dynamics remains open and is formulated as a research program.
title: Field-Dependent Kinetics, Exact Kinks, and a Moduli-Space Route from Self-Dual Yang-Mills Theory

summary: We investigate the linear stability of energetic-particle (EP) driven Alfvén eigenmodes and the wave-particle interaction in phase space, using the newly implemented energetic-particle module in the electromagnetic global full-f gyrokinetic code GYSELA. The coupled gyrokinetic-Maxwell system self-consistently evolves the EP species alongside thermal ions and kinetic electrons, retaining finite-orbit-width and global profile effects. To mitigate the relaxation of the initial distribution in global full-f models, a canonical Maxwellian initialisation is employed, which strongly reduces this relaxation and the associated change of the drive. The framework is verified against the ITPA-TAE and the reversed-shear NLED-AUG cases, including scans in EP temperature and density. The agreement with published multi-code results is quantitative for the ITPA-TAE case and qualitative for the NLED-AUG case, where a reversed-shear Alfvén eigenmode (RSAE) is found near $q_{\rm min}$. Beyond verification, we use a constants-of-motion (CoM) diagnostic to project the gyrocentre distribution and the local wave-particle power exchange ($P = -\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$) onto invariant space. This identifies the orbit classes and resonances that interact with the mode. For the ITPA-TAE, deeply co-passing orbits dominate the drive. summary: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for Bayesian inverse problems is expensive: the unknown is high-dimensional, every likelihood evaluation requires a forward solve, and gradients are often unavailable. The posterior typically differs from the prior in a few directions and is often approximately Gaussian in most of them but strongly non-Gaussian in a few. We propose the NQU sampler, a gradient-free MCMC method that splits the parameter space into non-Gaussian (N), approximately quadratic (Q) and uninformative (U) directions. The split is learned once, before sampling, from likelihood values, and each block is updated by a kernel suited to it; a collapsed update handles a global prior scale. Because the learned structure only shapes the proposals, every update leaves the exact posterior invariant, at the cost of one likelihood evaluation. We give a condition under which the blocks can be learned and show that, for likelihoods with exactly the learned structure, the spectral gap of the sampler does not depend on the dimension, whereas updating the scale given all coordinates can have a gap of order $1/d$. On the posterior axes, the NQU sampler, learning included, needed the fewest evaluations in four of five synthetic examples with $d=200$, among nine baselines including gradient-based ones; in those with non-Gaussian directions, gradient-free baselines needed at least ten times as many. On a methane ignition problem with 219 uncertain rate constants, it gave consistent estimates, whereas full-space robust adaptive Metropolis needed about 300 times as many evaluations and an ensemble sampler degenerated.
title: Gradient-free MCMC exploiting low-dimensional Gaussian and nonGaussian posterior structure
