summary: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation

summary: We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. NABLA combines an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners constructed from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+σ^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.
title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization

summary: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

summary: Knowledge-tracing benchmarks often compare models that have different access to a learner's previous responses. We examine how data provenance, history length, and representation affect those comparisons. First, we compare a pinned ASSISTments 2009 sequence mirror against the corrected official release. Of 4,148 learners represented in both, 817 have different ordered skill-response sequences; the mirror also contains fewer labeled events. Second, we retain earlier learner-disjoint model evaluations on the 2009 and 2015 datasets, distinguishing exploratory results from a corrective 2015 replication. Finally, we evaluate a new, nonoverlapping sample of 4,000 ASSISTments 2015 learners using three models constrained to the same one-event or 20-event prior-response window. On 20,592 test responses from 582 learners, the 20-event Brier scores were 0.17667 for count-based logistic regression, 0.17389 for an order-aware logistic model, and 0.17514 for a GRU. The GRU-minus-order-aware difference was 0.00125 (95% learner-cluster bootstrap interval [0.00008, 0.00243]); at one prior event, the corresponding difference was 0.00212 [0.00120, 0.00301]. Earlier comparisons had favored the GRU against simpler history summaries. The newer analysis instead favors a logistic comparator that represents order using the same permitted event stream. These results concern predictive performance on particular historical cohorts and model settings. They neither isolate an architectural effect nor establish generalization to contemporary classrooms.
title: When Knowledge-Tracing Rankings Depend on Available History: A Source-Correction and Matched-Information Audit on ASSISTments 2009 and 2015

summary: Embodied spatial intelligence requires agents to gather information through exploration and interaction, then use it to reason and act. Existing benchmarks insufficiently distinguish correct outcomes from completion of these task requirements. We introduce ROAM-Bench to evaluate these abilities under robot motion and collision constraints. Independent checks use simulation state and episode records to assess outcomes and task requirements, with stronger checks of geometry, coverage, or placement. It comprises 250 manually validated tasks across 11 types in five groups and 27 indoor environments, covering object and room search, counting, geometric judgments, direction reasoning, and relocation. Human evaluators achieve 84% strict task success on 100 sampled tasks, with every correct outcome satisfying the required checks. Across seven frontier vision-language models, we identify two complementary failure modes: correct outcomes with unmet task requirements, and incorrect outcomes despite passing stronger checks. Oracle-input diagnostics show that more complete target observations and calibrated feedback improve final spatial judgments.
title: ROAM-Bench: Evaluating Embodied Active Spatial Intelligence through Evidence Verification

summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems

summary: Auditing failed agent executions requires identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode. Representative supervised methods either focus on step localization or predict multiple attribution targets from shared trajectory representations. These methods do not use the localization result to select the text for mode diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose RecordRoute, which couples comparative localization with local diagnosis. Specifically, it represents each record with word and character features and learns to rank records through comparisons within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, while its text and metadata drive mode prediction. On controlled-injection Who&When Pro, RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon on all four official metrics. With actor and step predictions fixed, local diagnosis reaches 77.47% pooled joint accuracy versus 69.28% for full-trace diagnosis. On natural failures from TraceElephant and CatchBench POST, it outperforms these baselines and three open LLMs in localization.
title: RecordRoute: Auditing Agent Failures with Localization-Guided Diagnosis

summary: Terrain-modifying robot swarms operating in unstructured outdoor environments must coordinate under uncertain dynamics despite unreliable communication and incomplete global information. Stigmergy offers a decentralized alternative by allowing agents to coordinate indirectly through persistent environmental modifications, yet its application to large-scale terrain construction on real landscapes remains largely unexplored. Inspired by beaver canal construction, we present a minimal stigmergic framework for multi-agent systems in which decentralized agents follow local wetness cues, excavate terrain, and interact through a closed agent--environmental feedback loop. The framework couples agents with seasonal hydrology on a real digital elevation model (DEM). Across 110 simulations on an 862m x 1167m region spanning agent count and hydrological recession rate, the model produces emergent canal-like networks whose morphology varies predictably with environmental constraints. An alignment-invariant morphological evaluation against a field-annotated reference network identifies parameter regimes that reproduce key canal characteristics, while failure cases reveal over-canalization and fragmentation. These results demonstrate that simple local terrain-modifying behaviors can generate plausible landscape-scale structures through environmental feedback, providing a minimal framework for studying decentralized terrain construction and bio-inspired swarm coordination.
title: Multi-Agent Coordination Through Stigmergy for Canal Network Formation on Real Terrain

summary: Level 4 autonomous vehicles require fault-tolerant architectures that preserve critical driving functions under sensing, computing, communication, power, and actuation failures. As these systems progress toward industrial scalability, architectural complexity, validation burden, integration effort, and lifecycle cost become increasingly relevant. This study proposes an Operational Design Domain (ODD)-based, safety-constrained systems-engineering framework for architecture rationalization. ODD-specific capabilities, physical fault assumptions, post-fault operational policies, and spatial sensing requirements are propagated through an integrated safety-feasibility gate. Architecture transformations, including removal, relocation, functional reassignment, and consolidation, are evaluated only within the resulting safety-feasible design space, followed by lifecycle-cost sensitivity and robust multiobjective Pareto analysis. A generic, synthetically parameterized Level 4 architecture is used as a demonstrative computational case study. Within this modeled design space, direct ablation showed limited rationalization potential, whereas directional redistribution and functional consolidation generated a broader set of safety-feasible candidates. Under the illustrative lifecycle-cost model, the best nominal candidate achieved a 5.55% normalized cost reduction and remained cost-reducing across all 5,000 sampled points in the prescribed uncertainty domain. The analysis identified 15 non-dominated architecture-policy solutions representing seven physical transformations. The results support capability-based, policy-conditioned, and lifecycle-aware architecture rationalization under the stated assumptions, with safety retained as a non-compensatory feasibility constraint. The reported transformations are design candidates rather than validated production architectures.
title: From Safety-Driven Redundancy to Value-Driven Architecture: An ODD-Based Rationalization Framework for Level 4 Autonomous Vehicles

summary: Distributed runtime verification often requires combining evidence from several nodes to check properties that cannot be evaluated locally. However, when messages are delayed, lost, or deliberately suppressed, the verifier may not know whether a violation occurred or whether the relevant evidence is missing. This creates a risk of incorrectly reporting compliance. We study the requirements for sound monitoring under these conditions. We first show that a deadline-bounded monitor cannot be simultaneously sound, decisive, and available when an adversary can suppress evidence. The monitor must therefore be able to abstain. We then distinguish two sources of incomplete evidence. Sequence numbers and periodic reports can identify missing events, whereas detecting silent streams requires timing assumptions. We also examine how membership changes and coordinator failures affect verdict soundness and recovery. We implement these mechanisms in a three-tier monitoring architecture using MQTT and NATS JetStream. Experiments with an LLM-planned robot swarm demonstrate the failure modes, show how the proposed mechanisms prevent unsupported compliance verdicts, and measure their runtime and communication costs.

summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.
title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

summary: The dataset is a canonical, machine-readable compilation of 756 relinquishment reports for production licences on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, submitted by licensees and made public by the Norwegian Offshore Directorate (Sodir). Each report is represented by one structured JSON record and one GeoJSON file of its mapped features. The records were produced by a large-language-model extraction of the report PDFs and cover licence history (licensees, work commitments, milestones and reasons for relinquishment), the prospects and leads evaluated in each licence (play, trap, reservoir, risk factors and geological chance of success, volume distributions per evaluation stage, and drilling results), and the seismic data and studies used. A reproducible pipeline harmonised these records into a single canonical schema without altering any source value: all 2,016,399 source values were retained verbatim at their original paths, which was verified for every record by rebuilding the source file from the canonical record and comparing the two value by value, including data types, number formats and array order. Computed values are kept strictly separate from source content: 203,570 normalised values are stored in dedicated  _derived  objects next to the value they describe, and each records the source fields it was derived from, the rule applied and a status (exact 198,437; approximate 1,346; suggested 500; requiring review 2,766; not normalisable, unclassified or ambiguous 521). Normalisation comprises: conversion to common units: oil and oil-equivalent volumes in 10⁶ Sm³, gas in 10⁹ Sm³, depths in metres and ratios as fractions, with barrel and boe conversions labelled approximate (1 Sm³ o.e. = 6.29 boe); evidence-based orientation of probabilistic volumes to the convention that P10 is the high estimate, applied to 4 distributions, while 15 internally inconsistent distributions were flagged rather than reordered; parsing of dates with explicit precision; standardisation of licence identifiers, well names, lithostratigraphic and chronostratigraphic names, trap types, AVO classes and study categories. Ambiguous cases are never resolved by assumption, because the mapping tables are versioned and only entries approved by a person are applied; in the current version, for example, 1,319 company-name variants and 420 meeting types remain listed for review. The spatial component comprises 7,162 features (prospect and lead outlines, licence boundaries, well locations and seismic survey outlines) in EPSG:4326 with geometry unchanged from the source; it is provided both as a combined layer and as one file per report, and its attributes are reduced to identity and link information so that the JSON records are the single source of truth for all descriptive attributes. Features are linked to their report entities through explicit identifiers (5,644 prospect links) or through name-based matching flagged for review (29 links, including 6 segment-to-parent relations), and the attributes previously duplicated in the GeoJSON files were compared against the records in 250,664 value-level checks whose discrepancies, such as systematic unit-scale differences in 48 reports, are published as quality-control reports rather than corrected. Provenance is kept at every level: each record and feature carries its source file name, SHA-256 fingerprint, pipeline, schema and mapping-table versions; the source files are archived byte for byte; and the extraction's own uncertainty markers are preserved, with 48,200 values marked as stated in the report, 3,057 as inferred by the extractor and 467 as read from figures, extractor confidence levels for 863 prospects, and 2,757 of 7,162 features marked for review. Because the canonical dataset is faithful to the extracted records but has not been verified against the original PDFs, it should be used together with its validation, unresolved-field and consistency reports, and quantitative values should

summary: Unit-level audit of dataset reuse across 30 osteoporosis drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) studies. The record contains the frozen analysis tables, the adjudication ledger and the code that produced the figures, tables and numbers of the accompanying manuscript. What was measured - 128-study frozen corpus (musculoskeletal drug-target MR); 55 studies concerned osteoporosis or bone mineral density; 30 entered at least one candidate comparison (a target nominated in two or more studies). - 133 dataset units (one study x one dataset): 103 study-level rows plus 30 units expanded from two composite rows; 110 usable (84 as extracted, 26 after correction), 23 rejected because the resource name was absent from the supporting sentence. - 22 dataset families. Exposure concentrated in eQTLGen (9 studies), the deCODE plasma proteome (9) and the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (6); FinnGen supplied the outcome in 13 studies. - 34 study pairs share an exposure family and an outcome family: 11 identical dataset, 8 same endpoint with release unstated, 6 same endpoint at different releases, 7 not adjudicable, 2 demonstrably different. 25 of 34 (73.5%) analysed the same outcome endpoint; 92.6% among the 27 pairs where both studies named the endpoint; 94.1% only if every non-adjudicable pair shared it. - Endpoint identity was recoverable for 12 of the 13 FinnGen-outcome studies. Files - data/S1_unit_table.csv - the 133 units with the supporting sentence, verdict and naming correction flag (Table S1). - data/S2_pair_grades.csv - the 34 pairs with their five-level grade (Table S2). - data/S3_family_matrix.csv - the 22 families with exposure/outcome study counts (Table S3). - data/S4_naming_corrections.csv - the 19 naming corrections applied before grading (Table S4). - data/source_evidence.csv - evidence sentences with the locator used for each recorded dataset. - data/finnengen_endpoint_counts.csv, data/release_ladder.csv - release-specific case and control counts used to recover endpoint identity. - data/dataset_audit_full.csv, data/pair_matrix.csv - the full audit table and the pair matrix before grading. - data/corpus_128_studies.csv, data/target_nominations.csv - the frozen corpus and the target nominations from which the 30 comparative studies were selected. - data/analysis_summary.json - retrieval counts (4,446 records, 2,759 after de-duplication, 262 at screening). - data/references.csv - the reference table with PubMed identifiers. - code/ - the scripts that build the registries, the pair grades, the figures, the manuscript and the two self-checks (number registry; citation numbering). - docs/ - project.json (design type, frozen state, positive control), numbers.json (every number in the manuscript with its source), claim-ledger.tsv, figures.tsv. Provenance The corpus was assembled on 16 November 2026 by seven search batches over Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Crossref (Semantic Scholar could not be queried because of rate limiting) and frozen before any dataset-level extraction. 4,446 records were reduced to 2,759 after de-duplication and to 262 at title-and-abstract screening; 128 publications formed the main set. How to re-run Python 3.11; set F11_ROOT to the directory containing data/, code/ and docs/, then follow code/README_run_order.md. The two gates are lint of the manuscript (external tool) and code/145_refs45_align_numbered.py (citation numbering). Absolute paths and the local host name were replaced with environment variables in this deposit; no analysis input was altered. Licence Data and derived tables: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Quoted sentences in source_evidence.csv and S1_unit_table.csv come from the cited publications and remain under the copyright of their publishers; they are included only as the evidence locator for each extracted datum. Status Manuscript in preparation; not yet submitted. No DOI for the article exists at the time of deposit.
title: Dataset reuse in osteoporosis drug-target Mendelian randomization: unit-level audit tables, adjudication ledger and analysis code

summary: Unit-level audit of dataset reuse across 30 osteoporosis drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) studies. The record contains the frozen analysis tables, the adjudication ledger and the code that produced the figures, tables and numbers of the accompanying manuscript. What was measured - 128-study frozen corpus (musculoskeletal drug-target MR); 55 studies concerned osteoporosis or bone mineral density; 30 entered at least one candidate comparison (a target nominated in two or more studies). - 133 dataset units (one study x one dataset): 103 study-level rows plus 30 units expanded from two composite rows; 110 usable (84 as extracted, 26 after correction), 23 rejected because the resource name was absent from the supporting sentence. - 22 dataset families. Exposure concentrated in eQTLGen (9 studies), the deCODE plasma proteome (9) and the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (6); FinnGen supplied the outcome in 13 studies. - 34 study pairs share an exposure family and an outcome family: 11 identical dataset, 8 same endpoint with release unstated, 6 same endpoint at different releases, 7 not adjudicable, 2 demonstrably different. 25 of 34 (73.5%) analysed the same outcome endpoint; 92.6% among the 27 pairs where both studies named the endpoint; 94.1% only if every non-adjudicable pair shared it. - Endpoint identity was recoverable for 12 of the 13 FinnGen-outcome studies. Files - data/S1_unit_table.csv - the 133 units with the supporting sentence, verdict and naming correction flag (Table S1). - data/S2_pair_grades.csv - the 34 pairs with their five-level grade (Table S2). - data/S3_family_matrix.csv - the 22 families with exposure/outcome study counts (Table S3). - data/S4_naming_corrections.csv - the 19 naming corrections applied before grading (Table S4). - data/source_evidence.csv - evidence sentences with the locator used for each recorded dataset. - data/finnengen_endpoint_counts.csv, data/release_ladder.csv - release-specific case and control counts used to recover endpoint identity. - data/dataset_audit_full.csv, data/pair_matrix.csv - the full audit table and the pair matrix before grading. - data/corpus_128_studies.csv, data/target_nominations.csv - the frozen corpus and the target nominations from which the 30 comparative studies were selected. - data/analysis_summary.json - retrieval counts (4,446 records, 2,759 after de-duplication, 262 at screening). - data/references.csv - the reference table with PubMed identifiers. - code/ - the scripts that build the registries, the pair grades, the figures, the manuscript and the two self-checks (number registry; citation numbering). - docs/ - project.json (design type, frozen state, positive control), numbers.json (every number in the manuscript with its source), claim-ledger.tsv, figures.tsv. Provenance The corpus was assembled on 16 November 2026 by seven search batches over Europe PMC, OpenAlex and Crossref (Semantic Scholar could not be queried because of rate limiting) and frozen before any dataset-level extraction. 4,446 records were reduced to 2,759 after de-duplication and to 262 at title-and-abstract screening; 128 publications formed the main set. How to re-run Python 3.11; set F11_ROOT to the directory containing data/, code/ and docs/, then follow code/README_run_order.md. The two gates are lint of the manuscript (external tool) and code/145_refs45_align_numbered.py (citation numbering). Absolute paths and the local host name were replaced with environment variables in this deposit; no analysis input was altered. Licence Data and derived tables: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT. Quoted sentences in source_evidence.csv and S1_unit_table.csv come from the cited publications and remain under the copyright of their publishers; they are included only as the evidence locator for each extracted datum. Status Manuscript in preparation; not yet submitted. No DOI for the article exists at the time of deposit.

summary: Identifying fractal lattices of fractional (Hausdorff) dimension as geometric descendants of parent crystals, we showcase the successful realization of canonical topological insulators in one-, two-, and three-dimensional crystals on their self-similar descents using three complementary approaches, starting from lattice-regularized models in integer dimensions. (a) In the first approach, we construct the fractal Hamiltonian by removing all parent-lattice sites that do not belong to such a network (method of site elimination). (b) In the second one, we integrate or project out the same set of sites to obtain an effective Hamiltonian for the fractal lattice (method of projection or renormalization). (c) In the third approach, we retain the parent-crystal lattice intact but spatially pattern the on-site mass parameter, which controls the topology of the parent insulating system, such that it assumes two topologically distinct values on the fractal network and its complement (patterned fractal lattices). By numerically diagonalizing the resulting Hamiltonians and computing appropriate topological invariants or local markers, corroborating the bulk-boundary correspondence through gapless modes at outer or inner boundaries, we establish Su-Schrieffer-Heeger topology on the Cantor set using all three approaches, Haldane topology on the hexaflake [using (a) and (b)] and Qi-Wu-Zhang topology on the Sierpiński carpet [using (c)], and strong $Z_2$ topological insulating phases on the tiled Menger sponge from methods (a), (b), and (c). These findings complement and substantially extend the previously reported realization of Qi-Wu-Zhang topology on the Sierpiński carpet using methods (a) and (b) [Phys. Rev. B 110, L241302 (2024)].
title: Topological insulators on site-eliminated, projected, and patterned fractal lattices

summary: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.

summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report

summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.

summary: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.

summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.

summary: Representation-space generative models, such as Representation Autoencoders (RAEs), leverage pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) primarily to accelerate training and improve sample fidelity. Yet VFMs are more than reconstruction tokenizers, as they feature rich representation spaces that are highly organized and linearly readable. We observe that this removes a key obstacle of post-hoc guidance: by linearity of expectation, a clean probe applied to an ideal denoiser's prediction yields the exact posterior mean of the probe scores at any noise level. This regime, which we call Semantic Mean-Space, turns semantic guidance into a Bayesian linear inverse problem, bypassing the need for training-time conditioning. With this foundation, we propose LiSM, a unified framework for Linear Guidance in Semantic Mean-Space. To validate the framework, we developed and adapted different solvers, and characterized them based on how they estimate probe-space uncertainty and propagate the correction through the representation. summary: We study best arm identification (BAI) with post-action context in the fixed-confidence setting. After choosing an action, the learner observes a post-action context together with a reward whose distribution depends only on this context. Incorporating such intermediate information can substantially reduce the sample complexity of identifying the best arm. While Shahverdikondori et al. (2026a) analyzed the case where the distribution of contexts given actions is known, we address the more challenging and practically relevant case where this distribution is unknown. We derive an instance-dependent sample complexity lower bound and propose a Track-and-Stop algorithm that matches it asymptotically with access to an optimization oracle. Our stopping rule uses a new concentration inequality that jointly controls uncertainty in the context distributions and reward means, removing the factor of two incurred by separate concentration bounds. Implementing the algorithm generally requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. We propose a convex relaxation with instance-dependent approximation guarantees, including asymptotic tightness on hard Gaussian instances. Experiments demonstrate that exploiting post-action context reduces the sample complexity relative to baselines that ignore it, even when the context distributions are unknown.
title: Best Arm Identification with Unknown Post-Action Context Distribution

summary: Analysis code and pre-specified analysis plan for the study "Beyond Pooled Accuracy: Hospital-Level Validation of Smartphone Image-Based Anaemia Screening in Pregnant Women". The package contains Python scripts for data integrity checks, colour feature extraction, frozen image-encoder features (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DINOv2, BiomedCLIP), the pre-specified models, nested model selection over 73 configurations, the site-identification test, a protocol-matched comparison with a published study, and a simulation study of site-related inflation of pooled AUC. The analysis plan (version 2, with dated amendments) is included. No participant data or images are included. Participants did not consent to public sharing of their data, including de-identified data. The simulation script runs without participant data.                                     This record contains the analysis plan and code for the study "Does smartphone AI see anaemia or the hospital? Validation in pregnant women in Uzbekistan" (Islomova, Nishanova and Qodirov; manuscript under review). The study tested whether smartphone photographs of the eyelid, tongue, lips, nail bed and palm can screen pregnant women for anaemia, and whether reported accuracy reflects anaemia or the hospital where the photographs were taken. It compared accuracy pooled across two hospitals in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, with accuracy inside each hospital, used a simulation in which images carry no anaemia information, and repeated the main checks in a public conjunctival dataset. Version 1 contains: - the pre-specified analysis plan, written before modelling, with dated amendments; - all analysis code for the two-hospital study, including the simulation code, which runs without participant data. Version 2 adds the replication in the public Eyes-defy-anemia dataset: - Eyes_Defy_tahlil_rejasi.md: the replication analysis plan, written before any result was computed; - Eyes_Defy_tahlil_kodi.py: the replication code; - Eyes_Defy_natijalar.txt: the full output of the replication analysis; - a table of derived colour features (55 values per record: RGB, CIELAB and HSV statistics, chromaticity and channel ratios), computed from the conjunctival masks after erosion by 3 pixels; - README.md: file descriptions, run order and software requirements. Participant data are not included. Women in the two-hospital study did not consent to public sharing of their data, including de-identified data. Requests for access for verification may be sent to the corresponding author (m.islomova@tuit.uz) and require approval by the ethics committee. Source dataset: Eyes-defy-anemia, IEEE DataPort, https://doi.org/10.21227/t5s2-4j73, released under CC BY 4.0. The derived colour

summary: This paper examines the transmission of speculative activity across the Shanghai (SC), Brent, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil futures markets. Using daily trading volume and open interest data for nearby contracts from November 2018 to November 2025, we measure speculative intensity through a new ratio that extends existing volume- and open-interest-based proxies for speculative activity. Because SC settles approximately 12 hours before the Western benchmarks (Brent and WTI), standard connectedness frameworks that ignore non-synchronous trading may overstate its role as a transmitter. We address this problem with a block-recursive structural VAR in which the timing of settlements identifies the contemporaneous effect of SC on Brent and WTI, while common structural breaks enter as exogenous regressors. Our results indicate that SC is the most speculative market, while Brent is the least speculative. However, forecast error variance decompositions show that Brent is the main net transmitter of speculative volume shocks, WTI plays a broadly balanced role, and SC remains a net receiver whose speculative dynamics are largely self-contained. The results suggest that SC’s integration into global speculative activity is still limited and underscore the growing role of Brent futures in global crude oil markets.
title: Who moves the barrel? Speculative spillovers across global crude oil futures markets

summary: Code and Data Archive for "Extending Medium-Range Global Flood Forecasts: The Google Global Flood Forecasting Model Version 2" (v2.0.0) Overview This unified archive contains the frozen model training codebase ( OpenHydroNet ), the complete paper analysis and figure-generation codebase, and all evaluation data and pre-computed metric caches accompanying the Geoscientific Model Development (GMD) manuscript, "Extending Medium-Range Global Flood Forecasts: The Google Global Flood Forecasting Model Version 2" . The manuscript evaluates operational version 2 (v2) of the Google Global Flood Forecasting system against version 1 (v1) and established third-party benchmarks across 1,222 global test basins. Key updates in v2 include replacing the Encoder-Decoder LSTM (ED-LSTM) with a continuous Mean Embedding LSTM (ME-LSTM) architecture, expanding global training data with the Caravan community dataset, and incorporating GraphCast AI-based weather forecasts. Relative to the v1 nowcast, v2 extends the reliable predictive horizon by 6 days in gauged basins and 1 day in ungauged basins (measured by Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency) and improves operational flood-event detection and peak-flow accuracy. summary: Reproducible v3 benchmark archive accompanying the research manuscript “CRISPR-TRIAGE: Multi-Seed Benchmarking and Parameter-Efficient Bi-Modal Neural Prioritisation of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Target Cleavage Under Constrained Screening Budgets” (Rashid Kadayil, Pondicherry University). What is new in v3.0.0 (superseding v1.0.0): Expanded from single-seed two-cohort evaluation to a five-seed ( s ∈ {42, 123, 456, 789, 1011}), three-cohort, exact-sequence guide-disjoint benchmark across Listgarten 2018 GUIDE-seq, deduplicated K562, and deduplicated HEK293T ( N = 31 cleavage-positive guides, 249,768 candidate records, 237 detected positives within a 417,833-record, 41-guide universe; 16 model and ablation configurations). Principal pooled results: controlled reference CRISPR-TRIAGE (Full) (35,409 parameters) achieves 0.6899 Macro Recall@20 (Micro 0.5949), 0.8569 Recall@50, 0.9225 Recall@100, and 0.4484 Macro AP; 11-fold smaller Tabular-Only MLP (RankLoss) (3,217 parameters) achieves 0.6791 Recall@20 ( p = 0.7843); exploratory post-hoc pure-mismatch training ( No-Bulge Train , excluding 252,879 gap-containing CIRCLE-seq alignments) reaches 0.7243 Recall@20 ( p = 0.0022, p Holm = 0.0111). Archive contents ( crispr_triage_reproducible_release.zip , 38.71 MB, 233 files): Complete Python/PyTorch source code and post-hoc sensitivity audit scripts ( src/ , scripts/ ). 65 saved five-seed model checkpoints across 13 neural and gradient-boosted configurations plus 10 seed-fitted StandardScaler artifacts . Derived K562 and HEK293T cellular cohorts, Supplementary Tables S1–S7 (Online Resources 1–7), post-hoc audit CSVs, and complete upstream provenance/SHA-256 manifests ( DATA_MANIFEST.csv , RUN_MANIFEST.json verifying 232 registered artifacts, ENVIRONMENT_LOCK.txt ). Automated clean-room verification suite ( pytest tests/ -v : 12/12 tests passing offline with zero external downloads). summary: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
